abstract: We describe a new learning procedure for networks that contain groups of non(cid:173) linear units arranged in a closed loop. The aim of the learning is to discover codes that allow the activity vectors in a "visible" group to be represented by activity vectors in a "hidden" group. One way to test whether a code is an accurate representation is to try to reconstruct the visible vector from the hidden vector. The difference between the original and the reconstructed visible vectors is called the reconstruction error, and the learning procedure aims to minimize this error. The learning procedure has two passes. On the fust pass, the original visible vector is passed around the loop, and on the second pass an average of the original vector and the reconstructed vector is passed around the loop. The learning procedure changes each weight by an amount proportional to the product of the "presynaptic" activity and the difference in the post-synaptic activity on the two passes. This procedure is much simpler to implement than methods like back-propagation. Simulations in simple networks show that it usually converges rapidly on a good set of codes, and analysis shows that in certain restricted cases it performs gradient descent in the squared reconstruction error.

paragraphs: Recirculation learns a hidden representation by asking whether it can reproduce the original visible activity. Groups of nonlinear units form a closed loop, allowing activity to travel from the visible group through a hidden group and back. Learning aims to reduce the discrepancy between the starting visible vector and its reconstruction.

The procedure uses two passes around the loop. The first carries the original visible vector. The second carries a mixture of that original vector and the reconstruction. Each connection changes according to the activity on its sending side multiplied by the difference between its receiving unit’s activities on the two passes.

This rule turns changes in local activity into a learning signal, and the authors describe it as substantially simpler to implement than back-propagation. Simulations in simple networks usually find good codes quickly. The mathematical analysis establishes gradient descent on squared reconstruction error only in certain restricted cases. Together, these results support recirculation as a practical representation-learning procedure while identifying the narrower setting in which its optimization behavior is formally established.
summary.tldr: Recirculation learns hidden codes from activity differences across two passes through a loop, with gradient-descent guarantees in restricted cases.

title: Learning Representations by Recirculation

paragraphs: This paper studies how the learning rate should change during stochastic gradient descent. The learning rate determines the size of each parameter update, so its schedule influences both the progress of optimization and the solution eventually reached. The authors treat stochastic gradient descent as a general framework encompassing LMS, online backpropagation, and k-means clustering.

The supplied formulation seeks parameters that minimize an objective averaged over examples. Each stochastic update uses the most recent independently chosen random example, whereas the deterministic comparison uses the gradient of the average objective. The scheduling question therefore arises in an optimization process driven by individual sampled examples.

The authors introduce schedules described as search-then-converge and compare them with a fixed learning rate and a running-average schedule that decreases inversely with time. They report improvements in both convergence speed and solution quality. The contribution is the schedule itself: organizing the progression from search toward convergence changes how effectively the same broad update framework solves its optimization problem.
summary.tldr: Search-then-converge learning-rate schedules improve reported convergence speed and solution quality over constant and inverse-time schedules.

title: Note on Learning Rate Schedules for Stochastic Optimization

abstract: We have developed a VLSI silicon neuron and a corresponding mathe(cid:173) matical model that is a two state-variable system. We describe the cir(cid:173) cuit implementation and compare the behaviors observed in the silicon neuron and the mathematical model. We also perform bifurcation analy(cid:173) sis of the mathematical model by varying the externally applied current and show that the behaviors exhibited by the silicon neuron under corre(cid:173) sponding conditions are in good agreement to those predicted by the bifurcation analysis.
originalAbstract: We have developed a VLSI silicon neuron and a corresponding mathe(cid:173) matical model that is a two state-variable system. We describe the cir(cid:173) cuit implementation and compare the behaviors observed in the silicon neuron and the mathematical model. We also perform bifurcation analy(cid:173) sis of the mathematical model by varying the externally applied current and show that the behaviors exhibited by the silicon neuron under corre(cid:173) sponding conditions are in good agreement to those predicted by the bifurcation analysis.

paragraphs: The paper develops a silicon neuron implemented as a VLSI circuit and a corresponding mathematical description. The mathematical model uses two state variables to describe the system's changing condition. Having both a physical circuit and a compact model lets the authors compare measured behavior with behavior predicted through mathematical analysis.

The analysis focuses on what happens as the externally applied current changes. Using bifurcation analysis, the authors examine how changes in this control parameter alter the model's qualitative behavior. This addresses how the system's dynamics depend on its input current, extending the comparison beyond observing the circuit under one fixed operating condition.

The silicon neuron is examined under conditions corresponding to those used in the analysis. Its observed behavior agrees well with the mathematical predictions. This agreement supports the model as a description of the circuit under those conditions and shows the value of studying the hardware and its equations together: mathematical changes in behavior can be checked against a physical implementation.
summary.tldr: A two-state mathematical model predicts changes in a silicon neuron's behavior as applied current varies.

title: Bifurcation Analysis of a Silicon Neuron

abstract: We describe a joint probabilistic model for modeling the contents and inter-connectivity of document collections such as sets of web pages or research paper archives. The model is based on a probabilistic factor decomposition and allows identifying principal topics of the collection as well as authoritative documents within those topics. Furthermore, the relationships between topics is mapped out in order to build a predictive model of link content. Among the many applications of this approach are information retrieval and search, topic identification, query disambigua(cid:173) tion, focused web crawling, web authoring, and bibliometric analysis.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a joint probabilistic model for a collection's document contents and the connections between its documents. Web pages and research-paper archives are the stated examples. The modeling task brings together what documents discuss and how they link to one another within a single representation of the collection.

The approach uses a probabilistic factor decomposition to identify principal topics and authoritative documents within those topics. This associates document authority with topical structure, allowing the model to describe both subject matter and the documents that hold authority in each subject area. It also maps relationships between topics to construct a predictive model of link content.

The authors identify applications including retrieval, search, topic identification, query disambiguation, focused crawling, web authoring, and bibliometric analysis. These applications share a need to interpret documents in the context of their relationships. The contribution is a unified modeling framework that exposes topics, topic-specific authority, and connections among topics as related aspects of a linked document collection.
summary.tldr: A joint model of document content and links identifies topics, topic-specific authorities, and relationships among topics.

title: The Missing Link - A Probabilistic Model of Document Content and Hypertext Connectivity

abstract: We discuss the problem of ranking instances. In our framework each instance is associated with a rank or a rating, which is an integer from 1 to k. Our goal is to find a rank-prediction rule that assigns each instance a rank which is as close as possible to the instance's true rank. We describe a simple and efficient online al(cid:173) gorithm, analyze its performance in the mistake bound model, and prove its correctness. We describe two sets of experiments, with synthetic data and with the EachMovie dataset for collaborative filtering. In the experiments we performed, our algorithm outper(cid:173) forms online algorithms for regression and classification applied to ranking.

Our goal is to find a rank-prediction rule that assigns each instance a rank which is as close as possible to the instance's true rank. We describe a simple and efficient online al(cid:173) gorithm, analyze its performance in the mistake bound model, and prove its correctness. We describe two sets of experiments, with synthetic data and with the EachMovie dataset for collaborative filtering. paragraphs: The paper studies prediction when each instance has an ordered integer rating from one to k. The objective is to assign a rating as close as possible to the true one. This ordering matters because predicting a nearby rating is different from making a prediction far along the scale, giving the task a specific notion of prediction quality.

The authors propose a simple, efficient online algorithm for this problem. They analyze its performance using the mistake-bound model and prove its correctness. The theoretical component therefore accompanies the proposed learning procedure, providing a formal treatment of its behavior rather than relying entirely on empirical evaluation.

Experiments use both synthetic data and the EachMovie dataset for collaborative filtering. In those experiments, the ranking algorithm performs better than online regression and classification algorithms applied to the same ranking problem. The result supports treating ordered ratings as a learning task in their own right. Its empirical scope is the reported comparisons, showing that a method designed for rating prediction can outperform these alternative formulations.
summary.tldr: A simple online ranking algorithm has formal guarantees and outperforms tested regression and classification approaches on rating prediction.

title: Pranking with Ranking

abstract: We consider the learning problem of finding a dependency between a general class of objects and another, possibly different, general class of objects. The objects can be for example: vectors, images, strings, trees or graphs. Such a task is made possible by employing similarity measures in both input and output spaces using ker(cid:173) nel functions, thus embedding the objects into vector spaces. We experimentally validate our approach on several tasks: mapping strings to strings, pattern recognition, and reconstruction from par(cid:173) tial images.
originalAbstract: We consider the learning problem of finding a dependency between a general class of objects and another, possibly different, general class of objects. The objects can be for example: vectors, images, strings, trees or graphs. Such a task is made possible by employing similarity measures in both input and output spaces using ker(cid:173) nel functions, thus embedding the objects into vector spaces. We experimentally validate our approach on several tasks: mapping strings to strings, pattern recognition, and reconstruction from par(cid:173) tial images.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a relationship between one class of objects and another, potentially different class. The objects may be vectors, images, strings, trees, or graphs. This formulation makes the output itself part of the representation problem, rather than assuming that every prediction must already have a simple numerical form.

The approach uses kernel functions to measure similarities in both the input and output spaces. These kernels embed the respective objects into vector spaces, providing a mathematical setting in which their dependency can be learned. The central move is therefore to represent relationships among possible outputs as well as relationships among inputs.

The authors experimentally validate the approach on string-to-string mapping, pattern recognition, and reconstruction from partial images. These tasks illustrate its use across different kinds of input-output relationships. The contribution is a common kernel-based formulation for learning between object domains: suitable similarity measures provide a route from structured objects to vector-space learning, even when the two sides of the mapping contain different kinds of objects.
summary.tldr: Kernel dependency estimation uses similarities on both inputs and outputs to learn mappings between general objects such as strings and images.

title: Kernel Dependency Estimation

abstract: We visit the following fundamental problem: For a `generic model of consumer choice (namely, distributions over preference lists) and a limited amount of data on how consumers actually make decisions (such as marginal preference information), how may one predict revenues from offering a particular assortment of choices? This problem is central to areas within operations research, marketing and econometrics. We present a framework to answer such questions and design a number of tractable algorithms (from a data and computational standpoint) for the same.
originalAbstract: We visit the following fundamental problem: For a `generic model of consumer choice (namely, distributions over preference lists) and a limited amount of data on how consumers actually make decisions (such as marginal preference information), how may one predict revenues from offering a particular assortment of choices? This problem is central to areas within operations research, marketing and econometrics. We present a framework to answer such questions and design a number of tractable algorithms (from a data and computational standpoint) for the same.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to predict revenue from a particular assortment when information about consumer preferences is limited. The available evidence might describe individual preference relationships without revealing a complete picture of how everyone chooses. The challenge is to connect those partial observations to the financial consequences of offering a specific collection of alternatives.

The authors represent consumer choice through a distribution over preference lists. A preference list describes an ordering of alternatives, while the distribution allows different consumers to have different orderings. This gives the framework a broad way to describe variation in choice. Its central task is to use limited decision data within that representation to answer questions about assortment revenue.

The contribution is a framework together with several algorithms designed to be tractable in both their data requirements and computation. This matters because a flexible description of preferences is useful for decision-making only if it can support calculations from the information actually available. The paper positions this problem across operations research, marketing, and econometrics.
summary.tldr: The paper develops tractable algorithms for predicting assortment revenue from limited choice data using distributions over consumer preference lists.

title: A Data-Driven Approach to Modeling Choice

abstract: We develop unified information-theoretic machinery for deriving lower bounds for passive and active learning schemes. Our bounds involve the so-called Alexander's capacity function. The supremum of this function has been recently rediscovered by Hanneke in the context of active learning under the name of "disagreement coefficient." For passive learning, our lower bounds match the upper bounds of Gine and Koltchinskii up to constants and generalize analogous results of Massart and Nedelec. For active learning, we provide first known lower bounds based on the capacity function rather than the disagreement coefficient.
originalAbstract: We develop unified information-theoretic machinery for deriving lower bounds for passive and active learning schemes. Our bounds involve the so-called Alexander's capacity function. The supremum of this function has been recently rediscovered by Hanneke in the context of active learning under the name of "disagreement coefficient." For passive learning, our lower bounds match the upper bounds of Gine and Koltchinskii up to constants and generalize analogous results of Massart and Nedelec. For active learning, we provide first known lower bounds based on the capacity function rather than the disagreement coefficient.

paragraphs: Learning theory needs limits on what any method can achieve, as well as guarantees for particular algorithms. This paper develops a shared information-theoretic framework for proving such lower bounds in passive and active learning. It connects both settings through Alexander's capacity function, making the same mathematical quantity central to their analysis.

The capacity function is related to the disagreement coefficient used in active learning: the coefficient is its supremum. Working with the function itself retains information beyond that single summary value. The paper's active-learning contribution is to derive lower bounds based directly on the capacity function.

For passive learning, the resulting lower bounds match existing upper bounds up to constant factors and generalize earlier lower-bound results. This matching gives evidence that those upper bounds capture the achievable scale accurately. For active learning, the authors present the first known capacity-function-based lower bounds, extending the tools available for characterizing fundamental learning difficulty.
summary.tldr: A unified information-theoretic framework derives passive and active learning lower bounds using Alexander's capacity function.

title: Lower Bounds for Passive and Active Learning

abstract: Some of the most compelling applications of online convex optimization, including online prediction and classification, are unconstrained: the natural feasible set is R^n. Existing algorithms fail to achieve sub-linear regret in this setting unless constraints on the comparator point x* are known in advance. We present an algorithm that, without such prior knowledge, offers near-optimal regret bounds with respect to any choice of x*. In particular, regret with respect to x* = 0 is constant . We then prove lower bounds showing that our algorithm's guarantees are optimal in this setting up to constant factors.
originalAbstract: Some of the most compelling applications of online convex optimization, including online prediction and classification, are unconstrained: the natural feasible set is R^n. Existing algorithms fail to achieve sub-linear regret in this setting unless constraints on the comparator point x* are known in advance. We present an algorithm that, without such prior knowledge, offers near-optimal regret bounds with respect to any choice of x*. In particular, regret with respect to x* = 0 is constant . We then prove lower bounds showing that our algorithm's guarantees are optimal in this setting up to constant factors.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization evaluates a sequence of decisions against a fixed comparator chosen in hindsight. The paper focuses on problems where decisions naturally range over all of R^n, including online prediction and classification. In this unconstrained setting, existing algorithms required advance knowledge of restrictions on the comparator to obtain sublinear regret.

The authors introduce an algorithm that does not need that prior comparator information. It provides near-optimal regret bounds relative to any chosen comparator point. A particularly strong special case is the origin: regret relative to the zero vector remains constant. The guarantee therefore accommodates comparisons to different points without requiring a comparator constraint before learning begins.

The paper also proves lower bounds showing that these guarantees are optimal up to constant factors in the studied setting. This establishes both an achievable performance guarantee and a limit on how much it can be improved. The contribution removes the need to specify comparator restrictions in advance while retaining theoretically sharp control over cumulative performance.
summary.tldr: An unconstrained online optimization algorithm achieves near-optimal comparator-dependent regret without knowing comparator restrictions in advance.

title: No-Regret Algorithms for Unconstrained Online Convex Optimization

abstract: We present a probabilistic formulation of max-margin matrix factorization and build accordingly a nonparametric Bayesian model which automatically resolves the unknown number of latent factors. Our work demonstrates a successful example that integrates Bayesian nonparametrics and max-margin learning, which are conventionally two separate paradigms and enjoy complementary advantages. We develop an efcient variational algorithm for posterior inference, and our extensive empirical studies on large-scale MovieLens and EachMovie data sets appear to justify the aforementioned dual advantages.
originalAbstract: We present a probabilistic formulation of max-margin matrix factorization and build accordingly a nonparametric Bayesian model which automatically resolves the unknown number of latent factors. Our work demonstrates a successful example that integrates Bayesian nonparametrics and max-margin learning, which are conventionally two separate paradigms and enjoy complementary advantages. We develop an efcient variational algorithm for posterior inference, and our extensive empirical studies on large-scale MovieLens and EachMovie data sets appear to justify the aforementioned dual advantages.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization represents collaborative prediction data using latent factors, but the appropriate number of factors may be unknown. This paper presents a probabilistic formulation of max-margin matrix factorization and uses it to build a Bayesian nonparametric model. The resulting model automatically resolves how many latent factors are needed within its modeling framework.

The contribution brings together two approaches usually treated separately: max-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics. The former supplies the margin-based learning formulation, while the latter provides flexibility over the unknown latent dimension. Their integration lets the model address prediction and representation size as connected parts of the same learning problem.

The authors develop an efficient variational algorithm for posterior inference, making the combined formulation computationally usable. Extensive experiments use the large-scale MovieLens and EachMovie datasets. The authors describe those findings as appearing to support the complementary advantages of the two approaches. The evidence therefore supports the proposed integration while retaining a qualified claim about the benefits demonstrated by the empirical studies.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric formulation combines max-margin matrix factorization with automatic selection of the latent factor count.

title: Nonparametric Max-Margin Matrix Factorization for Collaborative Prediction

abstract: We propose a parameter server system for distributed ML, which follows a Stale Synchronous Parallel (SSP) model of computation that maximizes the time computational workers spend doing useful work on ML algorithms, while still providing correctness guarantees. The parameter server provides an easy-to-use shared interface for read/write access to an ML model's values (parameters and variables), and the SSP model allows distributed workers to read older, stale versions of these values from a local cache, instead of waiting to get them from a central storage. This significantly increases the proportion of time workers spend computing, as opposed to waiting. Furthermore, the SSP model ensures ML algorithm correctness by limiting the maximum age of the stale values. We provide a proof of correctness under SSP, as well as empirical results demonstrating that the SSP model achieves faster algorithm convergence on several different ML problems, compared to fully-synchronous and asynchronous schemes.

The parameter server provides an easy-to-use shared interface for read/write access to an ML model's values (parameters and variables), and the SSP model allows distributed workers to read older, stale versions of these values from a local cache, instead of waiting to get them from a central storage. This significantly increases the proportion of time workers spend computing, as opposed to waiting. paragraphs: Distributed learning workers need access to shared model values, but waiting for fresh values can consume time that could otherwise be spent computing. This paper proposes a parameter server organized around Stale Synchronous Parallel computation, or SSP. The server provides a shared interface for reading and writing model parameters and variables.

SSP allows workers to read older values from local caches instead of repeatedly waiting for central storage. It controls this flexibility by placing a maximum age on the values a worker may use. That bound makes staleness an explicit part of the computation model and supplies the mechanism through which the authors establish correctness.

The paper provides a correctness proof under SSP and evaluates the system on several machine-learning problems. The reported experiments show faster algorithm convergence than fully synchronous and asynchronous alternatives, alongside more time spent computing instead of waiting. The findings illustrate how bounded delays can improve distributed learning: workers gain freedom to continue useful computation while the system retains a defined constraint on how outdated their information can become.
summary.tldr: A parameter server with bounded stale reads reduces worker waiting while supporting correctness and faster convergence in reported experiments.

title: More Effective Distributed ML via a Stale Synchronous Parallel Parameter Server

abstract: Attention has long been proposed by psychologists to be important for efficiently dealing with the massive amounts of sensory stimulus in the neocortex. Inspired by the attention models in visual neuroscience and the need for object-centered data for generative models, we propose a deep-learning based generative framework using attention. The attentional mechanism propagates signals from the region of interest in a scene to an aligned canonical representation for generative modeling. By ignoring scene background clutter, the generative model can concentrate its resources on the object of interest. A convolutional neural net is employed to provide good initializations during posterior inference which uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Upon learning images of faces, our model can robustly attend to the face region of novel test subjects. More importantly, our model can learn generative models of new faces from a novel dataset of large images where the face locations are not known.

paragraphs: Generative models of objects benefit from inputs that center and align the object of interest. Large scenes make that difficult because the object appears alongside background clutter. This paper introduces a deep-learning framework that uses visual attention to send information from a selected scene region into an aligned, canonical representation for generative modeling.

The attention mechanism lets the generative model focus its resources on the object rather than the surrounding scene. Posterior inference uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, with a convolutional neural network supplying good starting points. The framework therefore combines attention, a generative representation, and learned initialization for its inference procedure.

The reported results focus on faces. After learning face images, the model can robustly attend to face regions belonging to previously unseen test subjects. It can also learn generative models of new faces from a separate dataset of large images without known face locations. These findings support the use of attention to connect scene-level inputs with object-centered generative learning, including a setting where object positions are not supplied.
summary.tldr: An attention-based generative framework learns face models from large images even when face locations are unknown.

title: Learning Generative Models with Visual Attention

abstract: Hashing has emerged as a popular technique for fast nearest neighbor search in gigantic databases. In particular, learning based hashing has received considerable attention due to its appealing storage and search efficiency. However, the performance of most unsupervised learning based hashing methods deteriorates rapidly as the hash code length increases. We argue that the degraded performance is due to inferior optimization procedures used to achieve discrete binary codes. This paper presents a graph-based unsupervised hashing model to preserve the neighborhood structure of massive data in a discrete code space. We cast the graph hashing problem into a discrete optimization framework which directly learns the binary codes. A tractable alternating maximization algorithm is then proposed to explicitly deal with the discrete constraints, yielding high-quality codes to well capture the local neighborhoods. Extensive experiments performed on four large datasets with up to one million samples show that our discrete optimization based graph hashing method obtains superior search accuracy over state-of-the-art unsupervised hashing methods, especially for longer codes.

paragraphs: Hashing supports fast nearest-neighbor search by representing data with compact binary codes. This paper focuses on a surprising difficulty in unsupervised hashing: search performance can deteriorate as codes become longer. The authors argue that poor optimization of the discrete codes is responsible, so providing more bits alone does not ensure a more useful representation.

Their model uses a graph to express which data points are neighbors and aims to preserve those relationships in binary code space. It formulates learning directly as a discrete optimization problem. A tractable alternating maximization algorithm explicitly handles the binary constraints, keeping the actual form of the final codes central to optimization.

Experiments cover four large datasets containing up to one million samples. The method achieves better search accuracy than the leading unsupervised hashing methods used in the comparison, especially with longer codes. The results support the paper’s argument that the optimization procedure matters substantially: additional code length is more useful when learning preserves local neighborhoods while respecting the discrete representation.
summary.tldr: Directly optimizing binary graph-hashing codes improves reported nearest-neighbor search accuracy, especially for longer codes.

title: Discrete Graph Hashing

abstract: In this paper we propose a general framework for learning distributed representations of attributes: characteristics of text whose representations can be jointly learned with word embeddings. Attributes can correspond to a wide variety of concepts, such as document indicators (to learn sentence vectors), language indicators (to learn distributed language representations), meta-data and side information (such as the age, gender and industry of a blogger) or representations of authors. We describe a third-order model where word context and attribute vectors interact multiplicatively to predict the next word in a sequence. This leads to the notion of conditional word similarity: how meanings of words change when conditioned on different attributes. We perform several experimental tasks including sentiment classification, cross-lingual document classification, and blog authorship attribution. We also qualitatively evaluate conditional word neighbours and attribute-conditioned text generation.

Attributes can correspond to a wide variety of concepts, such as document indicators (to learn sentence vectors), language indicators (to learn distributed language representations), meta-data and side information (such as the age, gender and industry of a blogger) or representations of authors. We describe a third-order model where word context and attribute vectors interact multiplicatively to predict the next word in a sequence. This leads to the notion of conditional word similarity: how meanings of words change when conditioned on different attributes. We perform several experimental tasks including sentiment classification, cross-lingual document classification, and blog authorship attribution. paragraphs: This paper learns vector representations for attributes of text alongside representations of words. Attributes can identify a document, a language, an author, or metadata such as a blogger’s age or industry. Putting these different kinds of information into a shared learning framework allows the model to represent how text varies with its surrounding circumstances.

The proposed third-order model predicts the next word through multiplicative interactions between word context and attribute vectors. An attribute therefore participates directly in how context influences prediction. This produces conditional word similarity: which words have similar meanings can depend on the attribute being considered, rather than being summarized by one fixed relationship across all text.

The authors investigate the framework through sentiment classification, cross-language document classification, and identifying blog authors. They also inspect how word neighbors change with attributes and examine text generated under attribute conditions. These evaluations explore both predictive uses and the representations’ behavior; the abstract does not claim a particular performance improvement. The central contribution is a common mechanism for learning attributes and their interactions with language.
summary.tldr: A multiplicative language model jointly learns word and attribute vectors, allowing word similarity and generation to depend on textual context and metadata.

title: A Multiplicative Model for Learning Distributed Text-Based Attribute Representations

abstract: We propose a Generalized Dantzig Selector (GDS) for linear models, in which any norm encoding the parameter structure can be leveraged for estimation. We investigate both computational and statistical aspects of the GDS. Based on conjugate proximal operator, a flexible inexact ADMM framework is designed for solving GDS. Thereafter, non-asymptotic high-probability bounds are established on the estimation error, which rely on Gaussian widths of the unit norm ball and the error set. Further, we consider a non-trivial example of the GDS using k-support norm. We derive an efficient method to compute the proximal operator for k-support norm since existing methods are inapplicable in this setting. For statistical analysis, we provide upper bounds for the Gaussian widths needed in the GDS analysis, yielding the first statistical recovery guarantee for estimation with the k-support norm. The experimental results confirm our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes the Dantzig selector for estimating parameters in linear models. The proposed framework allows any norm that encodes parameter structure to guide estimation. This separates the general estimation approach from the particular structural preference expressed by the chosen norm.

The authors address computation and statistical accuracy together. They design a flexible inexact ADMM solver using a conjugate proximal operator. They also derive finite-sample, high-probability bounds on estimation error. These bounds depend on Gaussian widths of the norm's unit ball and the error set, connecting the statistical guarantee to the geometry associated with the selected norm.

The k-support norm provides a concrete application of the framework. Existing proximal methods do not apply in this setting, so the paper develops an efficient alternative. It then bounds the Gaussian widths needed for the general analysis, obtaining what the authors identify as the first statistical recovery guarantee for estimation with this norm. Experiments support the theoretical analysis, linking the general framework to a worked computational and statistical example.
summary.tldr: A generalized Dantzig selector supports arbitrary structural norms, with an efficient solver and recovery guarantees developed for the k-support norm.

title: Generalized Dantzig Selector: Application to the k-support norm

abstract: We study the problem of minimizing the average of a large number of smooth convex functions penalized with a strongly convex regularizer. We propose and analyze a novel primal-dual method (Quartz) which at every iteration samples and updates a random subset of the dual variables, chosen according to an arbitrary distribution. In contrast to typical analysis, we directly bound the decrease of the primal-dual error (in expectation), without the need to first analyze the dual error. Depending on the choice of the sampling, we obtain efficient serial and mini-batch variants of the method. In the serial case, our bounds match the best known bounds for SDCA (both with uniform and importance sampling). With standard mini-batching, our bounds predict initial data-independent speedup as well as additional data-driven speedup which depends on spectral and sparsity properties of the data.

paragraphs: Quartz is a primal-dual optimization method for minimizing an average of many smooth convex functions together with a strongly convex regularizer. At each iteration, it samples a subset of dual variables and updates them. The sampling distribution is arbitrary, allowing the framework to accommodate different ways of selecting work.

The analysis directly bounds the expected decrease in primal-dual error. This avoids first establishing a separate result for dual error before relating it to the combined error. Different sampling choices yield serial and mini-batch versions, so the same analytical framework covers both individual updates and groups of updates.

For serial sampling, the bounds match the best known bounds for stochastic dual coordinate ascent with uniform or importance sampling. For standard mini-batches, the bounds predict an initial speedup independent of the data and an additional benefit influenced by its spectral and sparsity properties. These are theoretical speedup predictions, connecting the value of batching to both the sampling design and the structure of the optimization data.
summary.tldr: Quartz supports arbitrary sampling in primal-dual optimization, with matching serial convergence bounds and mini-batch speedup predictions tied partly to data structure.

title: Quartz: Randomized Dual Coordinate Ascent with Arbitrary Sampling

abstract: We show that natural classes of regularized learning algorithms with a form of recency bias achieve faster convergence rates to approximate efficiency and to coarse correlated equilibria in multiplayer normal form games. When each player in a game uses an algorithm from our class, their individual regret decays at $O(T^{-3/4})$, while the sum of utilities converges to an approximate optimum at $O(T^{-1})$--an improvement upon the worst case $O(T^{-1/2})$ rates. We show a black-box reduction for any algorithm in the class to achieve $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ rates against an adversary, while maintaining the faster rates against algorithms in the class. Our results extend those of Rakhlin and Shridharan~\cite{Rakhlin2013} and Daskalakis et al.~\cite{Daskalakis2014}, who only analyzed two-player zero-sum games for specific algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how quickly learning players approach efficient outcomes and coarse correlated equilibria in multiplayer normal-form games. It identifies classes of regularized learning algorithms with a form of recency bias. Their key advantage appears when every player uses an algorithm from the analyzed class, so the interacting learners have compatible behavior.

Under that condition, individual regret decays at O(T^(-3/4)), while the sum of players’ utilities approaches an approximate optimum at O(T^(-1)). Both improve on the O(T^(-1/2)) worst-case rates used for comparison. The efficiency claim remains approximate: faster convergence does not turn the destination into an exact optimum.

The authors also give a black-box reduction that preserves the faster rates against algorithms in the class while achieving a rate of roughly O(T^(-1/2)), up to logarithmic factors, against an adversary. This connects favorable interaction with protection against less predictable opponents. The analysis extends beyond earlier results restricted to particular algorithms in two-player zero-sum games, covering a broader multiplayer setting.
summary.tldr: Certain regularized learners converge faster when all players use the analyzed class, while a reduction retains adversarial regret guarantees.

title: Fast Convergence of Regularized Learning in Games

abstract: Clustering large data is a fundamental problem with a vast number of applications. Due to the increasing size of data, practitioners interested in clustering have turned to distributed computation methods. In this work, we consider the widely used k-center clustering problem and its variant used to handle noisy data, k-center with outliers. In the noise-free setting we demonstrate how a previously-proposed distributed method is actually an O(1)-approximation algorithm, which accurately explains its strong empirical performance. Additionally, in the noisy setting, we develop a novel distributed algorithm that is also an O(1)-approximation. These algorithms are highly parallel and lend themselves to virtually any distributed computing framework. We compare both empirically against the best known noisy sequential clustering methods and show that both distributed algorithms are consistently close to their sequential versions. The algorithms are all one can hope for in distributed settings: they are fast, memory efficient and they match their sequential counterparts.

Its motivation is the growing scale of datasets, which makes distributing computation attractive. The central question is whether this distribution can preserve strong clustering quality while providing practical speed and memory benefits.

For the noise-free problem, the authors prove that a previously proposed distributed method has a constant-factor approximation guarantee. This supplies a theoretical explanation for its observed empirical strength. For the setting with outliers, they develop a new distributed algorithm with another constant-factor guarantee. Both algorithms are highly parallel and designed to fit a broad range of distributed computing frameworks.

Empirical comparisons with leading noisy sequential clustering methods show that the distributed algorithms remain consistently close to their sequential versions. The authors also describe them as fast and memory efficient. Together, the results support distributed clustering through two forms of evidence: bounded approximation quality in the analysis and close agreement with sequential counterparts in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Distributed k-center algorithms achieve constant-factor approximation guarantees, including with outliers, and empirically stay close to sequential counterparts.

title: Fast Distributed k-Center Clustering with Outliers on Massive Data

abstract: The stochastic block model (SBM) has long been studied in machine learning and network science as a canonical model for clustering and community detection. In the recent years, new developments have demonstrated the presence of threshold phenomena for this model, which have set new challenges for algorithms. For the {\it detection} problem in symmetric SBMs, Decelle et al.\ conjectured that the so-called Kesten-Stigum (KS) threshold can be achieved efficiently. This was proved for two communities, but remained open from three communities. We prove this conjecture here, obtaining a more general result that applies to arbitrary SBMs with linear size communities. The developed algorithm is a linearized acyclic belief propagation (ABP) algorithm, which mitigates the effects of cycles while provably achieving the KS threshold in $O(n \ln n)$ time. This extends prior methods by achieving universally the KS threshold while reducing or preserving the computational complexity. ABP is also connected to a power iteration method on a generalized nonbacktracking operator, formalizing the spectral-message passing interplay described in Krzakala et al., and extending results from Bordenave et al.

paragraphs: The stochastic block model describes networks with underlying communities and provides a mathematical setting for studying community detection. Its detection problem exhibits thresholds that separate different levels of recoverable community information. This paper addresses whether an efficient algorithm can reach the Kesten-Stigum threshold, a conjecture previously proved for two symmetric communities but still open for three or more.

The authors prove the conjecture and obtain a broader result for arbitrary stochastic block models whose communities have sizes proportional to the network size. Their method is linearized acyclic belief propagation. It reduces the effects of cycles in the graph while achieving the threshold with a running time of O(n ln n).

The paper also connects this message-passing algorithm to power iteration on a generalized nonbacktracking operator. That connection gives a formal relationship between spectral calculations and message passing. Together, the results expand the models covered by an efficient threshold guarantee while preserving or improving the computational complexity of earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: Linearized acyclic belief propagation achieves the Kesten-Stigum detection threshold in O(n ln n) time for stochastic block models with linear-size communities.

title: Achieving the KS threshold in the general stochastic block model with linearized acyclic belief propagation

abstract: This paper describes InfoGAN, an information-theoretic extension to the Generative Adversarial Network that is able to learn disentangled representations in a completely unsupervised manner. InfoGAN is a generative adversarial network that also maximizes the mutual information between a small subset of the latent variables and the observation. We derive a lower bound to the mutual information objective that can be optimized efficiently, and show that our training procedure can be interpreted as a variation of the Wake-Sleep algorithm. Specifically, InfoGAN successfully disentangles writing styles from digit shapes on the MNIST dataset, pose from lighting of 3D rendered images, and background digits from the central digit on the SVHN dataset. It also discovers visual concepts that include hair styles, presence/absence of eyeglasses, and emotions on the CelebA face dataset. Experiments show that InfoGAN learns interpretable representations that are competitive with representations learned by existing fully supervised methods.

paragraphs: InfoGAN aims to learn interpretable factors of variation without labeled examples of those factors. It extends a generative adversarial network by encouraging a small subset of its latent variables to carry information about the generated observation. The intended result is a representation in which different variables correspond to distinct, understandable changes.

The added objective maximizes mutual information between those selected latent variables and observations. The authors derive a lower bound that can be optimized efficiently, making this information-based objective usable in training. They also show that the training procedure admits an interpretation as a variation of the Wake-Sleep algorithm.

The reported examples separate writing style from digit shape on MNIST, pose from lighting in rendered images, and background digits from the central digit on SVHN. On CelebA, the model discovers concepts including hairstyles, eyeglasses, and emotions. Experiments find interpretability competitive with existing fully supervised representations. These results demonstrate successful disentanglement in the studied examples without establishing that every latent factor will always be separated.
summary.tldr: InfoGAN adds an efficiently optimized information objective to GAN training to learn interpretable, disentangled visual representations without supervision.

title: InfoGAN: Interpretable Representation Learning by Information Maximizing Generative Adversarial Nets

abstract: Data augmentation is an essential part of the training process applied to deep learning models. The motivation is that a robust training process for deep learning models depends on large annotated datasets, which are expensive to be acquired, stored and processed. Therefore a reasonable alternative is to be able to automatically generate new annotated training samples using a process known as data augmentation. The dominant data augmentation approach in the field assumes that new training samples can be obtained via random geometric or appearance transformations applied to annotated training samples, but this is a strong assumption because it is unclear if this is a reliable generative model for producing new training samples. In this paper, we provide a novel Bayesian formulation to data augmentation, where new annotated training points are treated as missing variables and generated based on the distribution learned from the training set. For learning, we introduce a theoretically sound algorithm --- generalised Monte Carlo expectation maximisation, and demonstrate one possible implementation via an extension of the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). Classification results on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show the better performance of our proposed method compared to the current dominant data augmentation approach mentioned above --- the results also show that our approach produces better classification results than similar GAN models.

paragraphs: Deep learning often needs more labeled examples than are practical to collect. A common workaround creates additional examples by changing the geometry or appearance of existing ones. This paper questions whether those transformations reliably describe how new examples arise and develops a Bayesian alternative that learns how to generate annotated data from the training set.

The central move is to treat additional training examples as missing variables. Their values are generated according to a learned distribution, making augmentation part of the statistical learning problem. The authors introduce generalized Monte Carlo expectation maximization for this purpose and present an extension of a generative adversarial network as one possible implementation.

On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, the proposed method produces better classification results than the transformation-based augmentation approach described in the abstract and similar GAN models. These findings support learned augmentation in the evaluated settings: the generated examples help classification, connecting the quality of augmentation to the eventual task rather than only to the generation process.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian approach learns to generate labeled training examples and improves classification over the compared augmentation methods on three datasets.

title: A Bayesian Data Augmentation Approach for Learning Deep Models

abstract: In this work, we propose to apply trust region optimization to deep reinforcement learning using a recently proposed Kronecker-factored approximation to the curvature. We extend the framework of natural policy gradient and propose to optimize both the actor and the critic using Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) with trust region; hence we call our method Actor Critic using Kronecker-Factored Trust Region (ACKTR). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first scalable trust region natural gradient method for actor-critic methods. It is also the method that learns non-trivial tasks in continuous control as well as discrete control policies directly from raw pixel inputs. We tested our approach across discrete domains in Atari games as well as continuous domains in the MuJoCo environment. With the proposed methods, we are able to achieve higher rewards and a 2- to 3-fold improvement in sample efficiency on average, compared to previous state-of-the-art on-policy actor-critic methods. Code is available at https://github.com/openai/baselines

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning trains both an action-selecting policy and a component that evaluates behavior. This paper proposes ACKTR, which applies trust-region optimization to both components using Kronecker-factored approximate curvature, or K-FAC. The method extends the natural policy gradient framework with an approximation intended to make curvature-aware updates scalable.

Curvature information describes how the optimization landscape changes around the current parameters. ACKTR combines an approximation to that information with a trust region that controls the update. Applying the construction to both actor and critic gives the two parts of learning a shared optimization approach. The method handles continuous control and discrete policies learned directly from raw pixels.

The authors evaluate ACKTR on Atari games and MuJoCo control tasks. Against previous state-of-the-art on-policy actor-critic methods, they report higher rewards and an average two- to threefold improvement in sample efficiency. That average summarizes the evaluated comparisons; it is not a promise for every task. The findings support approximate curvature as a practical route to more efficient use of experience.
summary.tldr: ACKTR uses approximate curvature and trust regions for both actor and critic, reporting higher rewards and improved average sample efficiency.

title: Scalable trust-region method for deep reinforcement learning using Kronecker-factored approximation

abstract: We consider the problem of binary prediction with expert advice in settings where experts have agency and seek to maximize their credibility. This paper makes three main contributions. First, it defines a model to reason formally about settings with selfish experts, and demonstrates that ``incentive compatible'' (IC) algorithms are closely related to the design of proper scoring rules. Second, we design IC algorithms with good performance guarantees for the absolute loss function. Third, we give a formal separation between the power of online prediction with selfish experts and online prediction with honest experts by proving lower bounds for both IC and non-IC algorithms. In particular, with selfish experts and the absolute loss function, there is no (randomized) algorithm for online prediction---IC or otherwise---with asymptotically vanishing regret.

Second, we design IC algorithms with good performance guarantees for the absolute loss function. paragraphs: Online prediction with expert advice usually treats experts' reports as information a learner can combine. This paper studies binary prediction when experts act strategically to increase their own credibility. Their incentives become part of the learning problem, so a prediction algorithm must be analyzed together with the behavior it encourages.

The authors introduce a formal model and connect incentive-compatible algorithms to proper scoring rules. They also construct incentive-compatible algorithms with performance guarantees for absolute loss. This provides a positive result: it is possible to design prediction procedures that account for strategic reporting and still obtain meaningful guarantees.

The paper also proves lower bounds separating selfish experts from honest ones. Under the selfish-expert model and absolute loss, no online prediction algorithm, including randomized algorithms and algorithms that are not incentive compatible, achieves asymptotically vanishing regret. Thus, the obstruction is broader than a particular incentive design. The positive guarantees must be understood alongside this fundamental limit on what strategic expert advice permits.
summary.tldr: Strategic experts permit incentive-compatible prediction guarantees but impose a lower bound ruling out asymptotically vanishing regret under absolute loss.

title: Online Prediction with Selfish Experts

abstract: Hashing is a basic tool for dimensionality reduction employed in several aspects of machine learning. However, the perfomance analysis is often carried out under the abstract assumption that a truly random unit cost hash function is used, without concern for which concrete hash function is employed. The concrete hash function may work fine on sufficiently random input. The question is if it can be trusted in the real world when faced with more structured input. In this paper we focus on two prominent applications of hashing, namely similarity estimation with the one permutation hashing (OPH) scheme of Li et al. [NIPS'12] and feature hashing (FH) of Weinberger et al. [ICML'09], both of which have found numerous applications, i.e. in approximate near-neighbour search with LSH and large-scale classification with SVM. We consider the recent mixed tabulation hash function of Dahlgaard et al. [FOCS'15] which was proved theoretically to perform like a truly random hash function in many applications, including the above OPH. Here we first show improved concentration bounds for FH with truly random hashing and then argue that mixed tabulation performs similar when the input vectors are sparse. Our main contribution, however, is an experimental comparison of different hashing schemes when used inside FH, OPH, and LSH. We find that mixed tabulation hashing is almost as fast as the classic multiply-mod-prime scheme ax+b mod p. Mutiply-mod-prime is guaranteed to work well on sufficiently random data, but we demonstrate that in the above applications, it can lead to bias and poor concentration on both real-world and synthetic data. We also compare with the very popular MurmurHash3, which has no proven guarantees. Mixed tabulation and MurmurHash3 both perform similar to truly random hashing in our experiments. However, mixed tabulation was 40% faster than MurmurHash3, and it has the proven guarantee of good performance on all possible input making it more reliable.

The findings connect implementation choice to both practical reliability and computational speed.
summary.tldr: Mixed tabulation offers fast, theoretically supported hashing and avoids failures observed with multiply-mod-prime on structured data.

title: Practical Hash Functions for Similarity Estimation and Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: Non-parametric multivariate density estimation faces strong statistical and computational bottlenecks, and the more practical approaches impose near-parametric assumptions on the form of the density functions. In this paper, we leverage recent developments to propose a class of non-parametric models which have very attractive computational and statistical properties. Our approach relies on the simple function space assumption that the conditional distribution of each variable conditioned on the other variables has a non-parametric exponential family form.
originalAbstract: Non-parametric multivariate density estimation faces strong statistical and computational bottlenecks, and the more practical approaches impose near-parametric assumptions on the form of the density functions. In this paper, we leverage recent developments to propose a class of non-parametric models which have very attractive computational and statistical properties. Our approach relies on the simple function space assumption that the conditional distribution of each variable conditioned on the other variables has a non-parametric exponential family form.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of estimating a probability distribution over several variables without prescribing a rigid form for that distribution. Such nonparametric estimation faces both statistical and computational obstacles. The authors note that more practical approaches often obtain tractability by imposing assumptions that bring their models close to parametric ones, reducing the flexibility that motivates nonparametric modeling.

Their proposal is a class of models built around conditional distributions: the distribution of one variable when the values of the others are given. The central assumption is that each of these conditional distributions belongs to a nonparametric exponential family. This places structure on the functions describing the conditionals while retaining a nonparametric formulation.

The significance is the authors’ claim that this conditional construction yields attractive computational and statistical properties. It offers an approach to flexible multivariate density estimation whose organizing restriction is explicit. The proposed flexibility therefore depends on the stated exponential-family assumption for every variable’s conditional distribution; it does not amount to removing all assumptions about the density.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes nonparametric models with attractive computational and statistical properties by assuming that each variable’s conditional distribution has a nonparametric exponential-family form.

title: The Expxorcist: Nonparametric Graphical Models Via Conditional Exponential Densities

abstract: Digital presence in the world of online social media entails significant privacy risks. In this work we consider a privacy threat to a social network in which an attacker has access to a subset of random walk-based node similarities, such as effective resistances (i.e., commute times) or personalized PageRank scores. Using these similarities, the attacker seeks to infer as much information as possible about the network, including unknown pairwise node similarities and edges. For the effective resistance metric, we show that with just a small subset of measurements, one can learn a large fraction of edges in a social network. We also show that it is possible to learn a graph which accurately matches the underlying network on all other effective resistances. This second observation is interesting from a data mining perspective, since it can be expensive to compute all effective resistances or other random walk-based similarities. As an alternative, our graphs learned from just a subset of effective resistances can be used as surrogates in a range of applications that use effective resistances to probe graph structure, including for graph clustering, node centrality evaluation, and anomaly detection. We obtain our results by formalizing the graph learning objective mathematically, using two optimization problems. One formulation is convex and can be solved provably in polynomial time. The other is not, but we solve it efficiently with projected gradient and coordinate descent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods on a number of social networks obtained from Facebook. We also discuss how our methods can be generalized to other random walk-based similarities, such as personalized PageRank scores. Our code is available at https://github.com/cnmusco/graph-similarity-learning.

title: Inferring Networks From Random Walk-Based Node Similarities

abstract: This paper examines the long-run behavior of learning with bandit feedback in non-cooperative concave games. The bandit framework accounts for extremely low-information environments where the agents may not even know they are playing a game; as such, the agents’ most sensible choice in this setting would be to employ a no-regret learning algorithm. In general, this does not mean that the players' behavior stabilizes in the long run: no-regret learning may lead to cycles, even with perfect gradient information. However, if a standard monotonicity condition is satisfied, our analysis shows that no-regret learning based on mirror descent with bandit feedback converges to Nash equilibrium with probability 1. We also derive an upper bound for the convergence rate of the process that nearly matches the best attainable rate for single-agent bandit stochastic optimization.

In the bandit setting, agents receive limited feedback and may not even know they are interacting strategically. A natural response is no-regret learning, which aims to avoid doing persistently worse than a fixed alternative choice over time.

Low regret alone does not ensure stable behavior. Players can continue cycling, even when they receive perfect gradient information. The authors analyze a particular family of no-regret methods based on mirror descent with bandit feedback. They show that, when a standard monotonicity condition holds in a non-cooperative concave game, this learning process converges to a Nash equilibrium with probability one.

The paper also bounds the speed of convergence. Its upper bound nearly matches the best attainable rate for single-agent bandit stochastic optimization. This connects learning in a strategic environment to a simpler optimization benchmark, while retaining the monotonicity assumption that makes the equilibrium convergence result possible.
summary.tldr: Under a monotonicity condition, mirror-descent no-regret learning with bandit feedback converges almost surely to Nash equilibrium in concave games.

title: Bandit Learning in Concave N-Person Games

abstract: We consider semidefinite programs (SDPs) of size $n$ with equality constraints. In order to overcome scalability issues, Burer and Monteiro proposed a factorized approach based on optimizing over a matrix $Y$ of size $n\times k$ such that $X=YY^*$ is the SDP variable. The advantages of such formulation are twofold: the dimension of the optimization variable is reduced, and positive semidefiniteness is naturally enforced. However, optimization in $Y$ is non-convex. In prior work, it has been shown that, when the constraints on the factorized variable regularly define a smooth manifold, provided $k$ is large enough, for almost all cost matrices, all second-order stationary points (SOSPs) are optimal. Importantly, in practice, one can only compute points which approximately satisfy necessary optimality conditions, leading to the question: are such points also approximately optimal? To this end, and under similar assumptions, we use smoothed analysis to show that approximate SOSPs for a randomly perturbed objective function are approximate global optima, with $k$ scaling like the square root of the number of constraints (up to log factors). We particularize our results to an SDP relaxation of phase retrieval.

The price is non-convexity, raising the question of whether solutions reached in the factorized problem are good.

Practical algorithms, however, generally produce only approximate stationary points. This paper addresses the gap between an exact mathematical condition and the approximate conditions a numerical method can satisfy.

The required factor width scales like the square root of the number of constraints, up to logarithmic factors. They also specialize the results to a semidefinite relaxation of phase retrieval. The guarantee supports approximate computation while explicitly retaining the perturbation and structural assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under structural assumptions and random objective perturbation, approximate stationary points of low-rank SDP formulations are approximately globally optimal.

title: Smoothed analysis of the low-rank approach for smooth semidefinite programs

abstract: We develop new stochastic gradient methods for efficiently solving sparse linear regression in a partial attribute observation setting, where learners are only allowed to observe a fixed number of actively chosen attributes per example at training and prediction times. It is shown that the methods achieve essentially a sample complexity of $O(1/\varepsilon)$ to attain an error of $\varepsilon$ under a variant of restricted eigenvalue condition, and the rate has better dependency on the problem dimension than existing methods. Particularly, if the smallest magnitude of the non-zero components of the optimal solution is not too small, the rate of our proposed {\it Hybrid} algorithm can be boosted to near the minimax optimal sample complexity of {\it full information} algorithms. The core ideas are (i) efficient construction of an unbiased gradient estimator by the iterative usage of the hard thresholding operator for configuring an exploration algorithm; and (ii) an adaptive combination of the exploration and an exploitation algorithms for quickly identifying the support of the optimum and efficiently searching the optimal parameter in its support. Experimental results are presented to validate our theoretical findings and the superiority of our proposed methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse linear regression when a learner can inspect only a fixed number of actively chosen attributes per example. This restriction applies during both training and prediction. The challenge is to identify the relevant attributes and estimate their coefficients while working with incomplete observations of every example.

The proposed stochastic gradient methods construct an unbiased gradient estimate through repeated hard thresholding, which keeps a sparse selection of components. An exploration procedure searches for relevant attributes, while exploitation refines the solution on its identified support: the locations of nonzero coefficients. The Hybrid algorithm adaptively combines these activities to locate and optimize the useful parameter subset.

Under a variant of the restricted eigenvalue condition, the methods achieve essentially O(1/epsilon) sample complexity for error epsilon, with improved dependence on dimension compared with existing methods. If the smallest nonzero optimal coefficient is sufficiently large, Hybrid approaches the minimax-optimal sample complexity of full-information algorithms. Experiments support the theoretical findings and reported advantages. The stronger comparison with full-information learning depends on that additional coefficient-size condition.
summary.tldr: Sparse regression methods combine attribute exploration and exploitation to achieve strong conditional sample-complexity guarantees with limited observations.

title: Sample Efficient Stochastic Gradient Iterative Hard Thresholding Method for Stochastic Sparse Linear Regression with Limited Attribute Observation

abstract: Although the recent progress is substantial, deep learning methods can be vulnerable to the maliciously generated adversarial examples. In this paper, we present a novel training procedure and a thresholding test strategy, towards robust detection of adversarial examples. In training, we propose to minimize the reverse cross-entropy (RCE), which encourages a deep network to learn latent representations that better distinguish adversarial examples from normal ones. In testing, we propose to use a thresholding strategy as the detector to filter out adversarial examples for reliable predictions. Our method is simple to implement using standard algorithms, with little extra training cost compared to the common cross-entropy minimization. We apply our method to defend various attacking methods on the widely used MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, and achieve significant improvements on robust predictions under all the threat models in the adversarial setting.

This paper approaches the problem through detection: it trains the network to make adversarial and normal inputs easier to distinguish, then filters suspicious inputs at test time. The training procedure and detector are designed to work together.

Training minimizes reverse cross-entropy, an alternative to the usual cross-entropy objective. The intended effect is to shape the network's internal representations so that normal and adversarial examples are better separated. At test time, a thresholding rule uses the resulting distinction to filter adversarial inputs. The authors describe the procedure as straightforward to implement with standard algorithms and requiring little additional training cost.

Evaluation covers several attack methods on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The authors report significant improvements in robust prediction across all threat models considered in their adversarial evaluation. This supports the combination of representation-focused training and threshold detection in the tested settings. The reported scope is those evaluations, rather than an unconditional guarantee against every possible adversarial input.
summary.tldr: Reverse cross-entropy training and threshold-based detection improve robust predictions against the attacks evaluated on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

title: Towards Robust Detection of Adversarial Examples

abstract: We study the geometry of deep (neural) networks (DNs) with piecewise affine and convex nonlinearities. The layers of such DNs have been shown to be max-affine spline operators (MASOs) that partition their input space and apply a region-dependent affine mapping to their input to produce their output. We demonstrate that each MASO layer's input space partitioning corresponds to a power diagram (an extension of the classical Voronoi tiling) with a number of regions that grows exponentially with respect to the number of units (neurons). We further show that a composition of MASO layers (e.g., the entire DN) produces a progressively subdivided power diagram and provide its analytical form. The subdivision process constrains the affine maps on the potentially exponentially many power diagram regions with respect to the number of neurons to greatly reduce their complexity. For classification problems, we obtain a formula for a MASO DN's decision boundary in the input space plus a measure of its curvature that depends on the DN's nonlinearities, weights, and architecture. Numerous numerical experiments support and extend our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper studies deep networks with piecewise affine, convex nonlinearities through the geometry of their input spaces. Their layers can be represented as max-affine spline operators: each layer partitions its input into regions and applies a different affine mapping within each region. The question is how those regions are organized and change across layers.

The authors show that a layer's partition corresponds to a power diagram, an extension of a Voronoi tiling. The number of regions grows exponentially with the number of neurons. Composing layers produces progressive subdivisions, for which the paper gives an analytical form. These subdivisions also constrain the affine maps, reducing their complexity despite the potentially enormous number of regions.

For classification, the analysis yields a formula for the network's decision boundary and a curvature measure depending on its nonlinearities, weights, and architecture. Numerical experiments support and extend the theoretical results. The contribution connects layer composition to an explicit geometric description of both internal partitions and the resulting classification boundary.
summary.tldr: For a specified class of networks, power-diagram subdivisions describe layer geometry, constrain local mappings, and characterize decision boundaries.

title: The Geometry of Deep Networks: Power Diagram Subdivision

abstract: The knockoff filter introduced by Barber and Cand\`es 2016 is an elegant framework for controlling the false discovery rate in variable selection. While empirical results indicate that this methodology is not too conservative, there is no conclusive theoretical result on its power. When the predictors are i.i.d.\ Gaussian, it is known that as the signal to noise ratio tend to infinity, the knockoff filter is consistent in the sense that one can make FDR go to 0 and power go to 1 simultaneously. In this work we study the case where the predictors have a general covariance matrix $\bsigma$. We introduce a simple functional called \emph{effective signal deficiency (ESD)} of the covariance matrix of the predictors that predicts consistency of various variable selection methods. In particular, ESD reveals that the structure of the precision matrix plays a central role in consistency and therefore, so does the conditional independence structure of the predictors. To leverage this connection, we introduce \emph{Conditional Independence knockoff}, a simple procedure that is able to compete with the more sophisticated knockoff filters and that is defined when the predictors obey a Gaussian tree graphical models (or when the graph is sufficiently sparse). Our theoretical results are supported by numerical evidence on synthetic data.
