paragraphs: The paper studies quantum optimization when a function is close to convex but need not itself be convex. Its assumption is precise: over a convex feasible set in n dimensions, the target function differs everywhere from some convex function by at most epsilon divided by n. Under this condition, the algorithm finds a point within epsilon of the target function's minimum.

The algorithm uses roughly cubic-in-n quantum evaluation queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed, giving a polynomial improvement over the best-known classical algorithms. Its construction combines a quantum simulated-annealing framework with a quantum version of the hit-and-run walk. The speedup is stated in quantum query complexity.

The authors also apply the approach to zeroth-order stochastic convex bandits. They obtain regret scaling as n to the fifth power times the square of log T, again suppressing logarithmic factors, compared with a classical lower bound growing as the square root of T. This improvement in time dependence comes from a quadratic quantum improvement in mean estimation's multiplicative error.
summary.tldr: Quantum algorithms speed up approximately convex optimization and achieve polylogarithmic-in-time regret for the studied stochastic convex bandit setting.

title: Quantum Speedups of Optimizing Approximately Convex Functions with Applications to Logarithmic Regret Stochastic Convex Bandits

abstract: We study the problem of clustering graphs with additional side-information of node features. The problem is extensively studied, and several existing methods exploit Graph Neural Networks to learn node representations. However, most of the existing methods focus on generic representations instead of their cluster-ability or do not scale to large scale graph datasets. In this work, we propose S3GC which uses contrastive learning along with Graph Neural Networks and node features to learn clusterable features. We empirically demonstrate that S3GC is able to learn the correct cluster structure even when graph information or node features are individually not informative enough to learn correct clusters. Finally, using extensive evaluation on a variety of benchmarks, we demonstrate that S3GC is able to significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of clustering accuracy -- with as much as 5% gain in NMI -- while being scalable to graphs of size 100M.

paragraphs: Graph clustering seeks groups of nodes using both their connections and any descriptive features attached to them. Existing neural approaches can learn representations that are useful in general without making clusters easy to recover. They may also become impractical on very large graphs. S3GC is designed to address both concerns.

The method combines contrastive learning, graph neural networks, and node features to produce representations intended for clustering. Its experiments show that the combination can recover the correct cluster structure even when graph connections alone or node features alone do not provide enough information. This demonstrates a benefit from combining the two information sources in the tested settings.

Across a variety of benchmarks, the authors report better clustering results than leading methods, including gains of as much as 5% in normalized mutual information. They also report scalability to graphs of size 100M. The stated contribution joins cluster-oriented representation learning with large-scale operation, rather than treating the quality of the learned features and the scale of the graph as separate objectives.
summary.tldr: S3GC learns clusterable graph representations by combining connections and node features, with strong benchmark results and scalability to graphs of size 100M.

title: S3GC: Scalable Self-Supervised Graph Clustering

abstract: Relative Positional Encoding (RPE), which encodes the relative distance between any pair of tokens, is one of the most successful modifications to the original Transformer. As far as we know, theoretical understanding of the RPE-based Transformers is largely unexplored. In this work, we mathematically analyze the power of RPE-based Transformers regarding whether the model is capable of approximating any continuous sequence-to-sequence functions. One may naturally assume the answer is in the affirmative---RPE-based Transformers are universal function approximators. However, we present a negative result by showing there exist continuous sequence-to-sequence functions that RPE-based Transformers cannot approximate no matter how deep and wide the neural network is. One key reason lies in that most RPEs are placed in the softmax attention that always generates a right stochastic matrix. This restricts the network from capturing positional information in the RPEs and limits its capacity. To overcome the problem and make the model more powerful, we first present sufficient conditions for RPE-based Transformers to achieve universal function approximation. With the theoretical guidance, we develop a novel attention module, called Universal RPE-based (URPE) Attention, which satisfies the conditions. Therefore, the corresponding URPE-based Transformers become universal function approximators. Extensive experiments covering typical architectures and tasks demonstrate that our model is parameter-efficient and can achieve superior performance to strong baselines in a wide range of applications. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/lsj2408/URPE.

The authors identify continuous sequence-to-sequence functions that the analyzed RPE-based Transformers cannot approximate, even when their depth and width are increased arbitrarily.

The resulting URPE-based Transformers are universal approximators under the theoretical formulation. Experiments across typical architectures and tasks also show parameter efficiency and improvements over strong baselines in a broad range of applications. These are complementary findings: the theory addresses which functions the architecture can represent, while the experiments assess the practical performance of the proposed attention module.
summary.tldr: URPE Attention addresses a positional-information bottleneck in RPE Transformers and satisfies sufficient conditions for universal sequence-to-sequence approximation.

title: Your Transformer May Not be as Powerful as You Expect

abstract: Despite impressive successes, deep reinforcement learning (RL) systems still fall short of human performance on generalization to new tasks and environments that differ from their training. As a benchmark tailored for studying RL generalization, we introduce Avalon, a set of tasks in which embodied agents in highly diverse procedural 3D worlds must survive by navigating terrain, hunting or gathering food, and avoiding hazards. Avalon is unique among existing RL benchmarks in that the reward function, world dynamics, and action space are the same for every task, with tasks differentiated solely by altering the environment; its 20 tasks, ranging in complexity from eat and throw to hunt and navigate, each create worlds in which the agent must perform specific skills in order to survive. This setup enables investigations of generalization within tasks, between tasks, and to compositional tasks that require combining skills learned from previous tasks. Avalon includes a highly efficient simulator, a library of baselines, and a benchmark with scoring metrics evaluated against hundreds of hours of human performance, all of which are open-source and publicly available. We find that standard RL baselines make progress on most tasks but are still far from human performance, suggesting Avalon is challenging enough to advance the quest for generalizable RL.

paragraphs: Avalon is a benchmark for testing whether reinforcement learning agents can use learned skills in unfamiliar situations. Agents inhabit procedurally generated three-dimensional worlds, where survival involves finding food, navigating terrain, and avoiding hazards. Its 20 tasks span relatively simple actions, such as eating and throwing, through more involved activities such as hunting and navigation.

The benchmark holds the reward function, world dynamics, and available actions constant across tasks. Different tasks arise entirely from changes to the environment. This shared structure lets researchers study generalization to new worlds within a task, transfer between tasks, and combinations that require previously learned skills to work together. The environment becomes the controlled source of variation.

Avalon includes an efficient simulator, baseline implementations, and scoring metrics evaluated against hundreds of hours of human performance. These resources are publicly available and open source. Standard reinforcement learning baselines improve on most tasks, but remain well below human performance. Those results suggest the benchmark provides substantial room to investigate generalization, including whether agents can compose skills beyond the situations used for training.
summary.tldr: Avalon tests reinforcement learning generalization through diverse survival tasks that share actions, dynamics, and rewards.

title: Avalon: A Benchmark for RL Generalization Using Procedurally Generated Worlds

abstract: We study best-of-both-worlds algorithms for bandits with switching cost, recently addressed by Rouyer et al., 2021. We introduce a surprisingly simple and effective algorithm that simultaneously achieves minimax optimal regret bound (up to logarithmic factors) of $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ in the oblivious adversarial setting and a bound of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{\log (T)/\Delta^2,T^{2/3}\})$ in the stochastically-constrained regime, both with (unit) switching costs, where $\Delta$ is the gap between the arms. In the stochastically constrained case, our bound improves over previous results due to Rouyer et al., 2021, that achieved regret of $\mathcal{O}(T^{1/3}/\Delta)$. We accompany our results with a lower bound showing that, in general, $\tilde{\mathcal{\Omega}}(\min\{1/\Delta^2,T^{2/3}\})$ switching cost regret is unavoidable in the stochastically-constrained case for algorithms with $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ worst-case switching cost regret.

We introduce a surprisingly simple and effective algorithm that simultaneously achieves minimax optimal regret bound (up to logarithmic factors) of $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ in the oblivious adversarial setting and a bound of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{\log (T)/\Delta^2,T^{2/3}\})$ in the stochastically-constrained regime, both with (unit) switching costs, where $\Delta$ is the gap between the arms. In the stochastically constrained case, our bound improves over previous results due to Rouyer et al., 2021, that achieved regret of $\mathcal{O}(T^{1/3}/\Delta)$. We accompany our results with a lower bound showing that, in general, $\tilde{\mathcal{\Omega}}(\min\{1/\Delta^2,T^{2/3}\})$ switching cost regret is unavoidable in the stochastically-constrained case for algorithms with $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ worst-case switching cost regret.

paragraphs: Bandit learning involves repeatedly choosing among options while learning from the outcomes of those choices. Here, changing options also incurs a unit cost. The paper asks whether one algorithm can retain strong worst-case protection while exploiting the more favorable structure of a stochastically constrained setting. Regret measures the performance shortfall, including the cost of switching.

The proposed algorithm achieves regret of order T^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors, against an oblivious adversary. This matches the minimax rate at that level of precision. In the stochastically constrained regime, its bound becomes order min{log(T)/Δ², T^(2/3)}, where Δ is the gap between arms. This improves the previous order T^(1/3)/Δ guarantee stated in the abstract.

The paper also proves a complementary lower bound. Algorithms retaining the stated worst-case guarantee must, in general, incur stochastic-regime regret of at least order min{1/Δ², T^(2/3)}, ignoring logarithmic factors. Thus, the favorable-case improvement comes close to the unavoidable tradeoff imposed by preserving worst-case performance when switching is costly.
summary.tldr: A simple bandit algorithm improves stochastic regret with switching costs while retaining near-optimal worst-case protection.

title: Better Best of Both Worlds Bounds for Bandits with Switching Costs

abstract: Existing weak supervision approaches use all the data covered by weak signals to train a classifier. We show both theoretically and empirically that this is not always optimal. Intuitively, there is a tradeoff between the amount of weakly-labeled data and the precision of the weak labels. We explore this tradeoff by combining pretrained data representations with the cut statistic to select (hopefully) high-quality subsets of the weakly-labeled training data. Subset selection applies to any label model and classifier and is very simple to plug in to existing weak supervision pipelines, requiring just a few lines of code. We show our subset selection method improves the performance of weak supervision for a wide range of label models, classifiers, and datasets. Using less weakly-labeled data improves the accuracy of weak supervision pipelines by up to 19% (absolute) on benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Weak supervision trains classifiers using imperfect labeling signals, often taking every example those signals cover. This paper shows theoretically and empirically that using all such data is not always optimal. More examples provide more training information, but inaccurate weak labels can reduce the value of that additional data.

The proposed method combines pretrained representations with a cut statistic to select a subset intended to have higher-quality weak labels. It makes the tradeoff between data quantity and label precision an explicit part of the training pipeline. The selection step can be used with any label model and classifier, and the authors describe it as requiring only a few lines of integration code.

Evaluations span a wide range of label models, classifiers, and datasets. Selecting fewer weakly labeled examples improves accuracy by as much as 19 percentage points on benchmark tasks. That maximum is an observed result across the evaluations. The broader finding is that choosing training examples can be a useful component of weak supervision alongside constructing and combining labeling signals.
summary.tldr: Selecting higher-quality subsets of weakly labeled data can improve accuracy, with reported gains of up to 19 percentage points.

title: Training Subset Selection for Weak Supervision

abstract: Panchromatic (PAN) and multi-spectral (MS) image fusion, named Pan-sharpening, refers to super-resolve the low-resolution (LR) multi-spectral (MS) images in the spatial domain to generate the expected high-resolution (HR) MS images, conditioning on the corresponding high-resolution PAN images. In this paper, we present a simple yet effective alternating reverse filtering network for pan-sharpening. Inspired by the classical reverse filtering that reverses images to the status before filtering, we formulate pan-sharpening as an alternately iterative reverse filtering process, which fuses LR MS and HR MS in an interpretable manner. Different from existing model-driven methods that require well-designed priors and degradation assumptions, the reverse filtering process avoids the dependency on pre-defined exact priors. To guarantee the stability and convergence of the iterative process via contraction mapping on a metric space, we develop the learnable multi-scale Gaussian kernel module, instead of using specific filters. We demonstrate the theoretical feasibility of such formulations. Extensive experiments on diverse scenes to thoroughly verify the performance of our method, significantly outperforming the state of the arts.

The paper introduces a network that approaches this fusion through alternating reverse filtering. Its starting intuition is to undo filtering, moving an image toward the state it had before filtering reduced its detail.

The authors formulate fusion as an iterative process, giving the network an interpretable computational structure. The approach avoids dependence on predefined exact priors, which existing model-driven methods may require alongside degradation assumptions. To support stable, convergent iteration, the network uses a learnable multiscale Gaussian kernel module rather than relying on specific fixed filters.

summary.tldr: An alternating reverse-filtering network uses learnable Gaussian kernels for theoretically supported pan-sharpening and improved reported image-fusion results.

title: Panchromatic and Multispectral Image Fusion via Alternating Reverse Filtering Network

abstract: Developing deep generative models has been an emerging field due to the ability to model and generate complex data for various purposes, such as image synthesis and molecular design. However, the advance of deep generative models is limited by the challenges to generate objects that possess multiple desired properties because: 1) the existence of complex correlation among real-world properties is common but hard to identify; 2) controlling individual property enforces an implicit partially control of its correlated properties, which is difficult to model; 3) controlling multiple properties under variour manners simultaneously is hard and underexplored. We address these challenges by proposing a novel deep generative framework that recovers semantics and correlation of properties through disentangled latent vectors. The correlation is handled via an explainable mask pooling layer, and properties are precisely retained by the generated objects via the mutual dependence between latent vectors and properties. Our generative model preserves properties of interest while handles correlation and conflicts of properties under a multi-objective optimization framework. The experiments demonstrate our model's superior performance in generating objects with desired properties.

paragraphs: Generating an object with several desired properties is difficult when those properties are correlated. Changing one property can partly change others, and multiple requested properties may conflict. This paper addresses that joint-control problem with a deep generative framework designed to recover both the meaning of properties and the relationships among them.

The framework uses disentangled latent vectors to represent properties and an explainable mask pooling layer to handle their correlations. It also connects the latent vectors and properties through mutual dependence so that generated objects retain the properties of interest. These components make the relationships between requested attributes part of the generation process.

A multi-objective optimization framework manages simultaneous property requirements, including their correlations and conflicts. The experiments report superior performance in producing objects with desired properties. The central contribution is a mechanism for coordinated control: the generator accounts for how property requests interact, helping it preserve requested characteristics while handling dependencies that make separate control of each property difficult.
summary.tldr: A generative framework models correlations between properties to better produce objects satisfying multiple interacting requirements.

title: Multi-objective Deep Data Generation with Correlated Property Control

abstract: Consider a bandit algorithm that recommends actions to self-interested users in a recommendation system. The users are free to choose other actions and need to be incentivized to follow the algorithm's recommendations. While the users prefer to exploit, the algorithm can incentivize them to explore by leveraging the information collected from the previous users. All published work on this problem, known as incentivized exploration, focuses on small, unstructured action sets and mainly targets the case when the users' beliefs are independent across actions. However, realistic exploration problems often feature large, structured action sets and highly correlated beliefs. We focus on a paradigmatic exploration problem with structure: combinatorial semi-bandits. We prove that Thompson Sampling, when applied to combinatorial semi-bandits, is incentive-compatible when initialized with a sufficient number of samples of each arm (where this number is determined in advance by the Bayesian prior). Moreover, we design incentive-compatible algorithms for collecting the initial samples.

paragraphs: A recommendation algorithm benefits from exploring uncertain actions, but its users may prefer choices they currently expect to be best. Because users can ignore recommendations, exploration must respect their incentives. This paper studies how information gathered from earlier users can make exploratory recommendations worth following.

The focus is combinatorial semi-bandits, a structured exploration setting that moves beyond small collections of unrelated actions. Such structure matters because practical recommendation problems can involve large action spaces and strongly correlated beliefs. The paper asks whether Thompson Sampling can remain incentive-compatible in this setting, meaning users have an incentive to follow its recommendations.

The authors prove that it can, provided it is initialized with sufficiently many samples of each arm. The required sample count is determined in advance by the Bayesian prior. They also design incentive-compatible algorithms to collect those initial samples. This second contribution addresses the startup stage needed by the theorem, yielding a route from incentive-respecting initialization to incentive-respecting exploration. The guarantee therefore depends on adequate initialization rather than holding for an arbitrary starting state.
summary.tldr: Thompson Sampling is incentive-compatible for combinatorial semi-bandits after sufficient prior-dependent initialization, which the paper also shows how to collect.

title: Incentivizing Combinatorial Bandit Exploration

abstract: Dynamic graph neural networks (DyGNNs) currently struggle with handling distribution shifts that are inherent in dynamic graphs.Existing work on DyGNNs with out-of-distribution settings only focuses on the time domain, failing to handle cases involving distribution shifts in the spectral domain. In this paper, we discover that there exist cases with distribution shifts unobservable in the time domain while observable in the spectral domain, and propose to study distribution shifts on dynamic graphs in the spectral domain for the first time.However, this investigation poses two key challenges: i) it is non-trivial to capture different graph patterns that are driven by various frequency components entangled in the spectral domain; and ii) it remains unclear how to handle distribution shifts with the discovered spectral patterns. To address these challenges, we propose Spectral Invariant Learning for Dynamic Graphs under Distribution Shifts (SILD), which can handle distribution shifts on dynamic graphs by capturing and utilizing invariant and variant spectral patterns. Specifically, we first design a DyGNN with Fourier transform to obtain the ego-graph trajectory spectrums, allowing the mixed dynamic graph patterns to be transformed into separate frequency components. We then develop a disentangled spectrum mask to filter graph dynamics from various frequency components and discover the invariant and variant spectral patterns. Finally, we propose invariant spectral filtering, which encourages the model to rely on invariant patterns for generalization under distribution shifts. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world dynamic graph datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method for both node classification and link prediction tasks under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Dynamic graphs can change in ways that undermine predictions learned from earlier data. This paper identifies cases where distribution shifts are not observable in the time domain but become visible in the spectral domain. That observation motivates examining frequency components of graph evolution rather than relying exclusively on time-domain analysis.

SILD applies a Fourier transform to trajectories of local graph neighborhoods, separating mixed dynamics into frequency components. A learned spectrum mask then distinguishes patterns that remain invariant from those that vary. Finally, invariant spectral filtering encourages the predictor to rely on the stable patterns when making predictions under distribution shifts.

The approach addresses both extracting useful spectral patterns and deciding which patterns should guide generalization. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dynamic graphs show superior performance for node classification and link prediction under distribution shifts. The findings support spectral analysis as a complementary way to expose changes that time-domain approaches can miss and to identify more stable predictive structure.
summary.tldr: SILD separates dynamic-graph frequency patterns and emphasizes invariant ones to improve prediction under distribution shifts.

title: Spectral Invariant Learning for Dynamic Graphs under Distribution Shifts

abstract: While Vision Transformers (ViTs) have undoubtedly made impressive strides in computer vision (CV), their intricate network structures necessitate substantial computation and memory resources. A decision-making process for CV tasks typically entails performing computations with low latency, which is a tricky problem for ViT models.Model quantization is a widely-used technique to optimize the hardware efficiency of deep neural networks.Full quantization under Sub-8-bit precision, in particular, is a promising solution to reduce inference latency significantly. Unfortunately, current commodity hardware, such as CPUs and GPUs, still struggles to efficiently execute these sub-8-bit quantized networks, as their SIMD instructions only support a granularity of 8 bits or wider.Also, there is a scarcity of literature that presents a full quantization paradigm for ViTs.In this paper, we propose an activation-aware fully sub-8-bit quantization-aware training (QAT) framework called PackQViT for efficient yet accurate ViT acceleration on mobile devices to facilitate real-time AI-powered decision-making.Specifically, in revisiting data activation within the ViT dataflow, two characteristics are relevant to quantization strategy and precision: the long-tailed distribution and systematic channel-wise outliers.In response, we employ either log2 quantization or clipping to address the long-tailed distribution and incorporate outlier-aware training for residual link quantization to regulate the various channel-wise outliers more consistently.Notably, due to the systematic fixed pattern, outlier-aware training approach can predict the channel indices and regularized scales of outliers in advance, thus avoiding the runtime data-adaptive selection during inference.Furthermore, we employ Int-$2^{n}$-Softmax, Int-LayerNorm, and Integer GELU to enable integer-only computation flow. Finally, we develop a SIMD-based 4-bit packed multiplier to achieve end-to-end ViT acceleration on mobile phones.Compared to prior studies on ViT quantization using 8-bit precision, PackQViT surpasses other works by an improved accuracy ranging from 0.4\% to 17.9\% for various widely used ViTs on ImageNet dataset; under 4-bit precision, PackQViT demonstrates 0.4%$\sim$2.8% higher accuracy. Compared to the baseline multiplier, our implementations on the Realme GT Android smartphone with Snapdragon 870 SoC CPU achieve 2.6x$\sim$3.7x speedup under 8-bit scenario and 3.8x$\sim$5.9x speedup under 4-bit which ensures practical real-time performance.

paragraphs: Reducing numerical precision can make vision Transformers smaller and faster, but sub-8-bit values do not automatically produce faster execution. Commodity processors commonly offer SIMD instructions operating at eight bits or wider. PackQViT addresses both the model's sensitivity to quantization and the hardware challenge of executing low-precision operations efficiently.

Its quantization-aware training handles long-tailed activations with log2 quantization or clipping and regulates recurring channel-wise outliers in residual connections. Because those outliers have systematic patterns, their channels and regularized scales can be anticipated without runtime adaptive selection. Integer implementations of Softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU support an integer-only computation flow, while a packed 4-bit multiplier targets mobile acceleration.

On ImageNet, the authors report accuracy improvements over prior quantization work of 0.4%–17.9% at eight-bit precision and 0.4%–2.8% at four-bit precision. On a Realme GT phone with a Snapdragon 870 CPU, multiplier comparisons show speedups of 2.6–3.7 times and 3.8–5.9 times in the respective precision settings. These findings demonstrate benefits from coordinating quantization-aware modeling with concrete execution support.
summary.tldr: PackQViT combines activation-aware quantization training, integer operations, and packed multiplication to accelerate vision Transformers on mobile hardware.

title: PackQViT: Faster Sub-8-bit Vision Transformers via Full and Packed Quantization on the Mobile

abstract: Scaling laws have been recently employed to derive compute-optimal model size (number of parameters) for a given compute duration. We advance and refine such methods to infer compute-optimal model shapes, such as width and depth, and successfully implement this in vision transformers. Our shape-optimized vision transformer, SoViT, achieves results competitive with models that exceed twice its size, despite being pre-trained with an equivalent amount of compute. For example, SoViT-400m/14 achieves 90.3% fine-tuning accuracy on ILSRCV2012, surpassing the much larger ViT-g/14 and approaching ViT-G/14 under identical settings, with also less than half the inference cost. We conduct a thorough evaluation across multiple tasks, such as image classification, captioning, VQA and zero-shot transfer, demonstrating the effectiveness of our model across a broad range of domains and identifying limitations. Overall, our findings challenge the prevailing approach of blindly scaling up vision models and pave a path for a more informed scaling.

paragraphs: Choosing a model for a fixed training budget involves more than deciding how many parameters it should have. This paper extends scaling-law methods to choose model shape, including width and depth. The authors apply this approach to vision transformers, producing a shape-optimized model called SoViT.

The resulting model competes with models containing more than twice as many parameters despite using an equivalent pretraining compute budget. In the highlighted example, SoViT-400m/14 reaches 90.3% fine-tuning accuracy on ILSRCV2012. The central finding is that increasing parameter count alone is an incomplete strategy for scaling vision models: selecting how capacity is distributed across the architecture can improve the relationship between training resources, model size, and inference cost.
summary.tldr: Scaling laws that optimize transformer width and depth produce SoViT models competitive with much larger models at lower inference cost.

title: Getting ViT in Shape: Scaling Laws for Compute-Optimal Model Design

abstract: Whole-body pose and shape estimation aims to jointly predict different behaviors (e.g., pose, hand gesture, facial expression) of the entire human body from a monocular image. Existing methods often exhibit suboptimal performance due to the complexity of in-the-wild scenarios. We argue that the prediction accuracy of these models is significantly affected by the quality of the _bounding box_, e.g., scale, alignment. The natural discrepancy between the ideal bounding box annotations and model detection results is particularly detrimental to the performance of whole-body pose and shape estimation.In this paper, we propose a novel framework to enhance the robustness of whole-body pose and shape estimation. Our framework incorporates three new modules to address the above challenges from three perspectives: (1) a **Localization Module** enhances the model's awareness of the subject's location and semantics within the image space; (2) a **Contrastive Feature Extraction Module** encourages the model to be invariant to robust augmentations by incorporating a contrastive loss and positive samples; (3) a **Pixel Alignment Module** ensures the reprojected mesh from the predicted camera and body model parameters are more accurate and pixel-aligned. We perform comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework on body, hands, face and whole-body benchmarks.

paragraphs: Whole-body pose and shape estimation predicts body posture, hand gestures, and facial expression from a single image. The paper focuses on a source of error in realistic scenes: the bounding box around the person. Its scale and alignment can strongly affect predictions, especially when detector outputs differ from ideal annotated boxes.

The proposed framework addresses this sensitivity with three modules. Localization improves awareness of the subject's position and semantic information within the image. Contrastive feature extraction uses positive samples and a contrastive loss to encourage invariance to augmentations. Pixel alignment improves how the predicted body mesh, projected using the predicted camera, lines up with the image.

These components address subject localization, feature stability, and geometric alignment as complementary parts of the estimation problem. Experiments across body, hand, face, and whole-body benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The approach matters because it explicitly accounts for the imperfect image regions supplied to the estimator, connecting robustness to detection differences with the accuracy of detailed whole-body predictions.
summary.tldr: Three complementary modules improve whole-body pose estimation by addressing localization, augmentation invariance, and image alignment under imperfect bounding boxes.

title: Towards Robust and Expressive Whole-body Human Pose and Shape Estimation

abstract: To improve the robustness of deep classifiers against adversarial perturbations, many approaches have been proposed, such as designing new architectures with better robustness properties (e.g., Lipschitz-capped networks), or modifying the training process itself (e.g., min-max optimization, constrained learning, or regularization). These approaches, however, might not be effective at increasing the margin in the input (feature) space. In this paper, we propose a differentiable regularizer that is a lower bound on the distance of the data points to the classification boundary. The proposed regularizer requires knowledge of the model's Lipschitz constant along certain directions. To this end, we develop a scalable method for calculating guaranteed differentiable upper bounds on the Lipschitz constant of neural networks accurately and efficiently. The relative accuracy of the bounds prevents excessive regularization and allows for more direct manipulation of the decision boundary. Furthermore, our Lipschitz bounding algorithm exploits the monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity of the activation layers, and the resulting bounds can be used to design new layers with controllable bounds on their Lipschitz constant. Experiments on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet data sets verify that our proposed algorithm obtains competitively improved results compared to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: A classifier becomes vulnerable when a small input change can cross its decision boundary. Methods intended to improve robustness do not necessarily enlarge the distance between examples and that boundary. This paper targets that distance directly through a differentiable regularizer that provides a lower bound on the input-space margin.

Computing the regularizer requires information about how rapidly the network can change along certain directions, expressed through Lipschitz constants. The authors develop a scalable procedure for obtaining guaranteed, differentiable upper bounds on those constants. Relatively accurate bounds help avoid excessive regularization and make it possible to influence the decision boundary more directly during training.

The bounding procedure uses the monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity of activation layers. Its bounds also support designing layers whose Lipschitz constants can be controlled. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet report competitive improvements relative to state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects a geometric robustness objective with a practical way to calculate the bounds that objective needs.
summary.tldr: A differentiable margin regularizer and improved Lipschitz bounds provide a practical approach to strengthening certified classifier robustness.

title: Certified Robustness via Dynamic Margin Maximization and Improved Lipschitz Regularization

abstract: 3D scene segmentation based on neural implicit representation has emerged recently with the advantage of training only on 2D supervision. However, existing approaches still requires expensive per-scene optimization that prohibits generalization to novel scenes during inference. To circumvent this problem, we introduce a \textit{generalizable} 3D segmentation framework based on implicit representation. Specifically, our framework takes in multi-view image features and semantic maps as the inputs instead of only spatial information to avoid overfitting to scene-specific geometric and semantic information. We propose a novel soft voting mechanism to aggregate the 2D semantic information from different views for each 3D point. In addition to the image features, view difference information is also encoded in our framework to predict the voting scores. Intuitively, this allows the semantic information from nearby views to contribute more compared to distant ones. Furthermore, a visibility module is also designed to detect and filter out detrimental information from occluded views. Due to the generalizability of our proposed method, we can synthesize semantic maps or conduct 3D semantic segmentation for novel scenes with solely 2D semantic supervision. Experimental results show that our approach achieves comparable performance with scene-specific approaches. More importantly, our approach can even outperform existing strong supervision-based approaches with only 2D annotations.

GNeSF addresses this obstacle by building a segmentation framework that can handle new scenes at inference. It conditions its representation on image features and semantic maps from multiple views, rather than relying only on spatial information.

For each 3D point, a soft voting mechanism combines semantic information from different images. Image features and differences between views determine the voting weights, allowing nearby views to contribute more than distant ones. A visibility module detects occluded views and filters out information that could harm the combined prediction.

This design connects 3D predictions to transferable image evidence while accounting for viewpoint and visibility. With only 2D semantic supervision, the framework can produce semantic maps and segment previously unseen 3D scenes. Experiments show performance comparable to methods optimized for individual scenes, and the approach can even outperform existing methods using stronger supervision. These findings support generalizable segmentation without expensive per-scene fitting.
summary.tldr: GNeSF combines semantic evidence across visible camera views to segment new 3D scenes using only 2D supervision.

title: GNeSF: Generalizable Neural Semantic Fields

abstract: While reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable successes in several domains, its real-world application is limited due to many methods failing to generalise to unfamiliar conditions. In this work, we consider the problem of generalising to new transition dynamics, corresponding to cases in which the environment's response to the agent's actions differs. For example, the gravitational force exerted on a robot depends on its mass and changes the robot's mobility. Consequently, in such cases, it is necessary to condition an agent's actions on extrinsic state information and pertinent contextual information reflecting how the environment responds. While the need for context-sensitive policies has been established, the manner in which context is incorporated architecturally has received less attention. Thus, in this work, we present an investigation into how context information should be incorporated into behaviour learning to improve generalisation. To this end, we introduce a neural network architecture, the Decision Adapter, which generates the weights of an adapter module and conditions the behaviour of an agent on the context information. We show that the Decision Adapter is a useful generalisation of a previously proposed architecture and empirically demonstrate that it results in superior generalisation performance compared to previous approaches in several environments. Beyond this, the Decision Adapter is more robust to irrelevant distractor variables than several alternative methods.

The authors introduce the Decision Adapter, a neural architecture that generates the weights of an adapter module from context. This makes context influence the policy through an adjustable component of its computation. The paper investigates this architectural choice and shows that the Decision Adapter generalizes a previously proposed architecture.

Experiments across several environments demonstrate better generalization than previous approaches in the evaluated settings. The method is also more robust to irrelevant contextual distractors than several alternatives. These findings suggest that the way context enters a policy matters, beyond simply making context available: an appropriate adaptive architecture can help behavior respond to meaningful changes in dynamics while reducing sensitivity to unrelated information.
summary.tldr: The Decision Adapter generates context-dependent adapter weights to improve policy generalization to unfamiliar dynamics and robustness to irrelevant context.

title: Dynamics Generalisation in Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Context-Aware Policies

abstract: Per-example gradient clipping is a key algorithmic step that enables practical differential private (DP) training for deep learning models. The choice of clipping threshold $R$, however, is vital for achieving high accuracy under DP. We propose an easy-to-use replacement, called automatic clipping, that eliminates the need to tune $R$ for any DP optimizers, including DP-SGD, DP-Adam, DP-LAMB and many others.The automatic variants are as private and computationally efficient as existing DP optimizers, but require no DP-specific hyperparameters and thus make DP training as amenable as the standard non-private training. We give a rigorous convergence analysis of automatic DP-SGD in the non-convex setting, showing that it can enjoy an asymptotic convergence rate that matches the standard SGD, under a symmetric gradient noise assumption of the per-sample gradients (commonly used in the non-DP literature). We demonstrate on various language and vision tasks that automatic clipping outperforms or matches the state-of-the-art, and can be easily employed with minimal changes to existing codebases.

paragraphs: Differentially private training commonly clips each example’s gradient, limiting its contribution to an update. This paper proposes automatic clipping as a replacement that removes the need to tune that threshold across optimizers including DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-LAMB.

The automatic versions preserve the privacy and computational efficiency of existing private optimizers. The authors describe them as requiring no privacy-specific optimization hyperparameters, making the training procedure easier to use alongside familiar optimization methods. This matters because the contribution addresses a practical source of complexity in applying private learning, rather than merely offering another threshold-selection procedure.

The theoretical analysis covers automatic DP-SGD for nonconvex optimization. Under a symmetric noise assumption on per-example gradients, its asymptotic convergence rate can match ordinary SGD. That condition is essential to interpreting the rate claim. Across the language and vision tasks evaluated, automatic clipping matches or exceeds the reported state of the art. The authors also report that adopting it requires only small changes to existing implementations.
summary.tldr: Automatic clipping removes clipping-threshold tuning from private optimizers while retaining privacy and reporting competitive accuracy.

title: Automatic Clipping: Differentially Private Deep Learning Made Easier and Stronger

abstract: In recent years, significant attention in deep learning theory has been devoted to analyzing when models that interpolate their training data can still generalize well to unseen examples. Many insights have been gained from studying models with multiple layers of Gaussian random features, for which one can compute precise generalization asymptotics. However, few works have considered the effect of weight anisotropy; most assume that the random features are generated using independent and identically distributed Gaussian weights, and allow only for structure in the input data. Here, we use the replica trick from statistical physics to derive learning curves for models with many layers of structured Gaussian features. We show that allowing correlations between the rows of the first layer of features can aid generalization, while structure in later layers is generally detrimental. Our results shed light on how weight structure affects generalization in a simple class of solvable models.

paragraphs: Models can fit their training data exactly and still perform well on unseen examples. To understand this behaviour, researchers study simplified models whose generalisation can be calculated precisely. This paper examines deep models built from Gaussian random features, focusing on how structure in their weights changes the resulting learning curves.

Earlier analyses largely assumed independently and identically distributed Gaussian weights, allowing structure mainly in the input data. The authors relax that weight assumption and consider many layers of structured Gaussian features. They use the replica trick from statistical physics to derive learning curves, making it possible to examine how the location of weight correlations affects generalisation.

The results distinguish the first layer from later ones. Correlations between rows of the first feature layer can help generalisation, whereas structure in subsequent layers is generally harmful in the models studied. This shows that weight structure's effect depends on where it appears. The findings concern a tractable class of random-feature models and provide insight into that setting.
summary.tldr: An analysis of deep Gaussian-feature models finds that first-layer weight correlations can help generalisation, while later-layer structure is generally detrimental.

title: Learning Curves for Deep Structured Gaussian Feature Models

abstract: Partitioning a set of elements into an unknown number of mutually exclusive subsets is essential in many machine learning problems.However, assigning elements, such as samples in a dataset or neurons in a network layer, to an unknown and discrete number of subsets is inherently non-differentiable, prohibiting end-to-end gradient-based optimization of parameters.We overcome this limitation by proposing a novel two-step method for inferring partitions, which allows its usage in variational inference tasks.This new approach enables reparameterized gradients with respect to the parameters of the new random partition model.Our method works by inferring the number of elements per subset and, second, by filling these subsets in a learned order.We highlight the versatility of our general-purpose approach on three different challenging experiments: variational clustering, inference of shared and independent generative factors under weak supervision, and multitask learning.

paragraphs: Many learning problems involve dividing elements into mutually exclusive groups without knowing the number of groups beforehand. The elements might be data samples or neurons in a network layer. Because group assignments and the number of groups are discrete, directly learning such partitions creates an obstacle for end-to-end gradient-based optimization.

This paper introduces a random partition model that separates the decision into two stages. It first infers how many elements belong in each subset, then fills those subsets according to a learned ordering. The construction enables reparameterized gradients with respect to the partition model’s parameters, allowing partition inference to participate in variational inference tasks.

The authors demonstrate the approach in three settings: variational clustering, learning shared and independent generative factors with weak supervision, and multitask learning. These applications illustrate the breadth of a common underlying operation: learning how elements should be grouped as part of a larger model. The contribution is a general-purpose way to make that operation compatible with gradient-based learning, supported by demonstrations across distinct tasks.
summary.tldr: A two-stage random partition model enables gradient-based learning of groupings with an unknown number of subsets.

title: Differentiable Random Partition Models

abstract: Cross-modality registration between 2D images captured by cameras and 3D point clouds from LiDARs is a crucial task in computer vision and robotic. Previous methods estimate 2D-3D correspondences by matching point and pixel patterns learned by neural networks, and use Perspective-n-Points (PnP) to estimate rigid transformation during post-processing. However, these methods struggle to map points and pixels to a shared latent space robustly since points and pixels have very different characteristics with patterns learned in different manners (MLP and CNN), and they also fail to construct supervision directly on the transformation since the PnP is non-differentiable, which leads to unstable registration results. To address these problems, we propose to learn a structured cross-modality latent space to represent pixel features and 3D features via a differentiable probabilistic PnP solver. Specifically, we design a triplet network to learn VoxelPoint-to-Pixel matching, where we represent 3D elements using both voxels and points to learn the cross-modality latent space with pixels. We design both the voxel and pixel branch based on CNNs to operate convolutions on voxels/pixels represented in grids, and integrate an additional point branch to regain the information lost during voxelization. We train our framework end-to-end by imposing supervisions directly on the predicted pose distribution with a probabilistic PnP solver. To explore distinctive patterns of cross-modality features, we design a novel loss with adaptive-weighted optimization for cross-modality feature description. The experimental results on KITTI and nuScenes datasets show significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Aligning camera images with LiDAR point clouds requires identifying corresponding image pixels and three-dimensional locations, then estimating their relative transformation. Existing approaches face two difficulties: pixels and points have very different representations, and a separate, non-differentiable pose-estimation stage prevents direct training supervision on the final transformation.

The proposed method represents the three-dimensional input using both voxels and individual points. Voxel and image branches use convolutional networks on grid-structured inputs, helping connect their representations. An additional point branch recovers information lost when points are grouped into voxels. Together, these three branches learn a shared space for matching three-dimensional elements to image pixels.

A differentiable probabilistic Perspective-n-Points solver lets the system train end to end using supervision on the predicted pose distribution. The authors also introduce an adaptively weighted loss for learning distinctive cross-modality features. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The approach joins representation learning and transformation estimation so that training can directly address the alignment result.
summary.tldr: Combining voxel, point, and pixel features with differentiable pose estimation improves camera–LiDAR alignment in reported experiments.

title: Differentiable Registration of Images and LiDAR Point Clouds with VoxelPoint-to-Pixel Matching

abstract: In some applications of reinforcement learning, a dataset of pre-collected experience is already availablebut it is also possible to acquire some additional online data to help improve the quality of the policy.However, it may be preferable to gather additional data with a single, non-reactive exploration policyand avoid the engineering costs associated with switching policies. In this paper we propose an algorithm with provable guarantees that can leverage an offline dataset to design a single non-reactive policy for exploration. We theoretically analyze the algorithm and measure the quality of the final policy as a function of the local coverage of the original dataset and the amount of additional data collected.

In this paper we propose an algorithm with provable guarantees that can leverage an offline dataset to design a single non-reactive policy for exploration. We theoretically analyze the algorithm and measure the quality of the final policy as a function of the local coverage of the original dataset and the amount of additional data collected.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning applications begin with recorded experience but also allow additional interaction to improve a policy. Collecting that extra experience can create engineering costs if the system repeatedly switches its exploration policy. This paper studies the option of choosing a single non-reactive exploration policy using the data already available.

The authors propose an algorithm with provable guarantees for designing that exploration policy from an offline dataset. The existing experience therefore informs how further data should be gathered. This connects policy improvement with experimental design: the method uses prior observations to guide an additional collection phase while respecting the preference for one exploration policy.

The theoretical analysis expresses final policy quality in terms of two quantities: the local coverage of the original dataset and the amount of new data collected. This makes the starting dataset’s coverage an explicit part of the guarantee, rather than treating all offline datasets as equally informative. The result provides a formal account of policy improvement under this constrained data-collection arrangement.
summary.tldr: The paper uses offline experience to design one non-reactive exploration policy, with policy-quality guarantees tied to initial coverage and additional data.

title: Policy Finetuning in Reinforcement Learning via Design of Experiments using Offline Data

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks-- subtle, perceptually indistinguishable perturbations of inputs that change the response of the model. In the context of vision, we hypothesize that an important contributor to the robustness of human visual perception is constant exposure to low-fidelity visual stimuli in our peripheral vision. To investigate this hypothesis, we develop RBlur, an image transform that simulates the loss in fidelity of peripheral vision by blurring the image and reducing its color saturation based on the distance from a given fixation point. We show that compared to DNNs trained on the original images, DNNs trained on images transformed by RBlur are substantially more robust to adversarial attacks, as well as other, non-adversarial, corruptions, achieving up to 25% higher accuracy on perturbed data.

The authors test a related training intervention for neural networks, which can change their predictions in response to visually subtle adversarial perturbations.

They introduce RBlur, an image transformation based on distance from a fixation point. Areas farther from that point are blurred and have their color saturation reduced, simulating the loss of visual fidelity in peripheral vision. Neural networks are then trained using these transformed images, making this variation in image quality part of their learning experience.

Compared with networks trained on the original images, RBlur-trained networks show substantially greater robustness to both adversarial attacks and ordinary image corruptions. The paper reports up to 25% higher accuracy on perturbed data. These experiments support the proposed transformation as a robustness intervention; the human-vision explanation remains the motivating hypothesis rather than an established result about human perception.
summary.tldr: Training on images blurred and desaturated away from a fixation point improves reported robustness to adversarial and ordinary corruptions.

title: Training on Foveated Images Improves Robustness to Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Due to the heterogeneous architectures and class skew, the global representation models training in resource-adaptive federated self-supervised learning face with tricky challenges: $\textit{deviated representation abilities}$ and $\textit{inconsistent representation spaces}$. In this work, we are the first to propose a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework, namely $\textit{FedMKD}$, to learn global representations with whole class knowledge from heterogeneous clients even under extreme class skew. Firstly, the adaptive knowledge integration mechanism is designed to learn better representations from all heterogeneous models with deviated representation abilities. Then the weighted combination of the self-supervised loss and the distillation loss can support the global model to encode all classes from clients into a unified space. Besides, the global knowledge anchored alignment module can make the local representation spaces close to the global spaces, which further improves the representation abilities of local ones. Finally, extensive experiments conducted on two datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of $\textit{FedMKD}$ which outperforms state-of-the-art baselines 4.78\% under linear evaluation on average.

paragraphs: Federated self-supervised learning must combine knowledge from clients whose models and data can differ substantially. Resource constraints lead to different model architectures, while class skew means clients see different mixtures of classes. These differences can produce unequal representation abilities and incompatible representation spaces, complicating the construction of a useful global model.

FedMKD treats the heterogeneous client models as multiple teachers. An adaptive integration mechanism combines their knowledge despite differences in representation quality. A weighted combination of self-supervised and distillation losses helps the global model encode knowledge about all client classes in one shared space, including under extreme class skew.

The method also uses global knowledge to align local representation spaces with the global space, improving local representations as well as the shared model. Experiments on two datasets report an average 4.78% advantage over state-of-the-art baselines under linear evaluation. The stated findings support combining adaptive knowledge transfer with representation alignment to address both uneven client capabilities and fragmented class knowledge.
summary.tldr: FedMKD combines knowledge from heterogeneous federated clients and aligns their representations, reporting improved linear evaluation even under extreme class skew.

title: Resource-Aware Federated Self-Supervised Learning with Global Class Representations

abstract: Due to the lack of state dimension optimization methods, deep state space models (SSMs) have sacrificed model capacity, training search space, or stability to alleviate computational costs caused by high state dimensions. In this work, we provide a structured pruning method for SSMs, Layer-Adaptive STate pruning (LAST), which reduces the state dimension of each layer in minimizing model-level output energy loss by extending modal truncation for a single system. LAST scores are evaluated using the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ norms of subsystems and layer-wise energy normalization. The scores serve as global pruning criteria, enabling cross-layer comparison of states and layer-adaptive pruning. Across various sequence benchmarks, LAST optimizes previous SSMs, revealing the redundancy and compressibility of their state spaces. Notably, we demonstrate that, on average, pruning 33\% of states still maintains performance with 0.52\% accuracy loss in multi-input multi-output SSMs without retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/msgwak/LAST.

paragraphs: Deep state space models can incur substantial computational costs when their internal states have many dimensions. Reducing those dimensions has involved compromises in model capacity, training search space, or stability. LAST introduces structured pruning that chooses how much state to remove separately for each layer.

The method extends modal truncation from an individual system to a deep model, aiming to minimize loss of output energy across the model. It scores states using subsystem H-infinity norms together with layer-wise energy normalization. Normalization makes scores comparable across layers, allowing a global pruning criterion to decide which states to remove and where to preserve more capacity.

Across several sequence benchmarks, LAST improves the efficiency of existing state space models and reveals redundancy in their state representations. For multi-input multi-output models, the authors report pruning 33% of states on average without retraining, with an average accuracy loss of 0.52%. The result demonstrates useful compression in the tested models while quantifying the associated performance change.
summary.tldr: LAST compares state importance across layers, pruning 33% of states on average in tested multi-input multi-output SSMs with 0.52% accuracy loss and no retraining.

title: Layer-Adaptive State Pruning for Deep State Space Models

abstract: Sparsity is a central aspect of interpretability in machine learning. Typically, sparsity is measured in terms of the size of a model globally, such as the number of variables it uses. However, this notion of sparsity is not particularly relevant for decision making; someone subjected to a decision does not care about variables that do not contribute to the decision. In this work, we dramatically expand a notion of *decision sparsity* called the *Sparse Explanation Value* (SEV) so that its explanations are more meaningful. SEV considers movement along a hypercube towards a reference point. By allowing flexibility in that reference and by considering how distances along the hypercube translate to distances in feature space, we can derive sparser and more meaningful explanations for various types of function classes. We present cluster-based SEV and its variant tree-based SEV, introduce a method that improves credibility of explanations, and propose algorithms that optimize decision sparsity in machine learning models.

paragraphs: A model can use many variables overall while an individual decision depends on a much smaller set. This paper focuses on that decision-level view of sparsity, motivated by the information relevant to someone receiving a particular outcome. It expands the Sparse Explanation Value, or SEV, to make such explanations more meaningful.

The authors introduce flexibility in choosing that reference and account for how movement on the hypercube translates into distances in feature space. The stated contribution spans multiple types of function classes. Its practical focus is on improving the explanations attached to particular decisions, rather than relying only on the total number of variables used anywhere in a model.
summary.tldr: The paper extends Sparse Explanation Value with flexible references and feature-space distances to produce sparser, more meaningful decision explanations.

title: Improving Decision Sparsity

abstract: Molecular representation learning has shown great success in advancing AI-based drug discovery. A key insight of many recent works is that the 3D geometric structure of molecules provides essential information about their physicochemical properties. Recently, denoising diffusion probabilistic models have achieved impressive performance in molecular 3D conformation generation. However, most existing molecular diffusion models treat each atom as an independent entity, overlooking the dependency among atoms within the substructures. This paper introduces a novel approach that enhances molecular representation learning by incorporating substructural information in the diffusion model framework. We propose a novel diffusion model termed SubgDiff for involving the molecular subgraph information in diffusion. Specifically, SubgDiff adopts three vital techniques: i) subgraph prediction, ii) expectation state, and iii) k-step same subgraph diffusion, to enhance the perception of molecular substructure in the denoising network. Experiments on extensive downstream tasks, especially the molecular force predictions, demonstrate the superior performance of our approach.

The findings support incorporating dependencies among atoms within substructures as a way to improve representations for subsequent molecular prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: SubgDiff incorporates molecular subgraphs into diffusion training to improve molecular representations, with particularly strong reported results for force prediction.

title: SubgDiff: A Subgraph Diffusion Model to Improve Molecular Representation Learning

abstract: Advanced diffusion models (DMs) perform impressively in image super-resolution (SR), but the high memory and computational costs hinder their deployment. Binarization, an ultra-compression algorithm, offers the potential for effectively accelerating DMs. Nonetheless, due to the model structure and the multi-step iterative attribute of DMs, existing binarization methods result in significant performance degradation. In this paper, we introduce a novel binarized diffusion model, BI-DiffSR, for image SR. First, for the model structure, we design a UNet architecture optimized for binarization. We propose the consistent-pixel-downsample (CP-Down) and consistent-pixel-upsample (CP-Up) to maintain dimension consistent and facilitate the full-precision information transfer. Meanwhile, we design the channel-shuffle-fusion (CS-Fusion) to enhance feature fusion in skip connection. Second, for the activation difference across timestep, we design the timestep-aware redistribution (TaR) and activation function (TaA). The TaR and TaA dynamically adjust the distribution of activations based on different timesteps, improving the flexibility and representation alability of the binarized module. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our BI-DiffSR outperforms existing binarization methods. Code is released at: https://github.com/zhengchen1999/BI-DiffSR.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce impressive image super-resolution results, but their memory and computational demands make deployment difficult. Binarization offers aggressive compression, yet applying existing methods to diffusion models substantially reduces performance. This paper addresses two sources of that difficulty: the network architecture and the changing behavior of its activations across diffusion steps.

BI-DiffSR uses a UNet designed specifically for binarization. Its downsampling and upsampling components maintain dimensional consistency and help transfer full-precision information. A separate channel-shuffling fusion component improves how features combine through skip connections. These changes adapt the paths through which information moves, rather than treating compression as an isolated replacement of numerical representations.

The method also introduces timestep-aware redistribution and activation functions. These adjust activation distributions at different diffusion steps, giving the binarized components more flexibility as the generation process evolves. Experiments show that BI-DiffSR outperforms existing binarization approaches. The stated result supports designing compression around both the architecture and the iterative behavior of diffusion models, rather than assuming that one fixed treatment works equally well throughout generation.
summary.tldr: BI-DiffSR improves binarized image super-resolution by adapting both the network architecture and activation handling to diffusion models.

title: Binarized Diffusion Model for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the growth rate of $H$-consistency bounds (and excess error bounds) for various surrogate losses used in classification. We prove a square-root growth rate near zero for smooth margin-based surrogate losses in binary classification, providing both upper and lower bounds under mild assumptions. This result also translates to excess error bounds. Our lower bound requires weaker conditions than those in previous work for excess error bounds, and our upper bound is entirely novel. Moreover, we extend this analysis to multi-class classification with a series of novel results, demonstrating a universal square-root growth rate for smooth *comp-sum* and *constrained losses*, covering common choices for training neural networks in multi-class classification. Given this universal rate, we turn to the question of choosing among different surrogate losses. We first examine how $H$-consistency bounds vary across surrogates based on the number of classes. Next, ignoring constants and focusing on behavior near zero, we identify *minimizability gaps* as the key differentiating factor in these bounds. Thus, we thoroughly analyze these gaps, to guide surrogate loss selection, covering: comparisons across different comp-sum losses, conditions where gaps become zero, and general conditions leading to small gaps. Additionally, we demonstrate the key role of minimizability gaps in comparing excess error bounds and $H$-consistency bounds.

paragraphs: Classification models often train with a smooth substitute for the error measure they ultimately care about. This paper studies mathematical bounds connecting progress on that substitute loss to progress on classification error. Its focus includes H-consistency bounds, which account for the particular family of predictors available to the learner.

For binary classification, the authors establish matching upper and lower square-root growth rates near zero for smooth margin-based losses, under mild assumptions. They also connect this result to excess error bounds. For multiclass classification, they establish the same type of rate for smooth comp-sum and constrained losses, including common neural-network training choices.

Sharing a growth rate does not make all these losses interchangeable. The paper examines how bounds depend on class count and, when constants are ignored near zero, identifies minimizability gaps as a key distinction. Its comparisons and conditions for zero or small gaps offer a theoretical basis for choosing among losses whose leading growth behavior looks similar.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes square-root error-bound growth for several smooth classification losses and identifies minimizability gaps as a key factor distinguishing them.

title: A Universal Growth Rate for Learning with Smooth Surrogate Losses

abstract: The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) viewpoint is widely employed to analyze the training dynamics of overparameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). However, unlike the case of linear Partial Differential Equations (PDEs), we show how the NTK perspective falls short in the nonlinear scenario. Specifically, we establish that the NTK yields a random matrix at initialization that is not constant during training, contrary to conventional belief. Another significant difference from the linear regime is that, even in the idealistic infinite-width limit, the Hessian does not vanish and hence it cannot be disregarded during training. This motivates the adoption of second-order optimization methods. We explore the convergence guarantees of such methods in both linear and nonlinear cases, addressing challenges such as spectral bias and slow convergence. Every theoretical result is supported by numerical examples with both linear and nonlinear PDEs, and we highlight the benefits of second-order methods in benchmark test cases.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions while incorporating differential-equation constraints. Their training is often analyzed through the neural tangent kernel, which describes aspects of how parameter changes affect outputs. This paper shows that familiar conclusions from linear differential equations do not carry over to nonlinear equations, even for extremely wide networks.

In the nonlinear setting, the authors establish that the kernel is random at initialization and changes during training. They also show that the Hessian does not vanish in the infinite-width limit. Consequently, curvature cannot simply be ignored in the training analysis. These findings motivate studying second-order optimization methods that account for that curvature.

The paper examines convergence guarantees for such methods in both linear and nonlinear cases, including issues of spectral bias and slow convergence. Numerical examples support each theoretical result, and benchmark cases demonstrate benefits from second-order methods. The contribution both revises the theoretical picture of nonlinear physics-informed training and connects that revised picture to a promising choice of optimization method.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear physics-informed networks retain changing kernels and nonvanishing curvature even at infinite width, motivating second-order optimization.

title: The Challenges of the Nonlinear Regime for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Recent advancements in text-to-image diffusion models have enabled the personalization of these models to generate custom images from textual prompts. This paper presents an efficient LoRA-based personalization approach for on-device subject-driven generation, where pre-trained diffusion models are fine-tuned with user-specific data on resource-constrained devices. Our method, termed Hollowed Net, enhances memory efficiency during fine-tuning by modifying the architecture of a diffusion U-Net to temporarily remove a fraction of its deep layers, creating a hollowed structure. This approach directly addresses on-device memory constraints and substantially reduces GPU memory requirements for training, in contrast to previous methods that primarily focus on minimizing training steps and reducing the number of parameters to update. Additionally, the personalized Hollowed Net can be transferred back into the original U-Net, enabling inference without additional memory overhead. Quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate that our approach not only reduces training memory to levels as low as those required for inference but also maintains or improves personalization performance compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Personalizing a text-to-image model requires adapting it to user-specific data so that it can generate images of a particular subject. On devices with limited resources, the memory required for this training can be a major obstacle. Hollowed Net addresses that memory requirement within a LoRA-based personalization approach.

During fine-tuning, the method temporarily removes some deep layers from the diffusion model’s U-Net, creating a smaller training structure. This directly changes the architecture used during personalization, complementing approaches that focus on reducing training steps or the number of updated parameters. After training, the personalized components can be transferred back into the original U-Net for image generation without additional inference memory overhead.

Quantitative and qualitative analyses show that training memory can fall to levels as low as those needed for inference, while personalization quality is maintained or improved relative to existing methods. The findings indicate that temporarily simplifying the training architecture can make subject-specific adaptation more practical on memory-constrained devices.
summary.tldr: Hollowed Net temporarily removes deep diffusion-model layers during personalization to reduce training memory while preserving or improving quality.

title: Hollowed Net for On-Device Personalization of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

abstract: The recent introduction of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) has demonstrated exceptional capabilities in image generation by using a different backbone architecture, departing from traditional U-Nets and embracing the scalable nature of transformers. Despite their advanced capabilities, the wide deployment of DiTs, particularly for real-time applications, is currently hampered by considerable computational demands at the inference stage. Post-training Quantization (PTQ) has emerged as a fast and data-efficient solution that can significantly reduce computation and memory footprint by using low-bit weights and activations. However, its applicability to DiTs has not yet been explored and faces non-trivial difficulties due to the unique design of DiTs. In this paper, we propose PTQ4DiT, a specifically designed PTQ method for DiTs. We discover two primary quantization challenges inherent in DiTs, notably the presence of salient channels with extreme magnitudes and the temporal variability in distributions of salient activation over multiple timesteps. To tackle these challenges, we propose Channel-wise Salience Balancing (CSB) and Spearmen's $\rho$-guided Salience Calibration (SSC). CSB leverages the complementarity property of channel magnitudes to redistribute the extremes, alleviating quantization errors for both activations and weights. SSC extends this approach by dynamically adjusting the balanced salience to capture the temporal variations in activation. Additionally, to eliminate extra computational costs caused by PTQ4DiT during inference, we design an offline re-parameterization strategy for DiTs. Experiments demonstrate that our PTQ4DiT successfully quantizes DiTs to 8-bit precision (W8A8) while preserving comparable generation ability and further enables effective quantization to 4-bit weight precision (W4A8) for the first time.
