paragraphs: Deep-network training can spend much of its computation on examples the model already handles well. This paper proposes importance sampling to focus training effort on more informative examples and reduce the variance of stochastic gradients. The aim is to make better progress within a given amount of computation.

The method has two main ingredients. A tractable upper bound on each example’s gradient norm helps support the sampling scheme. An estimator of the variance reduction determines when enabling importance sampling will produce an actual speedup. This second ingredient matters because selecting examples has its own cost, so variance reduction must translate into a computational benefit.

The scheme requires only a few changes to standard stochastic gradient descent. Experiments cover image classification, convolutional-network fine-tuning, and recurrent-network training. Under fixed wall-clock budgets, the authors report training-loss reductions of up to an order of magnitude and relative test-error improvements between 5% and 17%. These are empirical gains for the evaluated training settings.
summary.tldr: An importance-sampling scheme estimates when focusing on informative examples will speed training and reports improved results under fixed time budgets.

title: Not All Samples Are Created Equal: Deep Learning with Importance Sampling

abstract: Spectral clustering is a widely studied problem, yet its complexity is prohibitive for dynamic graphs of even modest size. We claim that it is possible to reuse information of past cluster assignments to expedite computation. Our approach builds on a recent idea of sidestepping the main bottleneck of spectral clustering, i.e., computing the graph eigenvectors, by a polynomial-based randomized sketching technique. We show that the proposed algorithm achieves clustering assignments with quality approximating that of spectral clustering and that it can yield significant complexity benefits when the graph dynamics are appropriately bounded. In our experiments, our method clusters 30k node graphs 3.9$\times$ faster in average and deviates from the correct assignment by less than 0.1%.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering can be computationally expensive when a network changes over time, because repeated clustering repeatedly encounters the cost of computing graph eigenvectors. This paper asks how information from earlier cluster assignments can make subsequent clustering faster. The aim is to exploit continuity between successive network states while retaining assignments close in quality to spectral clustering.

The method builds on polynomial-based randomized sketching, which avoids directly computing the eigenvectors that form the main bottleneck. It combines this approach with reuse of information from past assignments. The analysis shows approximate spectral-clustering quality and potential reductions in computational complexity when the graph’s dynamics are appropriately bounded. The benefit therefore has an explicit connection to how the network changes.

In experiments on graphs with 30,000 nodes, the method is 3.9 times faster on average and differs from the correct assignment by less than 0.1%. These results illustrate the practical value of the approach in the tested setting. The broader contribution is a strategy for updating clusters using both a cheaper spectral approximation and information already obtained from earlier network states.
summary.tldr: Reusing past assignments with randomized spectral sketches accelerates dynamic graph clustering when graph changes are suitably bounded.

title: Fast Approximate Spectral Clustering for Dynamic Networks

abstract: Recent work has sought to understand the behavior of neural networks by comparing representations between layers and between different trained models. We examine methods for comparing neural network representations based on canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We show that CCA belongs to a family of statistics for measuring multivariate similarity, but that neither CCA nor any other statistic that is invariant to invertible linear transformation can measure meaningful similarities between representations of higher dimension than the number of data points. We introduce a similarity index that measures the relationship between representational similarity matrices and does not suffer from this limitation. This similarity index is equivalent to centered kernel alignment (CKA) and is also closely connected to CCA. Unlike CCA, CKA can reliably identify correspondences between representations in networks trained from different initializations.

paragraphs: Comparing internal representations can help explain how layers or independently trained networks relate to one another. This paper examines comparison methods based on canonical correlation analysis, or CCA. It identifies a fundamental problem with a broader family of similarity statistics that remain unchanged under arbitrary invertible linear transformations.

When representation dimension exceeds the number of data points, the authors show that no statistic with that invariance can measure meaningful similarities between the representations. This makes the choice of invariance consequential: ignoring certain transformations can also remove distinctions needed for a useful comparison in that dimensional regime.

The authors introduce an index based on relationships between representational similarity matrices. It is equivalent to centered kernel alignment, or CKA, and closely related to CCA, but avoids the identified limitation. They report that CKA reliably identifies corresponding representations in networks trained from different initializations, unlike CCA. The contribution combines an explanation of when a familiar comparison principle fails with an alternative that supports meaningful comparisons in the investigated setting.
summary.tldr: CKA avoids a high-dimensional limitation of CCA-based similarity measures and identifies corresponding representations across differently initialized networks.

title: Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited

abstract: Large-scale datasets may contain significant proportions of noisy (incorrect) class labels, and it is well-known that modern deep neural networks (DNNs) poorly generalize from such noisy training datasets. To mitigate the issue, we propose a novel inference method, termed Robust Generative classifier (RoG), applicable to any discriminative (e.g., softmax) neural classifier pre-trained on noisy datasets. In particular, we induce a generative classifier on top of hidden feature spaces of the pre-trained DNNs, for obtaining a more robust decision boundary. By estimating the parameters of generative classifier using the minimum covariance determinant estimator, we significantly improve the classification accuracy with neither re-training of the deep model nor changing its architectures. With the assumption of Gaussian distribution for features, we prove that RoG generalizes better than baselines under noisy labels. Finally, we propose the ensemble version of RoG to improve its performance by investigating the layer-wise characteristics of DNNs. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate the superiority of RoG given different learning models optimized by several training techniques to handle diverse scenarios of noisy labels.

paragraphs: RoG addresses classification when a neural network has already been trained on data containing incorrect labels. The method changes how predictions are made using the network’s hidden features. It is designed to apply to any pretrained discriminative neural classifier, allowing improvements without retraining the deep model or changing its architecture.

The authors construct a generative classifier on top of the hidden feature spaces and estimate its parameters using the minimum covariance determinant estimator. This robust estimation step is intended to produce a decision boundary less affected by noisy labels. Under a Gaussian assumption for the features, they prove better generalization than the baselines considered.

The paper also develops an ensemble version that draws on the differing characteristics of features at different network layers. Extensive experiments report improved classification across learning models, training techniques, and noisy-label scenarios. The practical contribution is an inference-stage way to improve an existing model, supported by experiments and a theoretical result whose guarantee depends on the stated feature-distribution assumption.
summary.tldr: RoG adds a robust generative classifier to pretrained neural features to improve noisy-label classification without retraining the deep network.

title: Robust Inference via Generative Classifiers for Handling Noisy Labels

abstract: A key problem in multi-label classification is to utilize dependencies among the labels. Chaining classifiers are a simple technique for addressing this problem but current algorithms all assume a fixed, static label ordering. In this work, we propose a multi-label classification approach which allows to choose a dynamic, context-dependent label ordering. Our proposed approach consists of two sub-components: a simple EM-like algorithm which bootstraps the learned model, and a more elaborate approach based on reinforcement learning. Our experiments on three public multi-label classification benchmarks show that our proposed dynamic label ordering approach based on reinforcement learning outperforms recurrent neural networks with fixed label ordering across both bipartition and ranking measures on all the three datasets. As a result, we obtain a powerful sequence prediction-based algorithm for multi-label classification, which is able to efficiently and explicitly exploit label dependencies.

Chaining classifiers are a simple technique for addressing this problem but current algorithms all assume a fixed, static label ordering. In this work, we propose a multi-label classification approach which allows to choose a dynamic, context-dependent label ordering. Our proposed approach consists of two sub-components: a simple EM-like algorithm which bootstraps the learned model, and a more elaborate approach based on reinforcement learning. Our experiments on three public multi-label classification benchmarks show that our proposed dynamic label ordering approach based on reinforcement learning outperforms recurrent neural networks with fixed label ordering across both bipartition and ranking measures on all the three datasets. As a result, we obtain a powerful sequence prediction-based algorithm for multi-label classification, which is able to efficiently and explicitly exploit label dependencies.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification assigns several labels to the same example, so relationships among labels can be useful for prediction. Classifier chains exploit those relationships by predicting labels in sequence. The paper questions the use of one fixed sequence for every context and proposes choosing the label ordering dynamically as part of the prediction approach.

The method has two components. A simple algorithm resembling expectation-maximization bootstraps the learned model, while a more elaborate reinforcement-learning approach learns context-dependent ordering. This makes the sequence itself part of the learning problem. The intended benefit is to exploit label dependencies explicitly without requiring the same order to work equally well for all contexts.

On three public benchmarks, the reinforcement-learning version outperforms recurrent neural networks that use fixed label orderings. The improvements occur on all three datasets for both bipartition measures, which assess label decisions, and ranking measures, which assess label ordering quality. These results support dynamic ordering as a useful ingredient in sequence-based multi-label classification within the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Learning context-dependent label orderings improves sequence-based multi-label classification over fixed-order recurrent models on three benchmarks.

title: Learning Context-dependent Label Permutations for Multi-label Classification

abstract: In this work we develop a novel Bayesian neural network methodology to achieve strong adversarial robustness without the need for online adversarial training. Unlike previous efforts in this direction, we do not rely solely on the stochasticity of network weights by minimizing the divergence between the learned parameter distribution and a prior. Instead, we additionally require that the model maintain some expected uncertainty with respect to all input covariates. We demonstrate that by encouraging the network to distribute evenly across inputs, the network becomes less susceptible to localized, brittle features which imparts a natural robustness to targeted perturbations. We show empirical robustness on several benchmark datasets.
originalAbstract: In this work we develop a novel Bayesian neural network methodology to achieve strong adversarial robustness without the need for online adversarial training. Unlike previous efforts in this direction, we do not rely solely on the stochasticity of network weights by minimizing the divergence between the learned parameter distribution and a prior. Instead, we additionally require that the model maintain some expected uncertainty with respect to all input covariates. We demonstrate that by encouraging the network to distribute evenly across inputs, the network becomes less susceptible to localized, brittle features which imparts a natural robustness to targeted perturbations. We show empirical robustness on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian neural network approach to adversarial robustness without requiring online adversarial training. The motivation is that randomness in network weights alone does not fully address how a model depends on its inputs. A network can still rely on localized, brittle features that make targeted perturbations effective.

The method supplements learning a distribution over parameters with a requirement to retain some expected uncertainty with respect to every input covariate. This goes beyond minimizing the divergence between the learned parameter distribution and a prior. The additional requirement encourages the network to distribute its dependence more evenly across inputs, reducing concentration on particularly fragile features.

The authors demonstrate that this encouragement makes the network less susceptible to localized features and gives it resistance to targeted perturbations. They report empirical robustness across several benchmark datasets. The contribution is therefore a training methodology that connects Bayesian uncertainty with how broadly a model uses input information, supported by experimental findings rather than a stated universal robustness guarantee.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian training method encourages uncertainty across inputs and shows empirical adversarial robustness without online adversarial training.

title: Defense Through Diverse Directions

abstract: Differentiable architecture search (DARTS) is a prevailing NAS solution to identify architectures. Based on the continuous relaxation of the architecture space, DARTS learns a differentiable architecture weight and largely reduces the search cost. However, its stability has been challenged for yielding deteriorating architectures as the search proceeds. We find that the precipitous validation loss landscape, which leads to a dramatic performance drop when distilling the final architecture, is an essential factor that causes instability. Based on this observation, we propose a perturbation-based regularization - SmoothDARTS (SDARTS), to smooth the loss landscape and improve the generalizability of DARTS-based methods. In particular, our new formulations stabilize DARTS-based methods by either random smoothing or adversarial attack. The search trajectory on NAS-Bench-1Shot1 demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach and due to the improved stability, we achieve performance gain across various search spaces on 4 datasets. Furthermore, we mathematically show that SDARTS implicitly regularizes the Hessian norm of the validation loss, which accounts for a smoother loss landscape and improved performance.

title: Stabilizing Differentiable Architecture Search via Perturbation-based Regularization

abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) demonstrate promising success in improving the robustness and uncertainty quantification of modern deep learning. However, they generally struggle with underfitting at scale and parameter efficiency. On the other hand, deep ensembles have emerged as alternatives for uncertainty quantification that, while outperforming BNNs on certain problems, also suffer from efficiency issues. It remains unclear how to combine the strengths of these two approaches and remediate their common issues. To tackle this challenge, we propose a rank-1 parameterization of BNNs, where each weight matrix involves only a distribution on a rank-1 subspace. We also revisit the use of mixture approximate posteriors to capture multiple modes, where unlike typical mixtures, this approach admits a significantly smaller memory increase (e.g., only a 0.4% increase for a ResNet-50 mixture of size 10). We perform a systematic empirical study on the choices of prior, variational posterior, and methods to improve training. For ResNet-50 on ImageNet, Wide ResNet 28-10 on CIFAR-10/100, and an RNN on MIMIC-III, rank-1 BNNs achieve state-of-the-art performance across log-likelihood, accuracy, and calibration on the test sets and out-of-distribution variants.

This paper seeks to combine advantages of these approaches through a more economical representation of uncertainty in network weights.

The proposed parameterization places a distribution on a rank-1 subspace associated with each weight matrix. This construction makes mixtures comparatively inexpensive: the abstract reports only a 0.4% memory increase for a ResNet-50 mixture with ten components.

summary.tldr: Rank-1 weight uncertainty and inexpensive posterior mixtures make Bayesian neural networks more scalable while delivering strong reported predictive and calibration results.

title: Efficient and Scalable Bayesian Neural Nets with Rank-1 Factors

abstract: Posterior inference with an intractable likelihood is becoming an increasingly common task in scientific domains which rely on sophisticated computer simulations. Typically, these forward models do not admit tractable densities forcing practitioners to rely on approximations. This work introduces a novel approach to address the intractability of the likelihood and the marginal model. We achieve this by learning a flexible amortized estimator which approximates the likelihood-to-evidence ratio. We demonstrate that the learned ratio estimator can be embedded in \textsc{mcmc} samplers to approximate likelihood-ratios between consecutive states in the Markov chain, allowing us to draw samples from the intractable posterior. Techniques are presented to improve the numerical stability and to measure the quality of an approximation. The accuracy of our approach is demonstrated on a variety of benchmarks against well-established techniques. Scientific applications in physics show its applicability.

paragraphs: Scientific simulators can generate observations even when the probability density of those observations cannot be evaluated tractably. This makes posterior inference difficult: the usual likelihood calculations are unavailable. The paper addresses this problem by learning an approximation to the likelihood-to-evidence ratio, avoiding a requirement to evaluate either of those quantities directly.

The learned estimator is amortized, allowing it to be reused across inference calculations. The authors embed it in Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers, where it approximates likelihood ratios between consecutive chain states. This provides a route to posterior sampling when the simulator’s likelihood is intractable, with the inference depending on the learned ratio approximation.

The work also presents methods for improving numerical stability and assessing approximation quality. Benchmarks against established techniques demonstrate the approach’s accuracy, while physics applications illustrate its scientific use. The key contribution is a reusable bridge between simulation and sampling: estimating the ratios needed by the inference procedure can make posterior inference feasible without a tractable likelihood model.
summary.tldr: A reusable learned likelihood-to-evidence ratio estimator enables approximate MCMC inference for simulators with intractable likelihoods.

title: Likelihood-free MCMC with Amortized Approximate Ratio Estimators

abstract: Disentangled generative models map a latent code vector to a target space, while enforcing that a subset of the learned latent codes are interpretable and associated with distinct properties of the target distribution. Recent advances have been dominated by Variational AutoEncoder (VAE)-based methods, while training disentangled generative adversarial networks (GANs) remains challenging. In this work, we show that the dominant challenges facing disentangled GANs can be mitigated through the use of self-supervision. We make two main contributions: first, we design a novel approach for training disentangled GANs with self-supervision. We propose contrastive regularizer, which is inspired by a natural notion of disentanglement: latent traversal. This achieves higher disentanglement scores than state-of-the-art VAE- and GAN-based approaches. Second, we propose an unsupervised model selection scheme called ModelCentrality, which uses generated synthetic samples to compute the medoid (multi-dimensional generalization of median) of a collection of models. The current common practice of hyper-parameter tuning requires using ground-truths samples, each labelled with known perfect disentangled latent codes. As real datasets are not equipped with such labels, we propose an unsupervised model selection scheme and show that it finds a model close to the best one, for both VAEs and GANs. Combining contrastive regularization with ModelCentrality, we improve upon the state-of-the-art disentanglement scores significantly, without accessing the supervised data.

paragraphs: A disentangled generative model aims to associate different latent variables with distinct, interpretable properties of its outputs. This paper addresses two related challenges: training such models and choosing a good trained model without labels that reveal the true underlying factors. Those labels are often assumed during tuning even though real datasets generally lack them.

For training, the authors introduce a contrastive regularizer inspired by latent traversal, the idea of inspecting how outputs change as latent codes vary. This self-supervised approach produces higher disentanglement scores than the compared VAE and GAN methods. For selection, ModelCentrality uses synthetic samples to identify the medoid of a collection of models, selecting a model that is central within the collection.

The authors report that ModelCentrality finds a model close to the best available one for both VAEs and GANs. Combining it with contrastive regularization significantly improves reported state-of-the-art disentanglement scores without accessing supervised data. The contribution therefore covers both learning useful latent structure and selecting among candidates when ground-truth factor labels are unavailable.
summary.tldr: Contrastive self-supervision and ModelCentrality improve disentangled generative modeling and model selection without ground-truth latent-factor labels.

title: InfoGAN-CR and ModelCentrality: Self-supervised Model Training and Selection for Disentangling GANs

abstract: Variational Bayesian Inference is a popular methodology for approximating posterior distributions over Bayesian neural network weights. Recent work developing this class of methods has explored ever richer parameterizations of the approximate posterior in the hope of improving performance. In contrast, here we share a curious experimental finding that suggests instead restricting the variational distribution to a more compact parameterization. For a variety of deep Bayesian neural networks trained using Gaussian mean-field variational inference, we find that the posterior standard deviations consistently exhibit strong low-rank structure after convergence. This means that by decomposing these variational parameters into a low-rank factorization, we can make our variational approximation more compact without decreasing the models’ performance. Furthermore, we find that such factorized parameterizations improve the signal-to-noise ratio of stochastic gradient estimates of the variational lower bound, resulting in faster convergence.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian inference approximates uncertainty over neural network weights using a manageable probability distribution. Much work makes that distribution richer. This paper investigates a different possibility: whether the parameters of a Gaussian mean-field approximation contain structure that allows a more compact representation.

Across a variety of deep Bayesian networks, the authors observe that posterior standard deviations develop strong low-rank structure after training converges. They use a low-rank factorization to represent these variational parameters with fewer independent quantities. The restriction is therefore motivated by a pattern observed in trained models.

In the reported experiments, the compact parameterization preserves model performance. It also improves the signal-to-noise ratio of stochastic gradients used to optimize the variational lower bound, leading to faster convergence. These findings suggest that a smaller uncertainty parameterization can help both representation efficiency and optimization in the studied networks. The evidence supports exploiting the observed structure, rather than assuming that a more expressive posterior approximation will always perform better.
summary.tldr: Low-rank factorization of posterior standard deviations makes studied Bayesian neural networks more compact while preserving performance and accelerating convergence.

title: The k-tied Normal Distribution: A Compact Parameterization of Gaussian Mean Field Posteriors in Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: Since the introduction of DQN, a vast majority of reinforcement learning research has focused on reinforcement learning with deep neural networks as function approximators. New methods are typically evaluated on a set of environments that have now become standard, such as Atari 2600 games. While these benchmarks help standardize evaluation, their computational cost has the unfortunate side effect of widening the gap between those with ample access to computational resources, and those without. In this work we argue that, despite the community’s emphasis on large-scale environments, the traditional small-scale environments can still yield valuable scientific insights and can help reduce the barriers to entry for underprivileged communities. To substantiate our claims, we empirically revisit the paper which introduced the Rainbow algorithm [Hessel et al., 2018] and present some new insights into the algorithms used by Rainbow.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement-learning research often evaluates new methods on established environments such as Atari games. These benchmarks provide common comparison points, but their computational demands can make participation harder for researchers with limited resources. This paper examines whether smaller, traditional environments can still support useful scientific investigation while lowering those barriers.

The authors revisit the empirical study that introduced Rainbow and investigate the algorithms it uses. Their purpose is to demonstrate that studying familiar methods at a smaller scale can reveal meaningful insights. The paper therefore treats the choice of experimental environment as part of research design, with consequences for both what can be learned and who can participate.

The empirical revisit produces new insights into Rainbow's component algorithms, supporting the argument that small-scale environments remain scientifically valuable. The abstract does not claim that these environments replace every role of larger benchmarks. Its stated contribution is evidence that useful reinforcement-learning research can also be conducted in settings with more accessible computational requirements.
summary.tldr: Revisiting Rainbow shows that small-scale environments can yield useful reinforcement-learning insights while lowering computational barriers.

title: Revisiting Rainbow: Promoting more insightful and inclusive deep reinforcement learning research

abstract: Biological systems understand the world by simultaneously processing high-dimensional inputs from modalities as diverse as vision, audition, touch, proprioception, etc. The perception models used in deep learning on the other hand are designed for individual modalities, often relying on domain-specific assumptions such as the local grid structures exploited by virtually all existing vision models. These priors introduce helpful inductive biases, but also lock models to individual modalities. In this paper we introduce the Perceiver {–} a model that builds upon Transformers and hence makes few architectural assumptions about the relationship between its inputs, but that also scales to hundreds of thousands of inputs, like ConvNets. The model leverages an asymmetric attention mechanism to iteratively distill inputs into a tight latent bottleneck, allowing it to scale to handle very large inputs. We show that this architecture is competitive with or outperforms strong, specialized models on classification tasks across various modalities: images, point clouds, audio, video and video+audio. The Perceiver obtains performance comparable to ResNet-50 and ViT on ImageNet without 2D convolutions by directly attending to 50,000 pixels. It is also competitive in all modalities in AudioSet.

paragraphs: Perception models often rely on assumptions specific to one kind of input, such as the two-dimensional grid structure used by vision systems. These assumptions can help learning but also tie architectures to particular modalities. Perceiver aims to retain the flexibility of transformers while handling inputs containing hundreds of thousands of elements.

Its central mechanism is asymmetric attention that repeatedly distills the input into a compact latent representation. This latent bottleneck provides a way to process very large inputs while making few architectural assumptions about how input elements relate to one another. Iterative attention lets the model build its representation through repeated interaction with the input.

The paper evaluates classification across images, point clouds, audio, video, and combined video and audio. Perceiver matches or exceeds strong specialized models in the reported tasks. On ImageNet, it performs comparably to ResNet-50 and ViT while attending directly to 50,000 pixels without two-dimensional convolutions. It is also competitive across AudioSet modalities, supporting the architecture’s usefulness across different input types.
summary.tldr: Perceiver repeatedly compresses large inputs through asymmetric attention, enabling one flexible architecture to compete across multiple perception modalities.

title: Perceiver: General Perception with Iterative Attention

abstract: Convex optimization with feedback is a framework where a learner relies on iterative queries and feedback to arrive at the minimizer of a convex function. The paradigm has gained significant popularity recently thanks to its scalability in large-scale optimization and machine learning. The repeated interactions, however, expose the learner to privacy risks from eavesdropping adversaries that observe the submitted queries. In this paper, we study how to optimally obfuscate the learner’s queries in convex optimization with first-order feedback, so that their learned optimal value is provably difficult to estimate for the eavesdropping adversary. We consider two formulations of learner privacy: a Bayesian formulation in which the convex function is drawn randomly, and a minimax formulation in which the function is fixed and the adversary’s probability of error is measured with respect to a minimax criterion. We show that, if the learner wants to ensure the probability of the adversary estimating accurately be kept below 1/L, then the overhead in query complexity is additive in L in the minimax formulation, but multiplicative in L in the Bayesian formulation. Compared to existing learner-private sequential learning models with binary feedback, our results apply to the significantly richer family of general convex functions with full-gradient feedback. Our proofs are largely enabled by tools from the theory of Dirichlet processes, as well as more sophisticated lines of analysis aimed at measuring the amount of information leakage under a full-gradient oracle.

Those queries can also reveal information to an eavesdropper. This paper studies how to obscure the query sequence so that the learner’s learned optimum remains difficult for an observer to estimate accurately.

In the minimax formulation, it is fixed and the adversary’s estimation performance is evaluated through a minimax criterion. The proof uses Dirichlet-process tools and information-leakage analysis for full-gradient feedback. The result shows that the chosen privacy formulation materially changes the optimization effort required.
summary.tldr: The query cost of hiding a convex optimizer’s learned optimum scales differently under Bayesian and minimax privacy formulations.

title: Learner-Private Convex Optimization

abstract: Existing reasoning tasks often have an important assumption that the input contents can be always accessed while reasoning, requiring unlimited storage resources and suffering from severe time delay on long sequences. To achieve efficient reasoning on long sequences with limited storage resources, memory augmented neural networks introduce a human-like write-read memory to compress and memorize the long input sequence in one pass, trying to answer subsequent queries only based on the memory. But they have two serious drawbacks: 1) they continually update the memory from current information and inevitably forget the early contents; 2) they do not distinguish what information is important and treat all contents equally. In this paper, we propose the Rehearsal Memory (RM) to enhance long-sequence memorization by self-supervised rehearsal with a history sampler. To alleviate the gradual forgetting of early information, we design self-supervised rehearsal training with recollection and familiarity tasks. Further, we design a history sampler to select informative fragments for rehearsal training, making the memory focus on the crucial information. We evaluate the performance of our rehearsal memory by the synthetic bAbI task and several downstream tasks, including text/video question answering and recommendation on long sequences.

paragraphs: Reasoning over a long sequence becomes costly when a system must keep the entire input available. Memory-augmented networks instead compress the sequence into a bounded memory during one pass and answer later queries from that memory. The paper highlights two problems: early information is gradually forgotten, and useful content is not distinguished from less important content.

Rehearsal Memory addresses both problems through self-supervised rehearsal. Recollection and familiarity tasks train the memory to retain earlier information. A history sampler selects informative fragments for this training, so rehearsal directs attention toward crucial material rather than treating every part of the sequence equally.

The approach connects memory preservation with selective review: the rehearsal tasks target forgetting, while the sampler determines what deserves reinforcement. The authors evaluate it on the synthetic bAbI task and downstream tasks involving text and video question answering and long-sequence recommendation. These evaluations examine the proposed memory mechanism across several uses of stored sequence information; the abstract states the evaluation scope without claiming a particular numerical improvement.
summary.tldr: Rehearsal Memory uses self-supervised review and selective history sampling to preserve important information from long sequences.

title: Learning to Rehearse in Long Sequence Memorization

abstract: Incorporating symmetry as an inductive bias into neural network architecture has led to improvements in generalization, data efficiency, and physical consistency in dynamics modeling. Methods such as CNNs or equivariant neural networks use weight tying to enforce symmetries such as shift invariance or rotational equivariance. However, despite the fact that physical laws obey many symmetries, real-world dynamical data rarely conforms to strict mathematical symmetry either due to noisy or incomplete data or to symmetry breaking features in the underlying dynamical system. We explore approximately equivariant networks which are biased towards preserving symmetry but are not strictly constrained to do so. By relaxing equivariance constraints, we find that our models can outperform both baselines with no symmetry bias and baselines with overly strict symmetry in both simulated turbulence domains and real-world multi-stream jet flow.

By relaxing equivariance constraints, we find that our models can outperform both baselines with no symmetry bias and baselines with overly strict symmetry in both simulated turbulence domains and real-world multi-stream jet flow.

paragraphs: Symmetry can help a neural network learn physical dynamics by telling it which transformations should preserve predictable relationships. Networks often enforce these relationships by sharing weights. This reduces what must be learned from data, but it also requires the observations to respect the imposed symmetry closely enough for that restriction to help.

The paper examines what happens when this requirement is too strong. Real observations can depart from mathematical symmetry because measurements are noisy or incomplete, or because the physical system itself contains symmetry-breaking features. The proposed approximately equivariant networks retain a preference for symmetry while allowing learned departures from it. Symmetry therefore guides the model without completely determining its permitted behavior.

In simulated turbulence and real multi-stream jet flow, the authors find that relaxing the constraints can outperform both networks without a symmetry bias and networks enforcing overly strict symmetry. The findings support treating the strength of a physical prior as a modeling choice: useful structure can improve prediction while flexibility accommodates departures present in the data.
summary.tldr: Networks that favor symmetry while allowing departures can better model imperfectly symmetric physical dynamics.

title: Approximately Equivariant Networks for Imperfectly Symmetric Dynamics

abstract: Sharpness of minima is a promising quantity that can correlate with generalization in deep networks and, when optimized during training, can improve generalization. However, standard sharpness is not invariant under reparametrizations of neural networks, and, to fix this, reparametrization-invariant sharpness definitions have been proposed, most prominently adaptive sharpness (Kwon et al., 2021). But does it really capture generalization in modern practical settings? We comprehensively explore this question in a detailed study of various definitions of adaptive sharpness in settings ranging from training from scratch on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 to fine-tuning CLIP on ImageNet and BERT on MNLI. We focus mostly on transformers for which little is known in terms of sharpness despite their widespread usage. Overall, we observe that sharpness does not correlate well with generalization but rather with some training parameters like the learning rate that can be positively or negatively correlated with generalization depending on the setup. Interestingly, in multiple cases, we observe a consistent negative correlation of sharpness with OOD generalization implying that sharper minima can generalize better. Finally, we illustrate on a simple model that the right sharpness measure is highly data-dependent, and that we do not understand well this aspect for realistic data distributions.

However, ordinary sharpness can change when the same network is represented with different parameters. This paper examines adaptive sharpness measures intended to address that problem and asks whether they explain generalization in practical settings.

The study spans training on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 and fine-tuning CLIP on ImageNet and BERT on MNLI, with particular attention to transformers. Across these settings, the authors find that sharpness does not correlate reliably with generalization. Instead, it often tracks training choices such as learning rate, whose relationship with generalization changes across setups.

In several cases, sharper solutions consistently generalize better to out-of-distribution data. This is an empirical observation in the studied settings, rather than a universal preference for sharp solutions. A simple model further illustrates that choosing an informative sharpness measure depends strongly on the data. Together, these findings challenge the reliability of sharpness as a general-purpose explanation of predictive performance.
summary.tldr: A broad empirical study finds that adaptive sharpness often tracks training choices more reliably than generalization, with sharper solutions sometimes generalizing better.

title: A Modern Look at the Relationship between Sharpness and Generalization

abstract: Contextual bandit algorithms appear in several applications, such as online advertisement and recommendation systems like personalized education or personalized medicine. Individually-tailored recommendations boost the performance of the underlying application; nevertheless, providing individual suggestions becomes costly and even implausible as the number of users grows. As such, to efficiently serve the demands of several users in modern applications, it is imperative to identify the underlying users’ clusters, i.e., the groups of users for which a single recommendation might be (near-)optimal. We propose CLUB-HG, a novel algorithm that integrates a game-theoretic approach into clustering inference. Our algorithm achieves Nash equilibrium at each inference step and discovers the underlying clusters. We also provide regret analysis within a standard linear stochastic noise setting. Finally, experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show the superior performance of our proposed algorithm compared to the state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Personalized recommendation becomes costly when a system must learn separately for very many users. One way to share that effort is to identify groups whose members can receive the same recommendation with near-optimal results. This paper studies that grouping problem within contextual bandit learning.

The proposed algorithm, CLUB-HG, incorporates a game-theoretic approach into cluster inference. It reaches a Nash equilibrium at each inference step and discovers the underlying user clusters. The equilibrium condition supplies a notion of stability for the grouping process, connecting online recommendation with a structured way to infer which users belong together.

The authors provide regret analysis under a standard linear setting with stochastic noise. That analysis addresses the cost of learning while making recommendations within the stated model. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. Together, the theory and experiments support clustering as a way to share learning across users while retaining the distinctions needed for useful personalization.
summary.tldr: CLUB-HG uses game-theoretic clustering to share contextual-bandit learning across users with similar recommendation needs.

title: Parallel Online Clustering of Bandits via Hedonic Game

abstract: The design of codes for feedback-enabled communications has been a long-standing open problem. Recent research on non-linear, deep learning-based coding schemes have demonstrated significant improvements in communication reliability over linear codes, but are still vulnerable to the presence of forward and feedback noise over the channel. In this paper, we develop a new family of non-linear feedback codes that greatly enhance robustness to channel noise. Our autoencoder-based architecture is designed to learn codes based on consecutive blocks of bits, which obtains de-noising advantages over bit-by-bit processing to help overcome the physical separation between the encoder and decoder over a noisy channel. Moreover, we develop a power control layer at the encoder to explicitly incorporate hardware constraints into the learning optimization, and prove that the resulting average power constraint is satisfied asymptotically. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our scheme outperforms state-of-the-art feedback codes by wide margins over practical forward and feedback noise regimes, and provide information-theoretic insights on the behavior of our non-linear codes. Moreover, we observe that, in a long blocklength regime, canonical error correction codes are still preferable to feedback codes when the feedback noise becomes high. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RCode1.

paragraphs: Feedback-enabled communication lets information return from the receiving side, but noise can affect both the forward and feedback channels. The paper develops nonlinear codes learned through an autoencoder architecture to improve robustness in this setting. Its encoder operates on consecutive blocks of bits, gaining denoising advantages over processing each bit individually.

The architecture also includes an encoder power-control layer that incorporates hardware constraints into training. The authors prove that the resulting average power constraint is satisfied asymptotically. This connects the learned communication scheme to a physical resource requirement while preserving the stated asymptotic scope of the guarantee.

Numerical experiments show large improvements over leading feedback codes across practical forward and feedback noise regimes and provide information-theoretic insights into the learned codes. The paper also reports a boundary to their usefulness: for long block lengths and sufficiently noisy feedback, conventional error-correcting codes remain preferable. The findings therefore support block-based learned feedback coding while identifying an evaluated regime where feedback coding loses its advantage.
summary.tldr: Block-based learned feedback codes improve noise robustness while satisfying an asymptotic average-power constraint.

title: Robust Non-Linear Feedback Coding via Power-Constrained Deep Learning

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech models such as wav2vec and HuBERT have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on automatic speech recognition (ASR) and proved to be extremely useful in low label-resource settings. However, the success of SSL models has yet to transfer to utterance-level tasks such as speaker, emotion, and language recognition, which still require supervised fine-tuning of the SSL models to obtain good performance. We argue that the problem is caused by the lack of disentangled representations and an utterance-level learning objective for these tasks. Inspired by how HuBERT uses clustering to discover hidden acoustic units, we formulate a factor analysis (FA) model that uses the discovered hidden acoustic units to align the SSL features. The underlying utterance-level representations are disentangled using probabilistic inference on the aligned features. Furthermore, the variational lower bound derived from the FA model provides an utterance-level objective, allowing error gradients to be backpropagated to the Transformer layers to learn highly discriminative acoustic units. When used in conjunction with HuBERT’s masked prediction training, our models outperform the current best model, WavLM, on all utterance-level non-semantic tasks on the SUPERB benchmark with only 20% of labeled data.

The authors argue that these tasks need more disentangled representations and an explicit utterance-level training objective.

This result supports linking feature alignment, probabilistic disentangling, and utterance-level training to improve the evaluated speech tasks beyond word recognition.
summary.tldr: Factor analysis adds disentangled utterance representations and a training objective that improve non-semantic speech tasks with limited labels.

title: Self-supervised Neural Factor Analysis for Disentangling Utterance-level Speech Representations

abstract: We propose Image-to-Image Schrödinger Bridge (I$^2$SB), a new class of conditional diffusion models that directly learn the nonlinear diffusion processes between two given distributions. These diffusion bridges are particularly useful for image restoration, as the degraded images are structurally informative priors for reconstructing the clean images. I$^2$SB belongs to a tractable class of Schrödinger bridge, the nonlinear extension to score-based models, whose marginal distributions can be computed analytically given boundary pairs. This results in a simulation-free framework for nonlinear diffusions, where the I$^2$SB training becomes scalable by adopting practical techniques used in standard diffusion models. We validate I$^2$SB in solving various image restoration tasks, including inpainting, super-resolution, deblurring, and JPEG restoration on ImageNet 256$\times$256 and show that I$^2$SB surpasses standard conditional diffusion models with more interpretable generative processes. Moreover, I$^2$SB matches the performance of inverse methods that additionally require the knowledge of the corruption operators. Our work opens up new algorithmic opportunities for developing efficient nonlinear diffusion models on a large scale. Project page and codes: https://i2sb.github.io/

paragraphs: Image restoration starts with an observation that is damaged but still contains useful structure. I²SB builds a conditional diffusion model around that information by learning a nonlinear process connecting degraded and clean image distributions directly. The degraded image therefore serves as an informative starting point for reconstruction, giving the generative process a clear relationship to the restoration task.

The method belongs to a tractable class of Schrödinger bridges. Given paired endpoints, its intermediate marginal distributions can be calculated analytically. This enables training without simulating the nonlinear diffusion process and lets the authors adopt practical training techniques from standard diffusion models. The analytic structure is what makes the proposed bridge framework scalable.

The authors evaluate inpainting, super-resolution, deblurring, and JPEG restoration on ImageNet at 256-by-256 resolution. They report better results than standard conditional diffusion models, alongside more interpretable generation processes. I²SB also matches inverse methods that additionally require knowledge of the corruption operators, showing that this direct distribution-to-distribution approach can be competitive across the tested restoration problems.
summary.tldr: I²SB learns diffusion bridges directly between degraded and clean images, enabling scalable training and strong results on several restoration tasks.

title: I$^2$SB: Image-to-Image Schrödinger Bridge

abstract: Independence testing is a classical statistical problem that has been extensively studied in the batch setting when one fixes the sample size before collecting data. However, practitioners often prefer procedures that adapt to the complexity of a problem at hand instead of setting sample size in advance. Ideally, such procedures should (a) stop earlier on easy tasks (and later on harder tasks), hence making better use of available resources, and (b) continuously monitor the data and efficiently incorporate statistical evidence after collecting new data, while controlling the false alarm rate. Classical batch tests are not tailored for streaming data: valid inference after data peeking requires correcting for multiple testing which results in low power. Following the principle of testing by betting, we design sequential kernelized independence tests that overcome such shortcomings. We exemplify our broad framework using bets inspired by kernelized dependence measures, e.g., the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion. Our test is also valid under non-i.i.d. time-varying settings. We demonstrate the power of our approaches on both simulated and real data.

paragraphs: Independence testing asks whether two quantities are statistically related. Traditional batch tests fix the sample size before data collection, while practitioners may want to keep collecting evidence until the problem is resolved. Repeatedly checking a batch test requires multiple-testing corrections to preserve validity, which can reduce its ability to detect dependence.

This paper develops sequential kernelized independence tests using the principle of testing by betting. Evidence can be incorporated as observations arrive, supporting continuous monitoring while controlling false alarms. The framework includes betting strategies inspired by kernel-based dependence measures, including the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion.

The aim is to adapt data collection to difficulty: easy cases can stop earlier, while harder ones can accumulate more evidence. The authors also establish validity in non-independent, non-identically distributed time-varying settings and demonstrate statistical power on simulated and real data. The contribution joins flexible stopping with a framework for measuring dependence, addressing the mismatch between fixed-sample procedures and the way evidence is often gathered in practice.
summary.tldr: Betting-based kernel tests support sequential independence testing with continuous evidence updates and false-alarm control.

title: Sequential Kernelized Independence Testing

abstract: Differentially Private methods for training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have progressed recently, in particular with the use of massive batches and aggregated data augmentations for a large number of training steps. These techniques require much more computing resources than their non-private counterparts, shifting the traditional privacy-accuracy trade-off to a privacy-accuracy-compute trade-off and making hyper-parameter search virtually impossible for realistic scenarios. In this work, we decouple privacy analysis and experimental behavior of noisy training to explore the trade-off with minimal computational requirements. We first use the tools of Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) to highlight that the privacy budget, when not overcharged, only depends on the total amount of noise (TAN) injected throughout training. We then derive scaling laws for training models with DP-SGD to optimize hyper-parameters with more than a $100\times$ reduction in computational budget. We apply the proposed method on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet and, in particular, strongly improve the state-of-the-art on ImageNet with a $+9$ points gain in top-1 accuracy for a privacy budget $\varepsilon=8$.

paragraphs: Differentially private neural-network training has improved through techniques involving large batches, aggregated data augmentations, and many training steps. These approaches can be computationally expensive, making hyperparameter search difficult. The paper therefore treats private training as a three-way trade-off among privacy, accuracy, and compute, and seeks a cheaper way to explore it.

The authors separate privacy accounting from the experimental behavior of noisy training. Using Rényi differential privacy, they show that the privacy budget depends only on total injected noise when the accounting is not overcharged. This qualified relationship motivates their total amount of noise, or TAN, perspective and scaling laws for choosing DP-SGD hyperparameters.

The proposed method reduces the computational budget for hyperparameter optimization by more than a factor of one hundred. Applications cover CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, with a reported nine-point gain in ImageNet top-1 accuracy over the state of the art at a privacy budget of epsilon eight. These results show how cheaper tuning can improve the practical privacy-accuracy-compute trade-off in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TAN-based scaling laws cut DP-SGD tuning compute by over 100 times and yield a reported nine-point ImageNet accuracy gain at epsilon eight.

title: TAN Without a Burn: Scaling Laws of DP-SGD

abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) exhibit exceptional general language processing capabilities but come with significant demands on memory and computational resources. As a powerful compression technology, binarization can extremely reduce model weights to a mere 1 bit, lowering the expensive computation and memory requirements. However, existing quantization techniques fall short of maintaining LLM performance under ultra-low bit-widths. In response to this challenge, we present BiLLM, a groundbreaking 1-bit post-training quantization scheme tailored for pretrained LLMs. Based on the weight distribution of LLMs, BiLLM first identifies and structurally selects salient weights, and minimizes the compression loss through an effective binary residual approximation strategy. Moreover, considering the bell-shaped distribution of the non-salient weights, we propose an optimal splitting search to group and binarize them accurately. BiLLM, for the first time, achieves high-accuracy inference (e.g. 8.41 perplexity on LLaMA2-70B) with only 1.08-bit weights across various LLM families and evaluation metrics, outperforms SOTA quantization methods of LLM by significant margins. Moreover, BiLLM enables the binarization process of a 7-billion LLM within 0.5 hours on a single GPU, demonstrating satisfactory time efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Aaronhuang-778/BiLLM .

paragraphs: BiLLM compresses pretrained language-model weights to roughly one bit each while trying to preserve useful prediction quality. Such aggressive compression targets the substantial memory and computation demands of large models. The challenge is that existing quantization methods struggle to retain performance when each weight has so few representable values.

The method treats weights differently according to their importance and distribution. It identifies structurally selected salient weights and uses a binary residual approximation to reduce compression loss. For the remaining weights, whose distribution is bell-shaped, it searches for a split that groups them for more accurate binarization. This separates two compression problems that would otherwise be handled with one uniform rule.

The reported results include perplexity of 8.41 on LLaMA2-70B with an effective weight precision of 1.08 bits, alongside substantial improvements over competing quantization methods across evaluated model families and metrics. A 7-billion-parameter model can be binarized within half an hour on one GPU. That timing measures the compression procedure, while the quality results demonstrate the feasibility of inference at extremely low weight precision.
summary.tldr: BiLLM uses separate binarization strategies for salient and other weights to compress language models to 1.08-bit weights with strong reported accuracy.

title: BiLLM: Pushing the Limit of Post-Training Quantization for LLMs

abstract: Transferring knowledge across diverse data modalities is receiving increasing attention in machine learning. This paper tackles the task of leveraging expert-derived, yet expensive, tabular data to enhance image-based predictions when tabular data is unavailable during inference. The primary challenges stem from the inherent complexity of accurately mapping diverse tabular data to visual contexts, coupled with the necessity to devise distinct strategies for numerical and categorical tabular attributes. We propose CHannel tAbulaR alignment with optiMal tranSport (Charms), which establishes an alignment between image channels and tabular attributes, enabling selective knowledge transfer that is pertinent to visual features. Specifically, Charms measures similarity distributions across modalities to effectively differentiate and transfer relevant tabular features, with a focus on morphological characteristics, enhancing the capabilities of visual classifiers. By maximizing the mutual information between image channels and tabular features, knowledge from both numerical and categorical tabular attributes are extracted. Experimental results demonstrate that Charms not only enhances the performance of image classifiers but also improves their interpretability by effectively utilizing tabular knowledge.

paragraphs: Expert-generated tables can contain valuable information for image classification, yet collecting that information can be expensive. This paper considers using such tables during learning so that predictions can later rely on images alone. The challenge is identifying which tabular attributes correspond to visual information and transferring them appropriately.

Charms aligns image channels with tabular attributes using optimal transport. It compares similarity distributions across the two modalities to select relevant information, especially morphological characteristics. This selective alignment matters because the usefulness of a tabular attribute depends on its relationship to the visual features available to the classifier.

The method also maximizes mutual information between image channels and tabular features, extracting knowledge from both numerical and categorical attributes. Experiments show improvements in image-classifier performance and interpretability. The contribution is a way to retain useful expert knowledge in an image-based predictor even when the accompanying table is unavailable at inference. The reported benefits come from making the correspondence between tabular expertise and visual representations part of learning.
summary.tldr: Charms transfers relevant expert tabular knowledge into image classifiers, improving reported performance and interpretability when tables are unavailable at inference.

title: Tabular Insights, Visual Impacts: Transferring Expertise from Tables to Images

abstract: In spite of their huge success, transformer models remain difficult to scale in depth. In this work, we develop a unified signal propagation theory and provide formulae that govern the moments of the forward and backward signal through the transformer model. Our framework can be used to understand and mitigate vanishing/exploding gradients, rank collapse, and instability associated with high attention scores. We also propose DeepScaleLM, an initialization and scaling scheme that conserves unit output/gradient moments throughout the model, enabling the training of very deep models with 1000 layers. We find that transformer models could be much deeper - our deep models with fewer parameters outperform shallow models in Language Modeling, Speech Translation, and Image Classification, across encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants, for both Pre-LN and Post-LN transformers, for multiple datasets and model sizes. These improvements also translate into improved performance on downstream Question Answering tasks and improved robustness for Image Classification.

paragraphs: Making transformers much deeper can destabilize the signals used for prediction and learning. This paper develops a unified theory describing moments of both forward signals and backward gradients throughout a transformer. The framework helps analyze vanishing or exploding gradients, rank collapse, and instability connected to large attention scores.

The authors use that theory to propose DeepScaleLM, an initialization and scaling scheme that preserves unit output and gradient moments across the model. This supports training models with one thousand layers. The contribution therefore connects a mathematical description of signal propagation with a concrete way to keep very deep transformer training stable.

In the reported experiments, deeper models with fewer parameters outperform shallower models across language modeling, speech translation, and image classification. The evaluations include encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder architectures, both pre-normalization and post-normalization variants, and multiple datasets and model sizes. The improvements also extend to downstream question answering and image classification robustness. These findings support greater depth as a productive design choice in the evaluated configurations.
summary.tldr: DeepScaleLM uses signal propagation theory to train thousand-layer transformers, with deeper models outperforming shallower ones in the reported evaluations.

title: Transformers Get Stable: An End-to-End Signal Propagation Theory for Language Models

abstract: We present an approach for estimating the fraction of text in a large corpus which is likely to be substantially modified or produced by a large language model (LLM). Our maximum likelihood model leverages expert-written and AI-generated reference texts to accurately and efficiently examine real-world LLM-use at the corpus level. We apply this approach to a case study of scientific peer review in AI conferences that took place after the release of ChatGPT: ICLR 2024, NeurIPS 2023, CoRL 2023 and EMNLP 2023. Our results suggest that between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to these conferences could have been substantially modified by LLMs, i.e. beyond spell-checking or minor writing updates. The circumstances in which generated text occurs offer insight into user behavior: the estimated fraction of LLM-generated text is higher in reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals. We also observe corpus-level trends in generated text which may be too subtle to detect at the individual level, and discuss the implications of such trends on peer review. We call for future interdisciplinary work to examine how LLM use is changing our information and knowledge practices.

summary.tldr: Corpus-level analysis suggests that 6.5%–16.9% of text in the studied conference reviews could have been substantially modified by LLMs.

title: Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews

abstract: Real-world datasets often exhibit long-tailed distributions, compromising the generalization and fairness of learning-based models. This issue is particularly pronounced in Image Aesthetics Assessment (IAA) tasks, where such imbalance is difficult to mitigate due to a severe distribution mismatch between features and labels, as well as the great sensitivity of aesthetics to image variations. To address these issues, we propose an Enhancer against Long-Tail for Aesthetics-oriented models (ELTA). ELTA first utilizes a dedicated mixup technique to enhance minority feature representation in high-level space while preserving their intrinsic aesthetic qualities. Next, it aligns features and labels through a similarity consistency approach, effectively alleviating the distribution mismatch. Finally, ELTA adopts a specific strategy to refine the output distribution, thereby enhancing the quality of pseudo-labels. Experiments on four representative datasets (AVA, AADB, TAD66K, and PARA) show that our proposed ELTA achieves state-of-the-art performance by effectively mitigating the long-tailed issue in IAA datasets. Moreover, ELTA is designed with plug-and-play capabilities for seamless integration with existing methods. To our knowledge, this is the first contribution in the IAA community addressing long-tail. All resources are available in here.

paragraphs: Image aesthetics assessment learns to judge aesthetic qualities from examples, but those examples can be unevenly distributed. Rare cases then receive weak representation. Correcting this imbalance is particularly difficult because changing an image can change its aesthetic qualities, and the distributions of learned features and aesthetic labels can differ substantially.

ELTA addresses these issues through three connected steps. First, a specialized mixup technique strengthens minority representations in a high-level feature space while preserving their aesthetic qualities. Second, a similarity-consistency mechanism aligns features with labels. Third, a strategy for refining the output distribution improves pseudo-labels, the labels produced by the model itself.

These components connect representation balance, feature-label agreement, and the quality of generated supervision. ELTA is designed as a plug-in for existing aesthetics methods, so its contribution can be incorporated into established models. Experiments on AVA, AADB, TAD66K, and PARA report state-of-the-art performance through mitigation of the long-tail problem. The authors also describe the work, to their knowledge, as the first contribution addressing this issue in image aesthetics assessment.
summary.tldr: ELTA improves aesthetics models by strengthening rare feature representations, aligning labels, and refining pseudo-labels.

title: ELTA: An Enhancer against Long-Tail for Aesthetics-oriented Models

abstract: Being the most classical generative model for serial data, state-space models (SSM) are fundamental in AI and statistical machine learning. In SSM, any form of parameter learning or latent state inference typically involves the computation of complex latent-state posteriors. In this work, we build upon the variational sequential Monte Carlo (VSMC) method, which provides computationally efficient and accurate model parameter estimation and Bayesian latent-state inference by combining particle methods and variational inference. While standard VSMC operates in the offline mode, by re-processing repeatedly a given batch of data, we distribute the approximation of the gradient of the VSMC surrogate ELBO in time using stochastic approximation, allowing for online learning in the presence of streams of data. This results in an algorithm, online VSMC, that is capable of performing efficiently, entirely on-the-fly, both parameter estimation and particle proposal adaptation. In addition, we provide rigorous theoretical results describing the algorithm’s convergence properties as the number of data tends to infinity as well as numerical illustrations of its excellent convergence properties and usefulness also in batch-processing settings.

paragraphs: State-space models describe sequential observations through underlying hidden states. Learning their parameters and inferring those states typically requires difficult posterior calculations. Variational sequential Monte Carlo combines particle methods with variational inference to make these calculations manageable, but its standard form repeatedly processes a fixed batch of observations.

This paper develops an online version for data streams. It uses stochastic approximation to distribute estimation of the variational objective’s gradient over time. The resulting algorithm updates model parameters and adapts the particle proposal mechanism entirely as observations arrive. This brings both learning tasks into the same on-the-fly procedure.

The authors provide rigorous convergence results describing behavior as the number of observations grows without bound. Numerical illustrations also show strong convergence behavior and usefulness when processing batches. The contribution is therefore both an algorithmic extension to streaming data and a theoretical account of its long-run behavior. Its reported batch usefulness suggests that the online construction can also be valuable when observations are already available together.
summary.tldr: Online VSMC learns state-space-model parameters and adapts particle proposals as data arrive, with asymptotic convergence guarantees.

title: Online Variational Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: A general belief in fair classification is that fairness constraints incur a trade-off with accuracy, which biased data may worsen. Contrary to this belief, Blum & Stangl (2019) show that fair classification with equal opportunity constraints even on extremely biased data can recover optimally accurate and fair classifiers on the original data distribution. Their result is interesting because it demonstrates that fairness constraints can implicitly rectify data bias and simultaneously overcome a perceived fairness-accuracy trade-off. Their data bias model simulates under-representation and label bias in underprivileged population, and they show the above result on a stylized data distribution with i.i.d. label noise, under simple conditions on the data distribution and bias parameters. We propose a general approach to extend the result of Blum & Stangl (2019) to different fairness constraints, data bias models, data distributions, and hypothesis classes. We strengthen their result, and extend it to the case when their stylized distribution has labels with Massart noise instead of i.i.d. noise. We prove a similar recovery result for arbitrary data distributions using fair reject option classifiers. We further generalize it to arbitrary data distributions and arbitrary hypothesis classes, i.e., we prove that for any data distribution, if the optimally accurate classifier in a given hypothesis class is fair and robust, then it can be recovered through fair classification with equal opportunity constraints on the biased distribution whenever the bias parameters satisfy certain simple conditions. Finally, we show applications of our technique to time-varying data bias in classification and fair machine learning pipelines.

paragraphs: Fairness constraints are often understood as imposing an accuracy cost. This paper investigates a different possibility: requiring fairness during learning can help undo distortions in the training data. It builds on a result showing recovery of an accurate, fair classifier despite underrepresentation and biased labels in an underprivileged population.

The authors develop a general method for extending such recovery results across fairness constraints, bias models, distributions, and classifier families. They strengthen the earlier result by allowing Massart label noise in its stylized setting. They also establish recovery for arbitrary data distributions using fair classifiers with a reject option, which can decline to classify some inputs.

The broadest stated result remains conditional. Within any given hypothesis class, the most accurate classifier can be recovered from biased data through equal opportunity constraints if that classifier is fair and robust and the bias parameters satisfy specified conditions. This shows circumstances where fairness and accuracy reinforce each other. Applications also cover changing data bias over time and fairness across machine learning pipelines.
summary.tldr: Under stated fairness, robustness, and bias conditions, fairness-constrained learning can recover an optimally accurate classifier from biased data.

title: How Far Can Fairness Constraints Help Recover From Biased Data?

abstract: Decision support systems for classification tasks are predominantly designed to predict the value of the ground truth labels. However, since their predictions are not perfect, these systems also need to make human experts understand when and how to use these predictions to update their own predictions. Unfortunately, this has been proven challenging. In this context, it has been recently argued that an alternative type of decision support systems may circumvent this challenge. Rather than providing a single label prediction, these systems provide a set of label prediction values constructed using a conformal predictor, namely a prediction set, and forcefully ask experts to predict a label value from the prediction set. However, the design and evaluation of these systems have so far relied on stylized expert models, questioning their promise. In this paper, we revisit the design of this type of systems from the perspective of online learning and develop a methodology that does not require, nor assumes, an expert model. Our methodology leverages the nested structure of the prediction sets provided by any conformal predictor and a natural counterfactual monotonicity assumption to achieve an exponential improvement in regret in comparison to vanilla bandit algorithms. We conduct a large-scale human subject study ($n = 2{,}751$) to compare our methodology to several competitive baselines. The results show that, for decision support systems based on prediction sets, limiting experts’ level of agency leads to greater performance than allowing experts to always exercise their own agency.
