paragraphs: A decision support system can offer experts a set of possible labels and require them to choose within it. This avoids asking experts to interpret a single imperfect prediction, but it creates a design question: how should the system select the set? Earlier approaches relied on simplified models of expert behavior, making their practical promise uncertain.

The authors develop an online learning methodology that does not require an expert model. It uses the nested structure of conformal prediction sets, where sets can be ordered by inclusion, together with a counterfactual monotonicity assumption. Those ingredients yield an exponential improvement in regret compared with ordinary bandit algorithms. The improvement depends on the stated structural assumption.

A study with 2,751 human participants compares the methodology with several competitive alternatives. Within these prediction-set support systems, limiting experts’ freedom to choose outside the offered set produces better performance than always allowing unrestricted agency. The finding concerns this form of decision support and its evaluation, while the methodological contribution shows how to adapt support without specifying a behavioral model of the expert.
summary.tldr: An online method learns prediction-set support without an expert model, and a human study finds benefits from restricting choices to those sets.

title: Designing Decision Support Systems using Counterfactual Prediction Sets

abstract: Machine learning models are routinely trained on a mixture of different data domains. Different domain weights yield very different downstream performances. We propose the Soup-of-Experts, a novel architecture that can instantiate a model at test time for any domain weights with minimal computational cost and without re-training the model. Our architecture consists of a bank of expert parameters, which are linearly combined to instantiate one model. We learn the linear combination coefficients as a function of the input domain weights. To train this architecture, we sample random domain weights, instantiate the corresponding model, and backprop through one batch of data sampled with these domain weights. We demonstrate how our approach obtains small specialized models on several language modeling tasks quickly. Soup-of-Experts are particularly appealing when one needs to ship many different specialist models quickly under a size constraint.

paragraphs: Training data often combines several domains, and changing their relative weights can substantially change downstream performance. Soup-of-Experts aims to produce a model suited to a requested domain mixture without retraining for each request. The architecture stores a bank of expert parameters and combines them linearly to instantiate one model.

The combination coefficients are learned as a function of the requested domain weights. During training, the system samples a random mixture, constructs the corresponding model, and backpropagates through a batch sampled according to that same mixture. This connects the desired data composition to the parameters of the resulting model, training the architecture to support different specialization choices.

The authors demonstrate rapid creation of small specialist models on several language-modeling tasks. At test time, the architecture can instantiate a model for any supplied domain weights with minimal computational cost and no retraining. Its stated appeal is strongest when many specialist models must be delivered quickly under a size constraint. The contribution is a reusable parameter bank that supports inexpensive construction of models tailored to different domain mixtures.
summary.tldr: Soup-of-Experts learns to combine expert parameters into small specialist models for requested domain mixtures without retraining.

title: Soup-of-Experts: Pretraining Specialist Models via Parameters Averaging

abstract: We develop a framework for capturing the instrumental value of data production processes, which accounts for two key factors: (a) the context of the agent’s decision-making; (b) how much data or information the buyer already possesses. We "micro-found" our data valuation function by establishing its connection to classic notions of signals and information design in economics. When instantiated in Bayesian linear regression, our value naturally corresponds to information gain. Applying our proposed data value in Bayesian linear regression for monopoly pricing, we show that if the seller can fully customize data production, she can extract the first-best revenue (i.e., full surplus) from any population of buyers, i.e., achieving first-degree price discrimination. If data can only be constructed from an existing data pool, this limits the seller’s ability to customize, and achieving first-best revenue becomes generally impossible. However, we design a mechanism that achieves seller revenue at most $\log(\kappa)$ less than the first-best, where $\kappa$ is the condition number associated with the data matrix. As a corollary, the seller extracts the first-best revenue in the multi-armed bandits special case.

paragraphs: The value of producing data depends on the decisions it will support and the information its buyer already has. This paper develops a valuation framework incorporating both factors. It connects the framework to economic theories of signals and information design, giving the valuation a foundation in how information helps an agent make decisions.

For Bayesian linear regression, the proposed value becomes information gain. The authors then study how a monopoly seller can price data in that setting. If the seller can completely customize data production, they show that the seller can capture the full available surplus from any population of buyers. This is the strongest revenue outcome considered, corresponding to first-degree price discrimination.

Restricting production to an existing data pool changes the result: full surplus extraction is generally impossible. The authors nevertheless construct a mechanism whose revenue falls short of that ideal by at most log(κ), where κ is the data matrix's condition number. In the special case of multi-armed bandits, their result yields full surplus extraction.
summary.tldr: A decision-dependent valuation of data shows how production flexibility determines a monopoly seller's ability to extract buyers' full surplus.

title: An Instrumental Value for Data Production and its Application to Data Pricing

abstract: Motivated by the recent success of time-series foundation models for zero-shot forecasting, we present a methodology for in-context fine-tuning of a time-series foundation model. In particular, we design a pretrained foundation model that can be prompted (at inference time) with multiple time-series examples, in order to forecast a target time-series into the future. Our foundation model is specifically trained to utilize examples from multiple related time-series in its context window (in addition to the history of the target time-series) to help it adapt to the specific distribution of the target domain at inference time. We show that such a foundation model that uses in-context examples at inference time can obtain much better performance on popular forecasting benchmarks compared to supervised deep learning methods, statistical models, and other time series foundation models. Interestingly, our in-context fine-tuning approach even matches the performance of a foundation model that is explicitly fine-tuned on the target domain.

paragraphs: A time-series forecasting model usually has the target series’ history available when predicting its future. This paper develops a foundation model that can also use multiple related time-series examples supplied in its inference-time context. The aim is to adapt predictions to the target domain by giving the model relevant examples when it is used.

The authors specifically train the model to make use of this additional context. Related series are therefore an intended adaptation mechanism, alongside the target series’ own history. They call the approach in-context fine-tuning because the examples help the pretrained model adjust to the domain through its input context, with adaptation occurring when forecasts are produced.

On popular forecasting benchmarks, the approach achieves substantially better performance than the compared supervised deep learning methods, statistical models, and other time-series foundation models. It also matches the performance of a foundation model explicitly fine-tuned on the target domain. These findings show that training a forecasting model to use related examples can make inference-time context a powerful source of domain adaptation.
summary.tldr: A specially trained forecasting model adapts through related time-series examples in its context, matching explicit fine-tuning in the reported evaluation.

title: In-Context Fine-Tuning for Time-Series Foundation Models

abstract: Most current precipitation nowcasting methods aim to capture the underlying spatiotemporal dynamics of precipitation systems by minimizing the mean square error (MSE). However, these methods often neglect effective constraints on the data distribution, leading to unsatisfactory prediction accuracy and image quality, especially for long forecast sequences. To address this limitation, we propose a precipitation nowcasting model incorporating perceptual constraints. This model reformulates precipitation nowcasting as a posterior MSE problem under such constraints. Specifically, we first obtain the posteriori mean sequences of precipitation forecasts using a precipitation estimator. Subsequently, we construct the transmission between distributions using rectified flow. To enhance the focus on distant frames, we design a frame sampling strategy that gradually increases the corresponding weights. We theoretically demonstrate the reliability of our solution, and experimental results on two publicly available radar datasets demonstrate that our model is effective and outperforms current state-of-the-art models.

paragraphs: Precipitation nowcasting predicts how rainfall will develop over a sequence of future frames. Many methods train by minimizing mean squared error, but the paper argues that this can neglect constraints on the forecast distribution. The resulting predictions can have disappointing accuracy and image quality, especially farther into a forecast sequence. The proposed model adds perceptual constraints to address this issue.

The method formulates forecasting as a posterior mean-squared-error problem subject to those constraints. A precipitation estimator first produces posterior mean forecast sequences. Rectified flow then constructs a transformation between distributions. To give distant forecast frames more attention, the authors also introduce a frame-sampling strategy whose corresponding weights increase gradually.

The paper provides a theoretical argument for the reliability of its solution and evaluates it on two public radar datasets. It reports better performance than current state-of-the-art models in those experiments. The approach connects numerical forecast estimation with distributional constraints, while explicitly adjusting training emphasis toward the later frames that motivate much of the problem.
summary.tldr: The model combines perceptual constraints, rectified flow, and increased emphasis on distant frames to improve precipitation nowcasting.

title: Perceptually Constrained Precipitation Nowcasting Model

abstract: As platforms increasingly rely on learning algorithms, collectives may form and seek ways to influence these platforms to align with their own interests. This can be achieved by coordinated submission of altered data. To evaluate the potential impact of such behavior, it is essential to understand the computations that collectives must perform to impact platforms in this way. In particular, collectives need to make a priori assessments of the effect of the collective before taking action, as they may face potential risks when modifying their data. Moreover they need to develop implementable coordination algorithms based on quantities that can be inferred from observed data. We develop a framework that provides a theoretical and algorithmic treatment of these issues and present experimental results in a product evaluation domain.

paragraphs: Groups of users may try to influence a learning platform by coordinating changes to the data they submit. This paper studies the computations needed to organize such collective action. The central question is how a group can assess its likely influence and coordinate an implementable strategy using information available from observations.

The framework addresses two connected needs. First, a collective should estimate the effects of its intervention before acting, because altering its data may carry risks. Second, its coordination algorithm must depend on quantities that can be inferred from observed data. Together, these requirements connect prospective impact assessment with the practical information needed to carry out a coordinated intervention.

The authors provide a theoretical and algorithmic treatment and present experiments in a product-evaluation setting. The stated contribution is a framework for analyzing and implementing collective influence under these informational requirements. It makes the group's own computational problem explicit: participants need a way to reason about anticipated platform responses and translate those assessments into coordinated data changes before accepting the risks of action.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a framework for collectives to estimate and coordinate their influence on learning platforms through altered data submissions.

title: Statistical Collusion by Collectives on Learning Platforms

abstract: Many commercial Large Language Models (LLMs) are often closed-source, limiting developers to prompt tuning for aligning content generation with specific applications. While these models currently do not provide access to token logits, we argue that if such access were available, it would enable more powerful adaptation techniques beyond prompt engineering. In this paper, we propose a token-level probability reweighting framework that, given access to logits and a small amount of task-specific data, can effectively steer black-box LLMs toward application-specific content generation. Our approach views next-token prediction through the lens of supervised classification. We show that aligning black-box LLMs with task-specific data can be formulated as a label noise correction problem, leading to Plugin model – an autoregressive probability reweighting model that operates solely on logits. We provide theoretical justification for why reweighting logits alone is sufficient for task adaptation. Extensive experiments with multiple datasets, LLMs, and reweighting models demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, advocating for broader access to token logits in closed-source models. We provide our code at this https URL.

paragraphs: Adapting a closed language model is difficult when developers cannot modify its internal parameters. This paper investigates what would become possible if providers exposed token logits, the scores underlying next-token probabilities. The proposal explicitly depends on that access, which the abstract says the commercial models under discussion do not currently provide.

The authors treat next-token prediction as a supervised classification problem and formulate task adaptation as label-noise correction. Their Plugin model learns to reweight token probabilities using logits and a small amount of task-specific data. Because it operates autoregressively, this correction can guide token choices throughout generation while leaving the underlying model closed.

The paper gives a theoretical justification for the sufficiency of logit reweighting for task adaptation and reports effective results across multiple datasets, language models, and reweighting models. The contribution is both an adaptation method and an argument about model interfaces: exposing token scores could support more powerful application-specific steering than prompt engineering alone, without requiring developers to access the model's internal weights.
summary.tldr: Given token-logit access, Plugin learns probability reweighting from limited task data to adapt a closed language model.

title: Logits are All We Need to Adapt Closed Models

abstract: Predicting labels directly from data has been the standard in label learning tasks, e.g., supervised learning, where models often prioritize feature compression and extraction from inputs under the assumption that label information is less complex. However, recent prediction tasks often face predicting complex labels, exacerbating the challenge of learning mappings from learned features to high-fidelity label representations. To this end, we draw inspiration from the consistency training concept in generative consistency models and propose predictive consistency learning (PCL), a novel learning paradigm that decomposes the full label information into a progressive learning procedure, mitigating the label capture challenge. Besides data inputs, PCL additionally receives input from noise-perturbed labels as an additional reference, pursuing predictive consistency across different noise levels. It simultaneously learns the relationship between latent features and a spectrum of label information, which enables progressive learning for complex predictions and allows multi-step inference analogous to gradual denoising, thereby enhancing the prediction quality. Experiments on vision, text, and graph tasks show the superiority of PCL over conventional supervised training in complex label prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Supervised learning commonly predicts labels directly from representations of the input. That arrangement becomes difficult when the labels themselves contain complex information and demand high-fidelity predictions. This paper proposes predictive consistency learning, or PCL, to distribute the challenge of learning that output information across a progressive procedure inspired by generative consistency training.

During learning, PCL receives the usual data input together with a noise-perturbed version of the label as an additional reference. It trains for consistent predictions across different noise levels, connecting input features to label information with varying amounts of corruption. This gives the model a spectrum of label information to learn from instead of relying solely on a direct mapping to the complete target.

The framework also permits multi-step inference resembling gradual denoising, allowing predictions to be progressively refined. Experiments on vision, text, and graph tasks report advantages over conventional supervised training for complex label prediction. The findings support using label structure itself as part of the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Predictive consistency learning uses noisy labels and consistency across noise levels to improve complex predictions through progressive learning.

title: Generative Modeling Reinvents Supervised Learning: Label Repurposing with Predictive Consistency Learning

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown promising capabilities but struggle under distribution shifts, where evaluation data differ from instruction tuning distributions. Although previous works have provided empirical evaluations, we argue that establishing a formal framework that can characterize and quantify the risk of MLLMs is necessary to ensure the safe and reliable application of MLLMs in the real world. By taking an information-theoretic perspective, we propose the first theoretical framework that enables the quantification of the maximum risk of MLLMs under distribution shifts. Central to our framework is the introduction of Effective Mutual Information (EMI), a principled metric that quantifies the relevance between input queries and model responses. We derive an upper bound for the EMI difference between in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) data, connecting it to visual and textual distributional discrepancies. Extensive experiments on real benchmark datasets, spanning 61 shift scenarios, empirically validate our theoretical insights.

By accounting for both input modalities, the framework makes it possible to study their distributional discrepancies within one risk analysis.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic framework bounds changes in multimodal query-response relevance using visual and textual distribution discrepancies.

title: Understanding Multimodal LLMs Under Distribution Shifts: An Information-Theoretic Approach

abstract: Predicting future scene representations is a crucial task for enabling robots to understand and interact with the environment. However, most existing methods rely on videos and simulations with precise action annotations, limiting their ability to leverage the large amount of available unlabeled video data. To address this challenge, we propose PlaySlot, an object-centric video prediction model that infers object representations and latent actions from unlabeled video sequences. It then uses these representations to forecast future object states and video frames. PlaySlot allows the generation of multiple possible futures conditioned on latent actions, which can be inferred from video dynamics, provided by a user, or generated by a learned action policy, thus enabling versatile and interpretable world modeling. Our results show that PlaySlot outperforms both stochastic and object-centric baselines for video prediction across different environments. Furthermore, we show that our inferred latent actions can be used to learn robot behaviors sample-efficiently from unlabeled video demonstrations. Videos and code are available on our project website.

PlaySlot learns from unlabeled video sequences instead. It extracts representations of individual objects together with latent actions that describe the changes observed between frames.

Those representations support predictions of future object states and video frames. The model can generate different possible futures depending on the latent actions supplied. Actions may be inferred from video dynamics, provided by a user, or produced by a learned policy, making the same predictive model useful under several forms of control.

The authors report better video prediction than the evaluated stochastic and object-centric baselines across different environments. They also show that the inferred actions support sample-efficient learning of robot behaviors from unlabeled video demonstrations. The contribution links observation and control: a video supplies more than examples of appearance, because its dynamics can also provide an action representation for predicting and learning behavior.
summary.tldr: PlaySlot learns objects and latent actions from unlabeled videos to support controllable future prediction and sample-efficient robot behavior learning.

title: PlaySlot: Learning Inverse Latent Dynamics for Controllable Object-Centric Video Prediction and Planning

abstract: Multi-player multi-armed bandit (MP-MAB) has been widely studied owing to its diverse applications across numerous domains. We consider an MP-MAB problem where $N$ players compete for $K$ arms in $T$ rounds. The reward distributions are heterogeneous where each player has a different expected reward for the same arm. When multiple players select the same arm, they collide and obtain zero rewards. In this paper, our target is to find the max-min fairness matching that maximizes the reward of the player who receives the lowest reward. This paper improves the existing max-min regret upper bound of $O(\exp(1/\Delta) + K^3 \log T\log \log T)$. More specifically, our decentralized fair elimination algorithm (DFE) deals with heterogeneity and collision carefully and attains a regret upper bound of $O((N^2+K)\log T / \Delta)$, where $\Delta$ is the minimum reward gap between max-min value and sub-optimal arms. In addition, this paper also provides an $\Omega(\max\\{ N^2, K \\} \log T / \Delta)$ regret lower bound for this problem, which indicates that our algorithm is optimal with respect to key parameters $T, N, K$, and $\Delta$. Additional numerical experiments also show the efficiency and improvement of our algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies several players learning to select among shared options over repeated rounds. Players can receive different expected rewards from the same option, and simultaneous selections of that option cause a collision with zero reward. The objective is max-min fairness: find an assignment that makes the lowest-reward player's expected outcome as large as possible.

The proposed decentralized fair elimination algorithm handles both differing player preferences and collisions. Its regret upper bound scales as (N² + K) log T divided by Δ, where N counts players, K counts arms, T counts rounds, and Δ measures the minimum gap between the max-min value and suboptimal arms. This improves the previously stated bound, which included exponential dependence on the inverse gap.

A matching lower bound scales with max{N², K} log T divided by Δ. Together, the bounds establish optimal dependence on the key parameters identified in the paper. Numerical experiments also show efficiency improvements. The result connects a fairness objective with a precise characterization of how difficult learning becomes as competition, available options, and reward gaps change.
summary.tldr: Decentralized fair elimination achieves optimal parameter dependence for learning assignments that maximize the worst-off player's reward.

title: Optimal Algorithm for Max-Min Fair Bandit

abstract: While language models have exceptional capabilities at text generation, they lack a natural inductive bias for emitting numbers and thus struggle in tasks involving quantitative reasoning, especially arithmetic. One fundamental limitation is the nature of the cross-entropy (CE) loss, which assumes a nominal scale and thus cannot convey proximity between generated number tokens. In response, we here present a regression-like loss that operates purely on token level. Our proposed Number Token Loss (NTL) comes in two flavors and minimizes either the $\mathcal{L}_p$ norm or the Wasserstein distance between the numerical values of the real and predicted number tokens. NTL can easily be added to any language model and extend the CE objective during training without runtime overhead. We evaluate the proposed scheme on various mathematical datasets and find that it consistently improves performance in math-related tasks. In a direct comparison on a regression task, we find that NTL can match the performance of a regression head, despite operating on token level. Finally, we scale NTL up to 3B parameter models and observe improved performance, demonstrating its potential for seamless integration into LLMs. We hope to inspire LLM developers to improve their pretraining objectives and distribute NTL as a minimalistic and lightweight PyPI package ntloss: https://ibm.biz/ntl-pypi-repo. Development code for full paper reproduction is available separately.

For numbers, that objective does not express how close a predicted value is to the correct one. The paper introduces Number Token Loss, or NTL, to add numerical proximity directly to training while keeping predictions at the token level.

NTL has two variants, based on an Lp norm or a Wasserstein distance between the numerical values associated with target and predicted number tokens. It supplements the existing cross-entropy objective and can be added without runtime overhead. This gives training a numerical signal while retaining the language model's ordinary token-generation interface.

Across mathematical datasets, the authors report consistent improvements on math-related tasks. In a direct regression comparison, NTL matches the performance of a regression head despite operating on tokens. Experiments also show improved performance when scaling to models with three billion parameters. These findings support the possibility of improving quantitative behavior through the training objective itself, without requiring a separate numerical output mechanism.
summary.tldr: Number Token Loss adds numerical proximity to language-model training and improves reported mathematical performance without runtime overhead.

title: Regress, Don’t Guess: A Regression-like Loss on Number Tokens for Language Models

abstract: We introduce Random Feature Representation Boosting (RFRBoost), a novel method for constructing deep residual random feature neural networks (RFNNs) using boosting theory. RFRBoost uses random features at each layer to learn the functional gradient of the network representation, enhancing performance while preserving the convex optimization benefits of RFNNs. In the case of MSE loss, we obtain closed-form solutions to greedy layer-wise boosting with random features. For general loss functions, we show that fitting random feature residual blocks reduces to solving a quadratically constrained least squares problem. Through extensive numerical experiments on tabular datasets for both regression and classification, we show that RFRBoost significantly outperforms RFNNs and end-to-end trained MLP ResNets in the small- to medium-scale regime where RFNNs are typically applied. Moreover, RFRBoost offers substantial computational benefits, and theoretical guarantees stemming from boosting theory.

paragraphs: RFRBoost constructs deep residual random-feature networks using boosting theory. At each layer, random features help learn a functional gradient of the network's representation: a direction for improving that representation. The method aims to gain the benefits of progressively improving a deep network while preserving the convex optimization advantages associated with random-feature models.

The optimization depends on the training loss. For mean squared error, the authors derive closed-form solutions for greedy layer-by-layer boosting. For general losses, fitting a random-feature residual block becomes a quadratically constrained least-squares problem. These results give the construction process an explicit optimization structure and connect the network's development to boosting-based theoretical guarantees.

Experiments cover tabular regression and classification in the small- to medium-scale setting where random-feature networks are typically used. The authors report significant improvements over random-feature networks and end-to-end trained multilayer-perceptron residual networks, together with substantial computational benefits. The demonstrated result is therefore scoped to this data regime, where representation boosting offers a promising combination of predictive performance and efficient optimization.
summary.tldr: RFRBoost builds residual random-feature networks layer by layer, improving tabular prediction while retaining structured, computationally efficient optimization.

title: Random Feature Representation Boosting

abstract: We propose LOGDIFF (Logical Guidance for the Exact Composition of Diffusion Models), a guidance framework for diffusion models that enables principled constrained generation with complex logical expressions at inference time. We study when exact score-based guidance for complex logical formulas can be obtained from guidance signals associated with atomic attributes and constraints. First, we derive an exact Boolean calculus that provides a sufficient condition for exact logical guidance. Specifically, if a formula admits a circuit representation in which conjunctions combine conditionally independent subformulas and disjunctions combine subformulas that are either conditionally independent or mutually exclusive, exact logical guidance is achievable. In this case, the guidance signal can be computed exactly from atomic scores and posterior probabilities using an efficient recursive algorithm. Moreover, we show that, for commonly encountered classes of distributions, any desired Boolean formula is compilable into such a circuit representation. Second, by combining atomic guidance scores with posterior probability estimates, we introduce a hybrid guidance approach that bridges classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance, applicable to both compositional logical guidance and standard conditional generation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on multiple image and protein structure generation tasks.

paragraphs: LOGDIFF studies how to guide diffusion models using complex logical requirements at generation time. The question is whether guidance for individual attributes or constraints can be combined into an exact guidance signal for a larger Boolean formula. The framework makes the conditions for that composition explicit.

The authors derive a Boolean calculus with a sufficient condition for exactness. A formula must admit a circuit in which conjunctions join conditionally independent subformulas, while disjunctions join subformulas that are conditionally independent or mutually exclusive. For commonly encountered classes of distributions, they also show that any Boolean formula can be compiled into a suitable circuit.

title: Logical Guidance for the Exact Composition of Diffusion Models

abstract: While Experience Replay—the practice of storing rollouts and reusing them multiple times during training—is a foundational technique in general RL, it remains largely unexplored in LLM post-training due to the prevailing belief that fresh, on-policy data is essential for high performance. In this work, we challenge this assumption. We present a systematic study of replay buffers for LLM post-training, formalizing the optimal design as a trade-off between staleness-induced variance, sample diversity and the high computational cost of generation. We show that strict on-policy sampling is suboptimal when generation is expensive. Empirically, we show that a well-designed replay buffer can drastically reduce inference compute without degrading – and in some cases even improving – final model performance, while preserving policy entropy.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language models often relies on newly generated responses from the model currently being trained. Generating those responses can be expensive. This paper studies whether storing past rollouts and using them again, a practice called experience replay, can reduce that cost while retaining the benefits of post-training.

The authors frame replay-buffer design as a balance among three factors: older data can increase variance as the model changes, a useful training collection needs diversity, and producing fresh samples consumes computation. This formulation makes data freshness one consideration within a broader efficiency problem. Their analysis shows that strict on-policy sampling is suboptimal when generation is expensive.

Empirically, a well-designed replay buffer substantially reduces inference computation without lowering final model performance in the reported study; some cases improve performance. It also preserves policy entropy, a measure of how varied the model’s choices remain. These findings support selective reuse of training experience and make buffer design central to achieving the reported savings.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed replay buffers reduce language-model RL generation costs while preserving, and sometimes improving, final performance.

title: Efficient RL Training for LLMs with Experience Replay

abstract: Diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art performance in generative modeling but are limited by their reliance on Gaussian noise and the high computational cost of iterative sampling. Star-shaped diffusion addresses the former by introducing a non-Markovian forward process, yet this comes at the expense of temporal coherence in the reverse process. We propose a novel framework that resolves this trade-off by learning a Markovian projection of a star-shaped forward process, and its reversal. This design enables learning over a broad class of exponential models and recovers DDPM as a special case. It is particularly well-suited for knowledge distillation, allowing few-step or even single-step generation. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our approach across multiple generative tasks. Code and demo are available at: https://oublalkhalid.github.io/MStar-Diffusion/.

paragraphs: Diffusion models face two challenges highlighted here: dependence on Gaussian noise and the cost of generating samples through many iterations. Star-shaped diffusion broadens the available noise processes with a non-Markovian forward construction, but the abstract identifies a resulting loss of temporal coherence in the reverse process.

M-Star addresses this trade-off by learning a Markovian projection of the star-shaped forward process together with its reversal. The framework supports a broad class of exponential models and includes DDPM as a special case. This connects the proposed construction to an established diffusion formulation while extending the range of distributions it can handle.

The authors emphasize that the design is particularly suitable for knowledge distillation, supporting generation in a few steps or even one step. Experiments across multiple generative tasks demonstrate effectiveness and flexibility. The contribution therefore links broader distributional modeling with a structure suited to reducing sampling steps, addressing both the modeling restriction and iterative generation cost described in the paper.
summary.tldr: M-Star learns a Markovian projection of star-shaped diffusion, supporting broader distribution families and distillation for few-step or single-step generation.

title: M-Star: Markovian Projection of Star-Shaped Diffusion for Exponential Family Distributions

abstract: Bioacoustic foundation models rely on large-scale citizen science platforms like Xeno-Canto for geographically and ecologically diverse data. Recent work has shown that supervision alone can produce SotA species detection models when trained on this large-scale data—however, there remains unutilized potential in the form of recording metadata readily available within these community-driven data hubs. In this work, we explore the use of metadata—such as location and time—as auxiliary supervision signals, allowing the model to leverage species-metadata correlations in its learned representation. Auxiliary metadata losses provide additional information beyond vocalizations alone that can encourage a richer, more robust representation that generalizes better to species distribution and acoustic domain shifts—important challenges for deployment in real-world passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) settings. We introduce MetaPerch, a new foundation model that achieves strong species identification performance across multiple challenging domains and present an extensive empirical study of the effects of 9 diverse metadata sources on 17 bioacoustic datasets.

paragraphs: Community recording platforms provide both animal sounds and contextual information such as recording location and time. Bioacoustic models already benefit from the scale and diversity of these collections, but their metadata offer additional supervision. MetaPerch investigates how learning from this context can improve the representations used to identify species.

The approach adds auxiliary metadata losses during training, encouraging the model to capture relationships between species and recording circumstances. Those relationships supply information beyond the vocalizations themselves. The motivation is to learn representations that generalize better when species distributions change or recordings come from different acoustic environments, both important challenges for passive acoustic monitoring.

The authors introduce MetaPerch as a foundation model and study nine metadata sources across 17 bioacoustic datasets. They report strong species-identification performance across several challenging domains. The contribution is both a model and an empirical investigation of metadata as an additional learning signal. It supports exploring recording context as a way to enrich acoustic representations, without implying that every metadata source provides the same benefit.
summary.tldr: MetaPerch uses recording metadata as auxiliary supervision to enrich bioacoustic representations and support species identification across challenging domains.

title: MetaPerch: Learning from metadata for bioacoustics foundation models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable breakthroughs across various applications. However, their architectures remain inefficient in pretraining due to two main limitations: (i) self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality, leading to redundant modeling of sequence-internal local information; (ii) mixture-of-experts (MoE) implicitly couples knowledge storage with computational pathways, hindering flexible access to sequence-external global knowledge. To overcome these limitations, we propose LoKiFormer, a novel LLM architecture that augments the standard decoder with two dedicated modules: 1) Local Fusion Attention (LFA), which incorporates a convolutional fusion to attention, explicitly capturing local patterns and allowing the attention to operate on more informative representations; 2) Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), which introduces a parametric key–value memory that explicitly stores global knowledge in addressable slots, decoupling storage from computation and enabling direct knowledge retrieval. Together, these modules enable LoKiFormer to achieve more efficient and effective integration of information at both levels. Experimental results show that LoKiFormer converges 1.33x faster in pre-training than baseline models, underscoring its superiority over existing LLM architectures.

To overcome these limitations, we propose LoKiFormer, a novel LLM architecture that augments the standard decoder with two dedicated modules: 1) Local Fusion Attention (LFA), which incorporates a convolutional fusion to attention, explicitly capturing local patterns and allowing the attention to operate on more informative representations; 2) Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), which introduces a parametric key–value memory that explicitly stores global knowledge in addressable slots, decoupling storage from computation and enabling direct knowledge retrieval. paragraphs: LoKiFormer addresses two proposed sources of inefficiency in language-model pretraining. Standard self-attention has no explicit preference for nearby patterns, which can lead to redundant modeling of local sequence information. Mixture-of-experts architectures also tie stored knowledge to computational pathways, limiting flexibility in how broader knowledge is accessed.

The architecture adds two specialized components to a standard decoder. Local Fusion Attention uses convolutional fusion to capture nearby patterns before attention works with the resulting representations. The Knowledge Memory Module stores global knowledge in learned key–value slots that can be addressed directly. This separates the role of retaining knowledge from the computational paths used to process a sequence.

Together, the modules provide dedicated mechanisms for local information within the current sequence and global knowledge stored in model parameters. Experiments report 1.33-times faster pretraining convergence than the baseline models. The finding supports the proposed division of architectural responsibilities in the evaluated setting: local structure receives explicit processing, while learned global knowledge becomes directly accessible through a separate memory component.
summary.tldr: LoKiFormer combines convolution-enhanced attention with addressable knowledge memory and reports 1.33-times faster pretraining convergence.

title: LoKiFormer: Locality-aware Attention with Decoupled Knowledge Memory for Efficient Large Language Model Pretraining

abstract: Accurate survival modeling in biomedical studies is often hindered by rare events, limited effective sample sizes, and settings with limited or partially observed information (e.g., covariates of interest that are difficult or expensive to collect, highly structured sampling designs, or nuisance parameters omitted by conditioning). Knowledge distillation can leverage external predictive information without sharing individual-level data, but existing approaches are largely built for fully specified likelihoods or probability-based survival models and do not extend to settings where outcome distributions are only partially specified. To address this challenge, we propose a knowledge distillation framework based on a composite-likelihood Kullback–Leibler divergence that aligns teacher and student models within components. Our key insight is that, although composite likelihoods do not define a global outcome distribution, each likelihood component induces a well-defined probability model on its restricted outcome space, enabling a principled KL divergence. Simulation studies and biomedical case studies show improved discrimination and predictive accuracy in rare-event, heterogeneous settings without requiring access to external individual-level data.

paragraphs: Survival modeling can be difficult when events are rare or information is only partially observed. Biomedical studies may also involve expensive covariates, structured sampling, or parameters removed through conditioning. External predictive models could help, but existing distillation approaches often expect a fully specified likelihood or an explicit probability model for the outcome.

The paper develops knowledge distillation around composite likelihoods, which combine separate likelihood components without necessarily defining one global outcome distribution. Its key observation is that each component still defines a valid probability model over a restricted outcome space. This makes it possible to measure teacher-student disagreement using a principled Kullback–Leibler divergence within individual components.

The resulting framework transfers external predictive information without requiring access to external individual-level records. Simulations and biomedical case studies report better discrimination and predictive accuracy in settings with rare events and heterogeneous information. The contribution is therefore a way to perform distillation when the model specifies useful pieces of the outcome process without specifying its complete distribution.
summary.tldr: Component-level probability models enable principled knowledge distillation for survival settings without fully specified outcome distributions.

title: Component-Wise Composite Likelihood Distillation for Censored Time-to-Event Data

abstract: The default paradigm of post-training text-to-image generators includes post-hoc selection of generated images, and subsequent training with one reward model to align the generator to the reward, typically user preference. This discards informative data as well as optimizes only for a single reward, hence harming diversity, semantic fidelity and efficiency. Instead, we propose MIRO, a method that conditions the model on multiple rewards during training, thus letting the model learn user preferences directly. MIRO pre-training both improves the visual quality of the generated images and speeds up the training, achieving state of the art on the GenEval compositional benchmark and user-preference scores (PickAScore, ImageReward, HPSv2).

The paper argues that this process throws away informative data and narrows optimization to one reward, which can harm diversity, fidelity to the prompt's meaning, and training efficiency.

MIRO makes multiple rewards part of the model's training conditions. This allows the generator to learn user preferences during pretraining, bringing reward information into the learning process itself. The central change concerns how preference information is supplied: several rewards guide learning together rather than reducing the available feedback to one post-training objective.

The authors report improved visual quality and faster training, along with state-of-the-art results on the GenEval compositional benchmark and the preference scores PickAScore, ImageReward, and HPSv2. These findings connect the training design to both compositional performance and preference-based assessment. The contribution is a way to incorporate richer reward information earlier in training, with reported benefits for image quality and efficiency.
summary.tldr: MIRO conditions text-to-image pretraining on multiple rewards, improving reported image quality, benchmark performance, and training efficiency.

title: MIRO: MultI-Reward cOnditioned pretraining improves T2I quality and efficiency

abstract: Temporal causal representation learning methods assume that causal mechanisms switch instantaneously between discrete domains, yet real-world systems often exhibit continuous mechanism transitions. For example, a vehicle’s dynamics evolve gradually through a turning maneuver, and human gait shifts smoothly from walking to running. We formalize this setting by modeling transitional mechanisms as convex combinations of finitely many atomic mechanisms, governed by time-varying mixing coefficients. Our theoretical contributions establish that both the latent causal variables and the continuous mixing trajectory are jointly identifiable. We further propose TRACE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework where each expert learns one atomic mechanism during training, enabling test-time recovery of mechanism trajectories, including intermediate mechanism states never observed during training. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that TRACE recovers mixing trajectories with up to 0.99 correlation, substantially outperforming discrete-switching baselines.

summary.tldr: TRACE models gradual causal changes as time-varying mixtures of atomic mechanisms and recovers their continuous trajectories.

title: TRACE: Trajectory Recovery for Continuous Mechanism Evolution in Causal Representation Learning

abstract: Semi-supervised learning faces significant challenges in realistic scenarios where labeled data is scarce and unlabeled data follows unknown, arbitrary distributions. We formalize this critical yet under-explored paradigm as Universal Semi-supervised Learning (UniSSL). Existing methods typically leverage unlabeled data via pseudo-labeling. However, they often rely on the idealized assumption of a uniform unlabeled data distribution or require sufficient labeled data to estimate it. In the UniSSL setting, such dependencies lead to numerous erroneous pseudo-labels, thereby triggering representation confusion. Fortunately, we observe that inter-sample relations captured by representations are more reliable than pseudo-labels. Leveraging this insight, we shift our focus to representation-level structural inference to bypass distribution estimation. Accordingly, we propose Simplex Anchored Graph-state Equipartition (SAGE), which captures high-order inter-sample dependencies to establish structural consensus for guiding representation learning. Meanwhile, to mitigate representation confusion, we employ vectors that satisfy a simplex equiangular tight frame to serve as a coordinate frame for guiding inter-class representation separation. Finally, we introduce a weighting strategy based on distribution-agnostic metrics to prioritize reliable pseudo-labels and an auxiliary branch to isolate potentially erroneous pseudo-labels. Evaluations on five standard benchmarks show that SAGE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with an average accuracy gain of 8.52%.

Across five standard benchmarks, SAGE consistently beats the compared state-of-the-art methods, with a reported average accuracy gain of 8.52%.
summary.tldr: SAGE uses representation relationships and geometric class anchors to improve semi-supervised learning when unlabeled-data distributions are unknown.

title: Beyond Distribution Estimation: Simplex Anchored Structural Inference Towards Universal Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Federated learning has emerged as the foremost approach for decentralized model training with privacy preserving. The global class imbalance and cross-client data heterogeneity naturally coexist, and the mismatch between local and global imbalances exacerbates the performance degradation of the aggregated model. The agnosticism of global class distribution poses significant challenges for data-level methods, especially under extreme conditions with severe class absence across clients. In this paper, we propose FedReLa, a novel data-level approach that tackles the coexistence of data heterogeneity and class imbalance in federated learning. By re-labeling samples with a feature-dependent label re-allocator, FedReLa corrects biased global decision boundaries without requiring knowledge of the global class distribution. This modular, model-agnostic approach can be integrated with algorithmic methods to deliver consistent improvements without additional communication overhead. Through extensive experiments, our method significantly improves the accuracy of minority classes and the overall accuracy on stepwise-imbalanced and long-tailed datasets, outperforming the previous state of the art.

paragraphs: FedReLa addresses federated learning when class imbalance and differences between clients occur together. A class may be rare across the full system yet have a different frequency locally, and some clients may lack it entirely. These mismatches can bias the combined model, while the unknown global class distribution makes data-level correction difficult.

The method uses a feature-dependent label re-allocator to relabel samples and correct biased global decision boundaries. Its distinguishing property is that it does not need the overall class distribution. Experiments on stepwise-imbalanced and long-tailed datasets show significant improvements in both minority-class accuracy and overall accuracy, exceeding the previous state of the art. The paper also reports consistent gains when integrating the method with algorithmic approaches, without extra communication overhead. This makes relabeling a complementary tool for handling imbalance and client heterogeneity within decentralized training.
summary.tldr: FedReLa uses feature-dependent relabeling to improve imbalanced federated learning without knowing global class frequencies or adding communication overhead.

title: FedReLa: Imbalanced Federated Learning via Re-Labeling

abstract: Noise-based certified machine unlearning currently faces a hard ceiling: the noise magnitude required to certify unlearning typically destroys model utility, particularly for large-scale deletion requests. While leveraging public data is a standard technique in differential privacy to relax this tension, its role in unlearning remains unexplored. We address this gap by introducing Asymmetric Langevin Unlearning (ALU), a framework that uses public data to mitigate privacy costs. We prove that public data injection suppresses the unlearning cost by a factor of $O(1/n_{\mathrm{pub}}^2)$, guaranteeing a strict computational advantage over retraining. This establishes a new control mechanism: practitioners can mitigate the need for high noise—and the associated utility loss—by increasing the volume of public data. Crucially, we analyze the realistic setting of distribution mismatch, explicitly characterizing how shifts between public and private sources impact utility. We show that ALU enables "mass unlearning” of constant dataset fractions – a regime where standard symmetric methods become impractical – while maintaining high utility. Empirical evaluations using variational Rényi divergence and membership inference attacks confirm that ALU effectively thwarts privacy attacks while preserving utility under reasonable distribution shifts.

This paper studies whether public data can ease that trade-off. It introduces Asymmetric Langevin Unlearning, or ALU, which uses public data to reduce the cost associated with unlearning private data.

This qualification matters because the usefulness of public data depends on how its distribution relates to the private source.
summary.tldr: ALU uses public data to reduce certified-unlearning costs and preserve utility, including large deletions under reasonable distribution mismatch.

title: Unlearning with Asymmetric Sources: Improved Unlearning-Utility Trade-off with Public Data

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has emerged as a popular paradigm for improving the performance of vision–language models (e.g., CLIP) on downstream tasks. Among existing CLIP-based TTA methods, Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) is a pioneering work that optimizes textual prompts using multiple test-time augmentations and remains a strong baseline to date. In this work, we revisit TPT and reveal that its optimization can be interpreted as implicitly learning from self-generated pseudo labels. Building on this perspective, we propose a unified self-ensembling framework (USE) that ensures consistency between the optimization and inference stages. During optimization, we introduce a simple yet effective self-ensembling (SE) strategy that emphasizes the test image itself over its augmented views adaptively to obtain more reliable pseudo labels. To fully exploit the potential of augmentations, we further apply the same strategy at inference time, unifying the objectives of both stages. Notably, SE can also act as a lightweight optimization-free TTA method. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that SE and USE outperform their counterparts, respectively. Furthermore, SE yields consistent performance gains when integrated with existing TTA methods. The code is available at https://github.com/sirujiang/USE.

paragraphs: Test-time prompt tuning adapts a vision–language model using several augmented versions of a test image. This paper revisits that procedure and interprets its optimization as learning from labels generated by the model itself. That perspective makes the reliability of those pseudo labels a central concern and motivates aligning how predictions are combined during adaptation and final inference.

The proposed self-ensembling strategy adaptively gives the original image greater emphasis than its augmented views when constructing pseudo labels. USE applies the same strategy at inference, keeping the two stages consistent while still exploiting the augmentations. The self-ensembling component can also operate independently as a lightweight adaptation method that requires no optimization.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report that self-ensembling and USE outperform their respective counterparts. Self-ensembling also produces consistent gains when added to existing test-time adaptation methods. The findings support treating prediction aggregation as part of adaptation design: how original and augmented views are combined affects both the supervision used for tuning and the final prediction.
summary.tldr: USE consistently combines original and augmented image predictions during prompt tuning and inference to improve test-time adaptation.

title: USE: A Unified Self-Ensembling Framework for Test-Time Prompt Tuning

abstract: Proteins are inherently dynamic, with biological functions often emerging from transitions between multiple conformational states. While recent breakthroughs have largely addressed the static structure prediction problem, no systematic benchmark exists to demonstrate how well current models capture functionally relevant dynamics. We introduce ProMiSE, the first benchmark that provides both a dataset and an evaluation scheme, based on native biological assemblies and integrating major conformational change mechanisms—intrinsic, ligand-induced, and protein-induced—within a single curated dataset. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art structure prediction models, including AlphaFold3 and recent generative approaches. Our findings reveal that current models exhibit a limited ability to sample intrinsic multi-states and are often insensitive to biological context in induced scenarios. Internal representation analysis suggests that training-data exposure can shift predictions toward dominant conformational states over alternative biologically relevant states, primarily at the structure module. In contrast, results from BioEmu indicate that reducing decoding-stage bias can substantially improve multi-state sampling without major changes to upstream pair representations.

paragraphs: Proteins often function by moving between different conformations, so predicting a single structure does not establish whether a model captures biologically relevant dynamics. ProMiSE provides a dataset and evaluation scheme for testing multiple protein states within native biological assemblies, bringing several causes of conformational change into one benchmark.

The benchmark covers intrinsic changes as well as changes induced by ligands or other proteins. The authors evaluate leading structure-prediction systems, including AlphaFold3 and recent generative approaches. They find limited sampling of intrinsic alternative states and frequent insensitivity to biological context in cases where surrounding molecules should help determine the conformation.

Results from BioEmu indicate that reducing bias during decoding can substantially improve multi-state sampling without major changes to upstream pair representations. This identifies decoding behavior as a promising intervention point while grounding evaluation in biological context and functionally meaningful alternatives.
summary.tldr: ProMiSE benchmarks biologically relevant protein states and finds shortcomings in current models, with decoding bias emerging as a promising improvement target.

title: ProMiSE: Protein Multi-State Evaluation Benchmark in Biological Contexts

abstract: Continual post-training (CPT) is a popular and effective technique for adapting foundation models like multimodal large language models to ever-evolving downstream tasks. While existing research primarily focuses on methods like data replay, model expansion, or parameter regularization, the fundamental role of the learning paradigm remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a comparative analysis of two core post-training paradigms: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), investigating their respective impacts on knowledge retention during CPT. Our experiments are conducted across multiple multimodal tasks, utilizing Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as the base model. The investigation yields two significant findings: (1) When continuously learning on downstream tasks, SFT leads to catastrophic forgetting of previously learned tasks. In contrast, RFT inherently preserves prior knowledge and achieves performance comparable to multi-task training. (2) RFT successfully protects and even enhances the model’s general knowledge on standard benchmarks, while SFT degrades general model capabilities severely. Further analysis reveals that this stability is not primarily due to explicit mechanisms like KL penalty or chain-of-thought reasoning. We investigate RFT’s learning dynamics and find that its selective update mechanism inherently prevents interference with established knowledge. Based on this insight, we propose a rollout-based instance filtering algorithm (RIF-RFT) that enhances the training efficiency of RFT by focusing on learnable samples. Our comprehensive study demonstrates the superiority of RFT as a robust paradigm for continual post-training.

title: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning Naturally Mitigates Forgetting in Continual Post-Training

abstract: Conditional time series generation plays a critical role in addressing data scarcity and enabling causal analysis in real-world applications. Despite its increasing importance, the field lacks a standardized and systematic benchmarking framework for evaluating generative models across diverse conditions. To address this gap, we introduce the Conditional Time Series Generation Benchmark (ConTSG-Bench). ConTSG-Bench comprises a suite of large-scale, well-aligned datasets spanning diverse conditioning modalities and levels of semantic abstraction, enabling systematic evaluation of representative generation methods across these dimensions with a comprehensive suite of metrics for generation fidelity and condition adherence. Both the quantitative benchmarking and in-depth analyses of conditional generation behaviors have revealed the traits and limitations of the current approaches, highlighting critical challenges and promising research directions, particularly with respect to precise structural controllability and downstream task utility under complex conditions.

paragraphs: Conditional time-series generation produces sequences guided by specified information. Its usefulness depends on both the quality of the generated sequence and whether it follows the requested condition. The paper addresses a lack of standardized evaluation across different kinds of conditioning, which makes systematic assessment of generation methods difficult.

ConTSG-Bench provides a collection of large-scale, aligned datasets covering multiple conditioning modalities and different levels of semantic abstraction. It evaluates representative generation methods using metrics for two distinct requirements: generation fidelity and condition adherence. This organization allows researchers to examine how methods behave as the form and meaning of the conditioning information change.

The contribution is therefore an evaluation framework that makes these challenges visible and provides a shared basis for studying progress on conditional generation.
summary.tldr: ConTSG-Bench evaluates conditional time-series generators for both realistic outputs and adherence to diverse conditioning information.

title: ConTSG-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for Conditional Time Series Generation

abstract: Surface reconstruction with differentiable rendering has achieved impressive performance in recent years, yet the pervasive photometric ambiguities have strictly bottlenecked existing approaches. This paper presents AmbiSuR, a framework that explores an intrinsic solution upon Gaussian Splatting for the photometric ambiguity-robust surface reconstruction with high performance. Started by revisiting the foundation, our investigation uncovers two built-in primitive-wise ambiguities in representation, while revealing an intrinsic potential for ambiguity self-indication in Gaussian Splatting. Stemming from these, a photometric disambiguation is first introduced, constraining ill-posed geometry solution for definite surface formation. Then, we propose an ambiguity indication module that unleashes the self-indication potential to identify and further guide correcting underconstrained reconstructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate our superior performance in surface reconstruction compared to existing methods across various challenging scenarios, while excelling in broad compatibility. Our code will be made open-source upon acceptance.

paragraphs: Surface reconstruction through differentiable rendering depends on connecting image appearance to geometry. Photometric ambiguity makes that connection underdetermined: matching appearance can leave the underlying surface insufficiently constrained. AmbiSuR investigates this problem within Gaussian Splatting, focusing on ambiguities built into its representation.

The authors identify two ambiguities at the level of individual primitives and find that Gaussian Splatting also contains information that can indicate ambiguity. Their framework first introduces photometric disambiguation to constrain ill-posed geometric solutions and support definite surface formation. It then uses an ambiguity indication module to identify reconstructions that remain underconstrained and guide their correction.

These components address both the formation of ambiguous geometry and the detection of unresolved regions. Experiments report better surface reconstruction than existing methods across challenging scenarios, alongside broad compatibility. The stated findings suggest that the representation can contribute to diagnosing its own reconstruction uncertainty, making ambiguity analysis useful for both preventing geometric errors and directing subsequent corrections.
summary.tldr: AmbiSuR improves Gaussian-Splatting surface reconstruction by constraining photometric ambiguities and identifying underconstrained geometry.

title: Revisiting Photometric Ambiguity for Accurate Gaussian-Splatting Surface Reconstruction

abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) ecosystems grow, routing queries to the most suitable model in a diverse pool has become a critical strategy for building efficient and high-performing AI systems. A common approach is to train a supervised router; however, this requires vast, expensive human-annotated preference data and creates models that are notoriously brittle, failing to generalize when faced with inevitable distribution shifts in user queries. Consequently, developing robust, unsupervised routing methods that adapt without retraining is a crucial research frontier. This challenge is severely amplified by Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), which introduce a dual problem for any label-free method: their outputs have a causal thinking $\to$ answer structure that must be modeled, and a structural imbalance where long reasoning text can dominate the final answer signal. We introduce ReasoningRouter, a novel framework that resolves these issues with a length-balanced embedding strategy and a probabilistic model capturing the thinking-to-answer dependency. The proposed Causal Triangulation Property enables the label-free estimation of component qualities and their causal link. Beyond competitive routing accuracy, ReasoningRouter offers unprecedented insights into model behavior, enabling separate quality assessment of reasoning and answer components while maintaining computational efficiency.

Consequently, developing robust, unsupervised routing methods that adapt without retraining is a crucial research frontier. This challenge is severely amplified by Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), which introduce a dual problem for any label-free method: their outputs have a causal thinking $\to$ answer structure that must be modeled, and a structural imbalance where long reasoning text can dominate the final answer signal. We introduce ReasoningRouter, a novel framework that resolves these issues with a length-balanced embedding strategy and a probabilistic model capturing the thinking-to-answer dependency. The proposed Causal Triangulation Property enables the label-free estimation of component qualities and their causal link. Beyond competitive routing accuracy, ReasoningRouter offers unprecedented insights into model behavior, enabling separate quality assessment of reasoning and answer components while maintaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Routing chooses which model in a pool should handle a query. Supervised routers need costly preference labels and can struggle when incoming queries change. Reasoning models add another complication: their output contains a thinking process followed by an answer, and the much longer thinking portion can overwhelm the answer when assessing the output.

ReasoningRouter addresses both the unequal lengths and the relationship between these components. It balances their contributions when constructing embeddings, then uses a probabilistic model to represent the dependency from thinking to answer. Its proposed Causal Triangulation Property enables estimation of the quality of each component and their causal connection without requiring labels.

The paper reports competitive routing accuracy together with computational efficiency. A further contribution is the ability to assess reasoning quality and answer quality separately, providing a more differentiated account of model behavior. This matters because a routing decision can then draw on the structure of a reasoning model’s output instead of treating the entire response as one undivided signal.
summary.tldr: ReasoningRouter routes without labels by balancing reasoning and answer representations and modeling their dependency.

title: Causal Dependency-Aware Unsupervised Routing for Large Reasoning Models

abstract: Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) enables single-pass uncertainty estimation by predicting Dirichlet evidence, but it can remain overconfident and poorly calibrated, and it often fails to represent multi-modal epistemic uncertainty. We introduce Gated Evidential Mixtures (GEM), a family of models that learns an in-model energy signal and uses it to gate evidential outputs end-to-end in a distance-informed manner. GEM-CORE learns a feature-level energy and maps it to a bounded gate that smoothly suppresses evidence when support is low. To capture epistemic multi-modality without multi-pass ensembling, GEM-MIX adds a lightweight mixture of evidential heads with learned routing weights while preserving single-pass inference. Finally, GEM-FI stabilizes mixture allocations via a Fisher-informed regularizer, reducing head collapse and producing smoother boundary uncertainty. Across image classification and OOD detection benchmarks, GEM improves calibration and ID/OOD separation with single-pass inference. On CIFAR-10, GEM-FI vs. DAEDL improves Acc. from 91.11 to 93.75 (+2.64 pp), reduces Brier $\times$100 from 14.27 to 6.81 (-7.46), and also improves misclassification-detection (AUPR) from 99.08 to 99.94 (+0.86). For epistemic OOD detection, GEM-FI achieves AUPR/AUROC of 92.59/95.09 on CIFAR-10$\rightarrow$SVHN and 90.20/89.06 on CIFAR-10$\rightarrow$CIFAR-100 (vs. 85.54/89.30 and 88.19/86.10 for DAEDL).

GEM-FI then uses a Fisher-informed regularizer to stabilize how examples are allocated among heads, reduce head collapse, and smooth uncertainty near boundaries.

It also improves the reported misclassification and out-of-distribution detection measures. The results show that richer uncertainty modeling can be built into one model evaluation without multi-pass ensembling.
summary.tldr: GEM-FI combines gated evidence, multiple prediction heads, and Fisher-informed regularization to improve single-pass uncertainty estimates.

title: GEM-FI: Gated Evidential Mixtures with Fisher Modulation

abstract: Simulation has become a key tool for training and evaluating home robots at scale, yet existing environments fail to capture the diversity and physical complexity of real indoor spaces. Current scene synthesis methods produce sparsely furnished rooms that lack the dense clutter, articulated furniture, and physical properties essential for robotic manipulation. We introduce SceneSmith, a hierarchical agentic framework that generates simulation-ready indoor environments from natural language prompts. SceneSmith constructs scenes through successive stages—from architectural layout to furniture placement to small object population—each implemented as an interaction among VLM agents: designer, critic, and orchestrator. The framework tightly integrates asset generation through text-to-3D synthesis for static objects, dataset retrieval for articulated objects, and physical property estimation. SceneSmith generates 3-6x more objects than prior methods, with $<$2% inter-object collisions and 96% of objects remaining stable under physics simulation. In a user study with 205 participants, it achieves 92% average realism and 91% average prompt faithfulness win rates against baselines. We further demonstrate that these environments can be used in an end-to-end pipeline for automatic robot policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Home-robot simulation needs rooms with realistic clutter, movable furniture parts, and usable physical properties. Sparse scene generation misses much of that complexity. SceneSmith creates indoor environments from natural-language prompts through a hierarchy of stages, moving from architectural layout to furniture placement and then to smaller objects.

Each stage involves vision-language agents acting as designer, critic, and orchestrator. The framework combines text-to-3D generation for static objects with dataset retrieval for articulated objects, and it estimates physical properties. These components connect scene composition to the requirements of simulation, where an object must have suitable physical behavior as well as an appropriate appearance.

The generated scenes contain three to six times as many objects as prior methods, with fewer than 2% inter-object collisions and 96% of objects remaining stable in physics simulation. In a study with 205 participants, SceneSmith achieves average win rates of 92% for realism and 91% for prompt faithfulness against baselines. The authors also demonstrate automatic robot-policy evaluation using the environments, showing their utility beyond visual scene presentation.
summary.tldr: SceneSmith coordinates vision-language agents to generate dense, physically usable indoor environments from text for robot simulation.

title: SceneSmith: Agentic Generation of Simulation-Ready Indoor Scenes

abstract: We study flow-matching transformers when data lie on a low-dimensional manifold. Our key insight is a flow decomposition that splits motion along the manifold from motion off the manifold. The scheme works for first and higher-order flow matching and ties model complexity to the intrinsic manifold dimension. Building on these, we establish tighter sample-complexity bounds for velocity approximation, velocity estimation, and distribution estimation. Our results show how flow-matching transformers escape the curse of dimensionality by utilizing intrinsic data structure.
