paragraphs: This paper studies flow-matching transformers when the data occupy a low-dimensional manifold within a larger space. The distinction is between the number of coordinates used to describe an example and the smaller number of dimensions needed to describe its underlying structure. The analysis asks how this structure changes the difficulty of learning.

The central construction separates the learned motion into a component along the manifold and a component off it. This decomposition applies to both first-order and higher-order flow matching. By treating these components separately, the framework connects model complexity to the manifold's intrinsic dimension, making the geometry of the data part of the theoretical analysis.

Using this construction, the authors derive tighter sample-complexity bounds for velocity approximation, velocity estimation, and distribution estimation. These results address several stages of learning, from representing the motion to estimating the resulting data distribution. Under the manifold setting studied, they explain how flow-matching transformers can exploit intrinsic structure to escape the curse of dimensionality.
summary.tldr: A decomposition of motion along and off a data manifold yields tighter learning bounds for flow-matching transformers.

title: Learning Manifold Data with Flow Matching

abstract: Why do adversarial examples exist, and why do they transfer between models? Existing explanations appeal to high-dimensional geometry, non-robust patterns in the input, and decision boundary structure, but none provides a representation-level mechanism that explains why specific perturbations succeed and why attacks transfer between models. In this paper, we show that adversarial vulnerability can stem from efficient information encoding in neural networks. Specifically, vulnerability can arise from superposition - the phenomenon where networks represent more concepts than they have dimensions, forcing non-orthogonal representation and thus interference. This interference causes perturbations targeting one representation to affect others, creating vulnerabilities determined by interference patterns. In synthetic settings with precisely controlled superposition, we establish that superposition suffices to create adversarial vulnerability. The resulting attacks are predictable: PGD-discovered perturbations align with theoretically optimal perturbations derived from the interference geometry. Models trained on similar data develop similar interference patterns, explaining attack transferability. We then show that successful attacks on image classifiers exhibit the structure predicted by our proposed mechanism. These findings reveal that adversarial vulnerability can be a byproduct of networks’ representational compression, complementing existing explanations based on data properties or architectural factors.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether adversarial vulnerability can arise from how a network compresses information internally. Its proposed mechanism is superposition: representing more concepts than there are available dimensions. Those representations cannot all remain independent, so changing the representation of one concept can interfere with others and create an opening for an adversarial perturbation.

In synthetic settings where the amount of superposition is precisely controlled, the researchers establish that superposition is sufficient to produce vulnerability. They also connect the mechanism to particular attacks: perturbations found by PGD align with theoretically optimal perturbations derived from the interference geometry. The theory therefore predicts attack structure, beyond suggesting that compression might cause problems.

Models trained on similar data develop similar interference patterns, providing an explanation for attacks that transfer between models. Successful attacks on image classifiers also exhibit structure predicted by the mechanism. These findings support representational compression as one possible source of vulnerability; they complement explanations involving data and architecture rather than establishing superposition as the cause of every adversarial example.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments show that interference between compressed feature representations can create adversarial vulnerability and help explain attack transfer.

title: Adversarial Vulnerability from Interference Between Features in Superposition

abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable success in ground-based embodied intelligence, their application to Aerial Manipulation Systems (AMS) remains a largely unexplored frontier. The inherent characteristics of AMS, including floating-base dynamics, strong coupling between the UAV and the manipulator, and the multi-step, long-horizon nature of operational tasks, pose severe challenges to existing VLA paradigms designed for static or 2D mobile bases. To bridge this gap, we propose AIR-VLA, the first VLA benchmark specifically tailored for aerial manipulation. We construct a physics-based simulation environment and release a high-quality multimodal dataset comprising 3000 manually teleoperated demonstrations, covering base manipulation, object & spatial understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Leveraging this platform, we systematically evaluate mainstream VLA models and state-of-the-art VLM models. Our experiments not only validate the feasibility of transferring VLA paradigms to aerial systems but also, through multi-dimensional metrics tailored to aerial tasks, reveal the capabilities and boundaries of current models regarding UAV mobility, manipulator control, and high-level planning. AIR-VLA establishes a standardized testbed and data foundation for future research in general-purpose aerial robotics. The resource of AIR-VLA will be available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AIR-VLA-dataset-B5CC/.

paragraphs: AIR-VLA provides a benchmark for robots that manipulate objects while flying. These systems combine a UAV with a manipulator, so movement of the flying base and movement of the arm are strongly coupled. Tasks can also require multiple steps and extended planning, creating challenges beyond those faced by models designed for stationary or ground-based robots.

The authors build a physics-based simulation environment and a multimodal dataset containing 3,000 manually teleoperated demonstrations. The tasks cover basic manipulation, understanding objects and spatial relationships, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. This combination makes it possible to examine both physical control and higher-level task understanding within the same aerial setting.

Using the platform, the paper evaluates mainstream vision-language-action models and state-of-the-art vision-language models. The results support the feasibility of transferring these approaches to aerial systems while revealing current capabilities and boundaries in UAV movement, manipulator control, and planning. The main contribution is a standardized experimental foundation for studying these connected demands.
summary.tldr: AIR-VLA benchmarks aerial manipulation with a physics simulator, 3,000 demonstrations, and evaluations of current vision-language models.

title: AIR-VLA: Vision-Language-Action Systems for Aerial Manipulation

abstract: Neural rough differential equations (NRDEs) stay accurate under irregular sampling while taking far fewer integration steps than standard neural differential equations, summarising a finely sampled driver by its log-signature and advancing the hidden state over coarse intervals using the log-ODE method. This efficiency rests on the shuffle algebra, the algebraic counterpart of Stratonovich calculus. This reliance means NRDEs cannot expose the quadratic-variation terms Itô dynamics require, nor the ordered covariant derivatives that govern Itô flows on connection-equipped manifolds. Ameliorating this, we introduce Branched Neural Rough Differential Equations (B-NRDEs), a Hopf-algebraic framework that recasts the NRDE log-ODE step as geometric numerical integration on the state-space manifold, matching the driving algebra to the governing calculus: Grossman–Larson rooted trees for Euclidean Itô dynamics, Munthe–Kaas–Wright planar rooted trees for ordered covariant derivatives on manifolds, and the shuffle algebra in the classical Stratonovich case. This yields intrinsic coarse-step dynamics that exactly preserve manifold constraints. Finally, we introduce a branched signature-kernel objective to enable Itô-consistent law matching by making quadratic-variation terms visible during training. On rough Bergomi volatility, sim-to-real $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ forecasting, and SPD covariance dynamics, B-NRDEs offer a unified, effective approach to stochastic and manifold-valued dynamics beyond the Euclidean–Stratonovich setting.

paragraphs: Neural rough differential equations summarize finely sampled inputs so that hidden states can advance in larger integration steps, retaining accuracy under irregular sampling. Their usual mathematical structure follows Stratonovich calculus. This creates a limitation for Itô dynamics, which require quadratic-variation terms, and for manifold-valued Itô flows, where the ordering of covariant derivatives matters.

Branched Neural Rough Differential Equations replace this single algebraic setup with structures matched to the governing calculus. Rooted trees represent Euclidean Itô dynamics, planar rooted trees support ordered derivatives on manifolds, and the classical shuffle algebra remains available for Stratonovich dynamics. The framework treats coarse integration steps geometrically and exactly preserves the manifold constraints of its intrinsic dynamics.

The paper also introduces a branched signature-kernel training objective that exposes quadratic-variation terms, enabling Itô-consistent matching of probability laws. Applications include rough Bergomi volatility, simulation-to-real rotation forecasting on SO(3), and positive-definite covariance dynamics. Together, these results support a unified approach to learning stochastic and geometrically constrained dynamics beyond the usual Euclidean–Stratonovich setting.
summary.tldr: B-NRDEs adapt rough differential equation models to Itô calculus and manifold geometry while preserving manifold constraints.

title: Learning Manifold and Itô Dynamics with Branched Neural Rough Differential Equations

abstract: Efficiently training recurrent neural networks on long sequences remains an open challenge. The standard global paradigm, backpropagation through time (BPTT), suffers from vanishing and exploding gradients and memory costs that scale linearly with sequence length. Conversely, biologically inspired local learning rules are memory-efficient but typically introduce severe bias. To bridge this gap, we introduce Criticality-driven Online Local Alignment (COLA). By leveraging the long-range spatiotemporal correlations inherent to the critical regime, COLA enables a strictly local learning rule to approximate global error propagation, thereby combining online efficiency with gradient descent precision. Theoretically, for a recurrent neural network with $H$ hidden units, COLA requires only an $O(H)$ auxiliary state and constant activation memory, completely independent of sequence length. Empirically, COLA is competitive with BPTT on standard benchmarks and demonstrates superior robustness on stability-sensitive tasks. Finally, we conduct a rigorous analysis of the approximation error to provide a theoretical foundation for reliable online learning. Code is available at https://github.com/Criticality-Cognitive-Computation-Lab/COLA

paragraphs: Training recurrent networks requires assigning responsibility for errors to computations that may have happened far earlier. Backpropagation through time performs this global assignment, but its activation memory grows with sequence length and its gradients can vanish or explode. Local learning rules save memory, yet often provide strongly biased updates.

Criticality-driven Online Local Alignment, or COLA, uses long-range correlations present when a network operates in a critical dynamical regime. These correlations allow a strictly local learning rule to approximate how errors would propagate globally. The critical regime is central to the mechanism: it supplies the relationships across space and time that make local information useful for estimating broader effects.

For a recurrent network with H hidden units, the theoretical memory requirements are O(H) auxiliary state and constant activation memory, both independent of sequence length. Experiments find COLA competitive with backpropagation through time on standard benchmarks and more robust on stability-sensitive tasks. An accompanying approximation-error analysis supports the method’s theoretical basis. The contribution is an efficient approximation to global credit assignment, rather than an assertion that local updates always equal exact gradients.
summary.tldr: COLA uses correlations in critical recurrent dynamics to approximate global learning with local updates and memory independent of sequence length.

title: Global Credit Assignment via Dynamical Criticality

abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are attractive for low-cost agent deployment, and their growing capabilities make them promising for procedure-centric workloads that repeatedly execute specialized task families with similar workflows. However, SLM agents still struggle in long-horizon interaction because limited context budgets make it difficult to reliably retain and reuse decision-relevant state across many steps. Existing working-memory methods attempt to mitigate context growth, but their reliance on unstructured natural-language summarization can discard critical facts, introduce state drift, and compound errors in SLM execution. We present LightWM, a training-free hierarchical working-memory framework that decomposes procedure-centric tasks into subgoals and organizes memory into task-level global memory and subtask-level local memory, where local memory directly conditions SLM action selection and is updated from new observations through structured updates. To instantiate such memories without training, a one-time offline LLM-based induction pipeline builds reusable schemas per task family from a few successful traces, requiring no SLM parameter updates or online LLM calls. On ALFWorld valid_unseen, Qwen3-4B reaches 0.910 success, whereas representative prompting and prior working-memory baselines under the same setting remain below 0.320.

paragraphs: Small language models are appealing for inexpensive agents, but long interactions can exceed their ability to retain decision-relevant state. Summarizing history in unstructured prose can also omit critical facts or gradually distort the state. LightWM addresses this problem for procedure-centric task families whose workflows recur, organizing memory around the structure of the work.

The framework decomposes a task into subgoals and maintains two memory levels: global memory for the overall task and local memory for the current subtask. Local memory directly guides action selection and receives structured updates from new observations. A one-time offline pipeline uses a larger language model and a few successful traces to induce reusable schemas for each task family. This result supports structured, reusable memory as an effective way to improve extended procedural execution in the evaluated small-model agent.
summary.tldr: LightWM equips small-model agents with reusable structured memories, substantially improving success on the reported ALFWorld evaluation without online large-model calls.

title: LightWM: Training-Free Hierarchical Working Memory for Small Language Model Agents

abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into ad auctions for dynamic creative enhancement presents a paradigm shift, yet introduces significant computational costs disrupting traditional mechanism design. This paper provides a comprehensive game-theoretic and algorithmic framework for such LLM-augmented auctions. We model the system as a dynamic Stackelberg game where the platform (leader) strategically invests in creative enhancement to maximize net revenue, while autobidding agents (followers) respond to enhanced ad qualities under budget constraints. To endogenize inference costs, we propose the Platform-Investment Mechanism (PIM). We develop the Online Dual-Descent Bidding with Regularization (ODDB-R) algorithm for agents to learn optimal bidding strategies in this non-stationary environment. For the platform, we formulate the investment problem as a continuous control task and solve it using a Two-Timescale Stackelberg Learning with Proximal Policy Optimization (TTSL-PPO) algorithm, which provably converges to a Stackelberg Stationary Point. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world datasets and state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms heuristic baselines in revenue, social welfare, and user engagement.

paragraphs: Using language models to improve advertising creatives changes an auction’s economics because generating those improvements costs computation. The platform must decide how much to invest in ad quality while advertisers’ automated bidding agents respond under budget constraints. The paper models this interaction as a dynamic leader–follower game, with the platform choosing investments and bidders reacting.

The proposed Platform-Investment Mechanism explicitly incorporates inference costs into the platform’s decisions. For bidders, an online dual-descent algorithm with regularization learns bidding strategies as the environment changes. For the platform, the researchers formulate investment as a continuous control problem and develop a two-timescale learning algorithm based on proximal policy optimization. This connects creative enhancement, its cost, and bidding behavior within one framework.

The platform algorithm is proved to converge to a Stackelberg stationary point, a qualified convergence result rather than a claim of global optimality. Experiments using large real-world datasets and contemporary language models report significant improvements over heuristic baselines in revenue, social welfare, and user engagement. The findings indicate that coordinating investment and bidding can improve several auction outcomes together.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly models costly LLM creative enhancement and automated bidding, improving auction outcomes over tested heuristic approaches.

title: Autobidding Auctions with LLM-Powered Creatives

abstract: Geo-temporal understanding, the ability to infer location, time, and contextual properties from visual input alone, underpins applications such as disaster management, traffic planning, embodied navigation, world modeling, and geography education. Although recent vision–language models (VLMs) have advanced image geo-localization using cues like landmarks and road signs, their ability to reason about temporal signals and physically grounded spatial cues remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce TimeSpot, a benchmark for evaluating real-world geo-temporal reasoning in VLMs. TimeSpot comprises 1,455 ground-level images from 80 countries and requires structured prediction of temporal attributes (season, month, time of day, daylight phase) and geographic attributes (continent, country, climate zone, environment type, latitude–longitude) directly from visual evidence. It also includes spatial–temporal reasoning tasks that test physical plausibility under real-world uncertainty. Evaluations of state-of-the-art open- and closed-source VLMs show low performance, particularly for temporal inference. While supervised fine-tuning yields improvements, results remain insufficient, highlighting the need for new methods to achieve robust, physically grounded geo-temporal understanding. TimeSpot is available at: https://TimeSpot-GT.github.io.
originalAbstract: Geo-temporal understanding, the ability to infer location, time, and contextual properties from visual input alone, underpins applications such as disaster management, traffic planning, embodied navigation, world modeling, and geography education. Although recent vision–language models (VLMs) have advanced image geo-localization using cues like landmarks and road signs, their ability to reason about temporal signals and physically grounded spatial cues remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce TimeSpot, a benchmark for evaluating real-world geo-temporal reasoning in VLMs. TimeSpot comprises 1,455 ground-level images from 80 countries and requires structured prediction of temporal attributes (season, month, time of day, daylight phase) and geographic attributes (continent, country, climate zone, environment type, latitude–longitude) directly from visual evidence. It also includes spatial–temporal reasoning tasks that test physical plausibility under real-world uncertainty. Evaluations of state-of-the-art open- and closed-source VLMs show low performance, particularly for temporal inference. While supervised fine-tuning yields improvements, results remain insufficient, highlighting the need for new methods to achieve robust, physically grounded geo-temporal understanding. TimeSpot is available at: https://TimeSpot-GT.github.io.

paragraphs: Understanding a photograph’s setting involves more than recognizing its location. A model may also need to infer the season, time of day, or whether spatial and temporal clues fit together physically. TimeSpot evaluates this broader ability using visual evidence alone, extending beyond location recognition from landmarks and road signs.

The benchmark contains 1,455 ground-level images from 80 countries. It requests structured predictions of temporal attributes, including season, month, time of day, and daylight phase. Geographic predictions include continent, country, climate zone, environment type, and coordinates. Additional reasoning tasks test physical plausibility while accounting for the uncertainty present in real-world images.

Evaluations of leading open- and closed-source vision-language models show low performance, especially on temporal inference. Supervised fine-tuning improves results, but the authors find the resulting performance still insufficient. The benchmark therefore exposes weaknesses in connecting visual cues to time and physical context, even when models can recognize geographic information. Its tasks provide a way to assess progress on these related capabilities together.
summary.tldr: TimeSpot tests location, time, and physical-context inference from images, revealing especially weak temporal understanding in evaluated vision-language models.

title: TimeSpot: Benchmarking Geo-Temporal Understanding in Vision–Language Models in Real-World Settings

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are strong passive responders, but learning to proactively elicit information—asking the right questions and stopping at the right time—remains difficult. Existing approaches, such as optimizing turn-level attributes or relying on user simulators to generate training trajectories, often struggle with a persistent reality gap. We propose Learn-to-Ask, a simulator-free framework that learns proactive questioning policies directly from offline expert conversations. Our key insight is to leverage the observed future of each expert trajectory to derive dense, turn-level rewards that reflect expert long-horizon strategy, reducing policy learning to a sequence of supervised learning tasks that jointly enable LLMs to know what to ask and when to stop. To ensure the LLM-generated contents, such as reward fidelity and sampling quality, align with expectations, we further introduce an automated pipeline that calibrates the prompts with minimal human supervision. Across multiple datasets and model scales, Learn-to-Ask consistently improves proactive information-seeking behavior. We also report a large-scale real-world deployment where the trained agent surpasses an internal expert baseline under professional audit, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our framework and our rewards as a reality-validated proxy metric for LLM proactivity.

Learn-to-Ask instead learns questioning policies from existing conversations conducted by experts.

The framework uses the observed continuation of each expert conversation to assign informative rewards to individual turns. These rewards are intended to capture how a question contributes to the expert’s longer-term strategy. Policy learning becomes a sequence of supervised learning tasks covering both question selection and stopping. An automated prompt-calibration pipeline uses minimal human supervision to improve generated rewards and sampling quality.

Across multiple datasets and model scales, the authors report consistent gains in proactive information seeking. They also describe a large-scale deployment in which the trained agent surpasses an internal expert baseline under professional audit. This supplies real-world evidence for the framework and supports the proposed rewards as a useful proxy for proactivity in that deployment.
summary.tldr: Learn-to-Ask uses the recorded futures of expert conversations to train better questioning and stopping policies without user simulators.

title: Grounded in Reality: Learning and Deploying Proactive LLM from Offline Logs

abstract: We propose Progressive Structure Adjustment for Homophily Shift (PSAHS), a lightweight method for Graph Domain Adaptation (GDA) that explicitly addresses cross-domain mismatch in node-level homophily. PSAHS enhances node homophily in the source graph to a prescribed level by reweighting edges and introducing additional intra-class connections for low-homophily nodes, and conservatively refines the target graph using agreement-consistent predictions from a structure-aware Graph Neural Network (GNN) and an attribute-only Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to ensure reliability under label scarcity. After each structural refinement, domain-adversarial training is employed to align node representations across domains. PSAHS employs a progressive training scheme that alternates between structure adjustment and representation alignment, where increasingly informative representations enable safer homophily correction, and the refined structure in turn improves representation learning. Extensive experiments on multiple GDA benchmarks demonstrate that PSAHS consistently outperforms strong baselines, with particularly large gains under severe homophily mismatch, highlighting the importance of explicit homophily alignment for effective cross-graph transfer.

paragraphs: Graph models can struggle to transfer when connected nodes share labels at different rates in the source and target graphs. This property is called homophily. PSAHS addresses the mismatch directly by progressively modifying graph structure alongside the representations used for prediction.

On the source graph, the method reweights edges and adds same-class connections for nodes with low homophily, aiming for a prescribed level. Target labels are scarce, so target changes rely on agreement between a graph neural network that uses structure and a multilayer perceptron that uses only node attributes. This agreement guides conservative refinement of the target graph.

After each refinement, domain-adversarial training aligns node representations across the two domains. Alternating these stages lets improved representations inform subsequent structural changes, while the revised structure supports further learning. Experiments across graph domain-adaptation benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines, with especially large gains under severe homophily mismatch. The results support explicitly adjusting connectivity patterns as part of transferring knowledge between graphs.
summary.tldr: PSAHS alternates graph-structure refinement and representation alignment to improve transfer when source and target graphs differ in homophily.

title: Progressive Graph Structure Adjustment for Homophily Shift Adaptation

abstract: In recent years, there has been growing interest in understanding neural architectures’ ability to learn to execute discrete algorithms, a line of work often referred to as neural algorithmic reasoning. The goal is to integrate algorithmic reasoning capabilities into larger neural pipelines. Many such architectures are based on (message-passing) graph neural networks (MPNNs), owing to their permutation equivariance and ability to deal with sparsity and variable-sized inputs. However, much existing work is either largely empirical and lacks formal guarantees or it focuses solely on expressivity, leaving open the question of when and how such architectures generalize beyond a finite training set. In this work, we propose a general theoretical framework that characterizes sufficient conditions under which MPNNs can learn an algorithm from a training set of small instances and provably approximate its behavior on inputs of arbitrary size with worst-case guarantees. Our framework applies to a broad class of algorithms, including single-source shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, and general dynamic programming problems, such as the $0$-$1$ knapsack problem. In addition, we establish impossibility results for a wide range of algorithmic tasks, showing that standard MPNNs cannot learn them and derive more expressive MPNN-like architectures that overcome these limitations. Finally, we refine our analysis for the Bellman–Ford algorithm, yielding substantially smaller required training sets and significantly extending the recent work of Nerem et al., 2025 by allowing for a differentiable regularization loss. Empirical results largely support our theoretical findings.

title: Which Algorithms Can Graph Neural Networks Learn?

abstract: The quadratic cost of attention limits the scalability of long-context LLMs, especially under limited hardware memory budgets. While attention is often sparse, existing static sparse methods cannot adapt to task- or input-dependent variations, and recent dynamic approaches rely on predefined templates or heuristics that may sacrifice generality. We propose Dynamic Hierarchical Sparse Attention (DHSA), a data-driven framework that predicts attention sparsity online while keeping the LLM backbone frozen. DHSA performs hierarchical routing by estimating importance at the chunk level and propagating it to token-level interactions, preserving causally important dependencies while enabling efficient sparsification. Across Needle-in-a-Haystack test, LongBench and RULER, DHSA maintains near-dense accuracy in highly sparse regimes, achieving 12–20% relative accuracy gains over Block Sparse Attention at comparable prefill cost. With a memory-efficient tiled backend, DHSA delivers up to $10\times$ prefill speedup at 128K context length. On LLaMA-3.1-8B (4-bit), DHSA scales to 100K context on a single 24GB GPU, where dense attention fails. We provide complementary GPU and CPU backends, enabling DHSA to run across diverse hardware environments and multiple open-weight model families. These results demonstrate DHSA as an efficient and adaptable solution for memory-constrained long-context LLM inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/xiongsiheng/DHSA.

Dynamic Hierarchical Sparse Attention predicts which interactions matter online while keeping the underlying language model frozen.

summary.tldr: DHSA predicts sparse attention hierarchically to preserve long-context accuracy while reducing prefill cost and memory requirements.

title: Long-Context Modeling with Dynamic Hierarchical Sparse Attention for Memory-Constrained LLM Inference

abstract: The advancement of artificial neural networks (ANNs) has been driven by diverse and well-established architectural designs, especially in connectivity. Biological neural networks, which exhibit a rich variety of neurodynamic circuits, offer a valuable source of inspiration for developing novel ANN models. In this study, we analyze the meta-connectivity structure and introduce a network motif-based approach, in which 13 distinct motifs are modeled as functional building blocks. These motifs represent low-dimensional, fundamental components of larger network architectures. Through rigorous theoretical analysis, we classify these motifs into a three-layer hierarchical classification of their dynamical regimes and demonstrate that their hierarchical proportions critically shape collective neural dynamics. Furthermore, by embedding motif distributions into recurrent neural networks (RNNs), we show that these motifs can selectively enhance either network robustness or flexibility. Collectively, our findings provide a theoretical framework—supported by extensive experiments—for understanding how specific network motifs influence the computational properties of artificial intelligence systems via their underlying dynamics. This motif-driven approach offers significant potential for analyzing and modulating neural dynamics in ANNs.

paragraphs: Neural-network connectivity affects how activity evolves, but large architectures can make that relationship difficult to interpret. This study examines smaller connectivity patterns, called motifs, as functional building blocks. Inspired by the variety of circuits in biological networks, the authors model 13 distinct motifs as low-dimensional components of larger artificial networks.

The theoretical analysis organizes these motifs into a three-layer hierarchy of dynamical regimes. It then shows that the proportions of motifs within this hierarchy critically shape the network’s collective dynamics. This connects local wiring patterns to behavior at the scale of the whole network: the relevant design choice includes how frequently different functional patterns appear.

The authors embed motif distributions into recurrent neural networks and show that these distributions can selectively improve robustness or flexibility. Extensive experiments support the theoretical framework. The contribution is a way to understand and potentially adjust computational properties through underlying dynamics, using distributions of small connectivity structures as a handle on larger architectural behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper links 13 small connectivity motifs to collective neural dynamics and shows how their distributions can enhance RNN robustness or flexibility.

title: Functional building blocks of neural networks: from network motifs to collective dynamics

abstract: Memory-based test-time adaptation (TTA) assigns streaming test samples into class-specific memory slots based on pseudo-labels predicted by models like CLIP, and retrieves them to facilitate subsequent predictions under distribution shift. However, this process introduces two challenges: (1) Each sample is hard-assigned to a single class based on CLIP’s prediction, where inaccurate CLIP prediction leads to memory contamination that biases subsequent prediction. (2) Samples are evicted under biased selection due to fixed memory capacity, which risks discarding informative samples and undermining the efficacy of the memory. To address these challenges, we propose A$^2$Memory (Attributive-Associative Memory for Test-time Adaptation). For challenge (1), we propose Attribute-centric Memory Construction that builds prior textual representations from class-shared representative and diverse visual attributes, and applies soft assignment to generate surrogate visual representations. For challenge (2), we design Class-wise Associative Memory that dynamically compresses streaming samples into fixed-capacity memory through gradient-based optimization and data-dependent retention, then retrieves sample-adaptive class prototypes for reliable inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods across 15 benchmarks.

paragraphs: Memory-based test-time adaptation uses incoming examples to improve later predictions when the data distribution changes. However, assigning each example to a single class using a model’s own prediction can store mistakes that bias future decisions. Limited memory capacity creates another problem when eviction discards informative examples.

A²Memory addresses class assignment through representations built from diverse visual attributes shared across classes. It uses these textual representations and soft assignment to construct surrogate visual representations, reducing reliance on a single predicted label. Its associative memory then compresses the incoming stream into fixed capacity through gradient-based optimization and data-dependent retention. Retrieval produces class prototypes adapted to the current sample.

Experiments across 15 benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The framework’s contribution is to treat both memory construction and retention as parts of adaptation that need careful design. Its results support using attribute information to handle uncertain assignments and learned compression to preserve useful information within a bounded memory, improving subsequent predictions under distribution shift.
summary.tldr: A²Memory improves online adaptation through attribute-based soft assignment and learned compression of a fixed-capacity memory.

title: Learning to Memorize with Attributive and Associative Memory for Online Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models

abstract: Radio Frequency (RF) sensing has emerged as a powerful, privacy-preserving alternative to vision-based methods for various perception tasks. However, building high-quality RF datasets in dynamic and diverse environments remains a major challenge. To address this, we introduce WaveVerse, a prompt-based, scalable framework that simulates realistic RF signals from generated indoor scenes with human motions guided by spatial paths, enabling diverse and feasible behaviors without manual trajectory design. WaveVerse features a language-guided 4D world generator and a physics-based signal simulator that enables realistic simulation of RF signals in diverse environments. It employs a phase-coherent ray tracer that preserves both spatial and temporal phase consistency. The simulated signals show high fidelity on phase-sensitive benchmarks, and closely align with both real-world collected measurements and simulations from a proprietary electromagnetic solver. When used for data augmentation, WaveVerse consistently improves performance in downstream tasks like RF imaging and human activity recognition, with gains that grow with the amount of simulated data and surpass existing methods. Code and additional materials are available on the webpage.

paragraphs: Radio-frequency sensing offers a privacy-preserving alternative to visual perception, but collecting varied data from changing environments is difficult. WaveVerse addresses this data problem through simulation. Given prompts, it generates indoor scenes with human motion guided by spatial paths, supporting diverse feasible behaviors without requiring manually designed trajectories.

The framework combines a language-guided generator of evolving three-dimensional worlds with a physics-based RF signal simulator. Its ray tracer preserves phase consistency across both space and time. That consistency is central to the paper's approach because the evaluation includes benchmarks sensitive to signal phase, tying the simulated environment to demanding signal-level behavior.

The simulated signals closely match collected real-world measurements and results from a proprietary electromagnetic solver, according to the reported evaluations. Using them for augmentation consistently improves RF imaging and human activity recognition, with gains increasing as more simulated data is added and exceeding existing methods. These results connect simulation fidelity with downstream usefulness, supporting generated dynamic environments as a scalable source of RF training data.
summary.tldr: WaveVerse generates dynamic indoor worlds and phase-consistent RF signals that improve downstream sensing tasks through data augmentation.

title: Scalable RF Simulation in Generative 4D Worlds

abstract: Many failures of deployed machine learning systems stem not from insufficient accuracy, but from neglecting responsibility as a core design requirement. While responsibility principles are widely studied, they are often treated as post-hoc checks rather than as integral factors of system design. This framework has reinforced the perception that responsible practices inherently trade-off with model performance. We challenge the assumption that responsibility necessarily reduces performance and argue that, in many practical settings, responsible practices improve robustness, reliability, and real-world effectiveness. We adopt a lifecycle-oriented perspective, identifying which responsible AI principles are most critical at each stage, from problem formulation and data curation to training, deployment, and monitoring. Drawing on real-world instances, we show how misaligned choices at specific stages can compound downstream risks and how alternative design choices could have mitigated these failures. Importantly, we argue for a system-level notion of performance that includes not only predictive accuracy, but also robustness, calibration, fairness, reliability, and deployability under real-world conditions.

The authors argue that many deployment failures arise because responsibility was treated as a final check instead of a design requirement. In many practical settings, attending to responsibility can improve robustness, reliability, and effectiveness under actual operating conditions.

The analysis follows the full system lifecycle, from defining the problem and curating data through training, deployment, and monitoring. It identifies which responsibility principles matter at different stages and draws on real-world cases to show how poor choices can create accumulating downstream risks. The authors also consider alternative design choices that could have reduced those failures.

The paper’s broader proposal is to evaluate performance at the system level. Predictive accuracy remains relevant, but the definition also includes calibration, fairness, reliability, robustness, and the ability to deploy successfully. Under this perspective, responsible design contributes directly to what makes a system useful. The claim is that responsibility and performance often reinforce one another; it does not assert that every design decision is free of tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: Integrating responsibility throughout development can improve real-world system performance, challenging the assumption of an inevitable tradeoff.

title: Position: Responsible Practices and Model Performance are *Not* Competing Goals

abstract: This paper presents a novel framework called proto-reinforcement learning (PRL), based on a mathematical model of a proto-value function: these are task-independent basis functions that form the building blocks of all value functions on a given state space manifold. Proto-value functions are learned not from rewards, but instead from analyzing the topology of the state space. Formally, proto-value functions are Fourier eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami diffusion operator on the state space manifold. Proto-value functions facilitate structural decomposition of large state spaces, and form geodesically smooth orthonormal basis functions for approximating any value function. The theoretical basis for proto-value functions combines insights from spectral graph theory, harmonic analysis, and Riemannian manifolds. Protovalue functions enable a novel generation of algorithms called representation policy iteration, unifying the learning of representation and behavior.

paragraphs: This paper proposes learning reusable building blocks for value functions from the structure of a state space. These building blocks, called proto-value functions, are independent of a particular reward task. The framework learns them by analyzing the topology of the state space rather than deriving them from rewards.

Mathematically, proto-value functions are Fourier eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami diffusion operator on the state-space manifold. They form an orthonormal basis whose smoothness follows the geometry of that space. The paper uses this structure both to decompose large state spaces and to provide basis functions for approximating value functions.

The theoretical framework brings together spectral graph theory, harmonic analysis, and Riemannian geometry. Its reinforcement-learning consequence is a family of algorithms called representation policy iteration, which connects learning a representation with learning behavior. The key contribution is to make the state space itself a source of representation: its topology supplies task-independent components that can be used when constructing value functions for particular rewards. This places representation learning inside the process of learning a policy.
summary.tldr: Proto-value functions learn task-independent value-function building blocks from state-space geometry, linking representation learning with policy learning.

title: Proto-value functions: developmental reinforcement learning
Learning algorithms for online principal-agent problems (and selling goods online)
A graphical model for predicting protein molecular function

abstract: We describe an algorithm for learning in the presence of multiple criteria. Our technique generalizes previous approaches in that it can learn optimal policies for any linear preference assignment over the multiple reward criteria. The algorithm can be viewed as an extension to standard reinforcement learning for MDPs where instead of repeatedly backing up maximal expected rewards, we back up the set of expected rewards that are maximal for some set of linear preferences (given by a weight vector, w). We present the algorithm, along with a proof of correctness showing that our solution gives the optimal policy for any linear preference function. The solution reduces to the standard value iteration algorithm for a specific weight vector.

paragraphs: A decision-making problem can have several reward criteria, with different preferences assigning different importance to each. This paper develops an algorithm that learns optimal policies across linear combinations of those criteria. Its target is a solution that supports any linear preference assignment, rather than requiring the entire problem to be expressed through one fixed weighting.

The algorithm extends the backup operation used in reinforcement learning for Markov decision processes. Instead of retaining only a maximal expected reward for a single objective, it backs up a set of expected reward outcomes. Each retained outcome is maximal for some set of preference weights, preserving alternatives that can matter under different linear preferences.

The authors provide a correctness proof showing that the solution yields an optimal policy for any linear preference function. For a specific weight vector, the approach reduces to standard value iteration. The linear form of the preferences is central to the stated result: the guarantee concerns weighted combinations of the reward criteria, not unrestricted ways of expressing preferences.
summary.tldr: Set-valued reward backups extend value iteration to recover an optimal policy for any linear weighting of multiple reward criteria.

title: Learning all optimal policies with multiple criteria

abstract: A broad class of boosting algorithms can be interpreted as performing coordinate-wise gradient descent to minimize some potential function of the margins of a data set. This class includes AdaBoost, LogitBoost, and other widely used and well-studied boosters. In this paper we show that for a broad class of convex potential functions, any such boosting algorithm is highly susceptible to random classification noise. We do this by showing that for any such booster and any nonzero random classification noise rate R, there is a simple data set of examples which is efficiently learnable by such a booster if there is no noise, but which cannot be learned to accuracy better than 1/2 if there is random classification noise at rate R. This negative result is in contrast with known branching program based boosters which do not fall into the convex potential function framework and which can provably learn to high accuracy in the presence of random classification noise.

paragraphs: Many boosting algorithms can be viewed as coordinate-wise gradient descent on a potential function of classification margins. This perspective includes AdaBoost, LogitBoost, and other established methods. The paper studies how algorithms in this framework behave when labels contain random classification noise.

For a broad class of convex potential functions, the authors prove a strong negative result. For every covered booster and every nonzero noise rate, there exists a simple dataset that the booster can learn efficiently without noise but cannot learn beyond one-half accuracy with that noise. The statement is existential: it establishes troublesome datasets for each covered method, not failure on every noisy dataset.

The result contrasts with known boosters based on branching programs, which lie outside the convex-potential framework and have guarantees of high accuracy under random classification noise. This distinction matters because the failure is tied to the studied algorithmic framework rather than to boosting in its entirety. Even an arbitrarily small positive noise rate can expose the demonstrated weakness on an appropriate dataset.
summary.tldr: For every booster in a broad convex-potential class, any positive random label-noise rate admits a learnable clean dataset on which noisy accuracy cannot exceed one-half.

title: Random classification noise defeats all convex potential boosters

abstract: Dyadic data arises in many real world applications such as social network analysis and information retrieval. In order to discover the underlying or hidden structure in the dyadic data, many topic modeling techniques were proposed. The typical algorithms include Probabilistic Latent Semantic Analysis (PLSA) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). The probability density functions obtained by both of these two algorithms are supported on the Euclidean space. However, many previous studies have shown naturally occurring data may reside on or close to an underlying submanifold. We introduce a probabilistic framework for modeling both the topical and geometrical structure of the dyadic data that explicitly takes into account the local manifold structure. Specifically, the local manifold structure is modeled by a graph. The graph Laplacian, analogous to the Laplace-Beltrami operator on manifolds, is applied to smooth the probability density functions. As a result, the obtained probabilistic distributions are concentrated around the data manifold. Experimental results on real data sets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Dyadic data describe relationships between pairs of entities and appear in applications such as social network analysis and information retrieval. Topic models can uncover hidden structure in these relationships. This paper argues that probabilistic modeling should also account for the possibility that naturally occurring data lie on or near a lower-dimensional manifold.

The proposed framework models topical structure together with the data's geometry. It represents local manifold structure using a graph, then uses the graph Laplacian to smooth probability density functions. The Laplacian serves as a discrete counterpart to a manifold-based smoothing operator, connecting nearby data through the graph during probabilistic modeling.

As a result, the learned distributions concentrate around the data manifold. This matters because the model can reflect the local organization of the observations alongside their hidden topical structure. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is the explicit integration of geometric information into probabilistic dyadic analysis, motivated by data whose structure may not be well represented by the surrounding Euclidean space alone.
summary.tldr: Graph-based smoothing helps probabilistic models of dyadic data capture both hidden topics and local manifold structure.

title: Probabilistic dyadic data analysis with local and global consistency

abstract: This paper proposes an efficient sparse metric learning algorithm in high dimensional space via an $\ell_1$-penalized log-determinant regularization. Compare to the most existing distance metric learning algorithms, the proposed algorithm exploits the sparsity nature underlying the intrinsic high dimensional feature space. This sparsity prior of learning distance metric serves to regularize the complexity of the distance model especially in the ``less example number $p$ and high dimension $d$" setting. Theoretically, by analogy to the covariance estimation problem, we find the proposed distance learning algorithm has a consistent result at rate $\mathcal O\left(\sqrt{\left( {m^2 \log d} \right)/n}\right)$ to the target distance matrix with at most $m$ nonzeros per row. Moreover, from the implementation perspective, this $\ell_1$-penalized log-determinant formulation can be efficiently optimized in a block coordinate descent fashion which is much faster than the standard semi-definite programming which has been widely adopted in many other advanced distance learning algorithms. We compare this algorithm with other state-of-the-art ones on various datasets and competitive results are obtained.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning fits a rule for measuring how far apart examples are. In a high-dimensional space, that rule can become complex, especially when relatively few examples are available. This paper introduces a sparse metric learning formulation that uses an L1 penalty together with log-determinant regularization to control the complexity of the learned distance model.

The approach explicitly uses an assumption of sparsity in the underlying feature relationships. Through an analogy with covariance estimation, the authors establish a consistency result for a target distance matrix with at most m nonzero entries per row. The stated convergence rate is O(sqrt((m² log d)/n)). Its dependence on sparsity and dimension makes the structural assumption central to the theoretical result.

For computation, the formulation supports block coordinate descent, which updates portions of the optimization variables in turn. The authors report that this is much faster than standard semidefinite programming approaches used for metric learning. Comparisons on several datasets yield competitive results, supporting the combination of sparse modeling and more efficient optimization.
summary.tldr: Sparse metric learning combines L1 and log-determinant regularization with efficient optimization and a consistency result for sparse target matrices.

title: An efficient sparse metric learning in high-dimensional space via l1-penalized log-determinant regularization

abstract: In a trend that reflects the increasing demand for intelligent applications driven by business data, IBM today is building out a significant number of applications that leverage machine learning technologies to optimize business process decisions. This talk highlights this trend; and describes the many different ways in which leading edge machine learning concepts are being utilized in business applications developed by IBM for its internal use and for clients.
originalAbstract: In a trend that reflects the increasing demand for intelligent applications driven by business data, IBM today is building out a significant number of applications that leverage machine learning technologies to optimize business process decisions. paragraphs: This talk describes how machine learning is being used in IBM applications to improve business-process decisions. Its starting point is growing demand for intelligent applications driven by business data. The abstract presents IBM's development of a substantial collection of such applications as an example of that broader demand.

The emphasis is on the connection between learning techniques and the decisions made within business processes. Machine learning appears here as a component of applications built to serve operational purposes. The talk covers applications developed for IBM's own use as well as those developed for clients, giving the discussion both internal and customer-facing settings.

The stated contribution is an overview of the different ways advanced machine-learning concepts are being applied in those systems. It highlights a deployment trend and describes practical uses, rather than presenting one shared algorithm as the focus of the talk. For readers, the central perspective is that business data can motivate machine-learning applications whose intended value lies in improving the decisions a process makes.
summary.tldr: This talk surveys IBM's use of machine learning in internal and client applications intended to improve business-process decisions.

title: The Role of Machine Learning in Business Optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of selecting, from among the arms of a stochastic n-armed bandit, a subset of size m of those arms with the highest expected rewards, based on efficiently sampling the arms. This “subset selection” problem finds application in a variety of areas. Kalyanakrishnan & Stone (2010) frame this problem under a PAC setting (denoting it “Explore-m”) and analyze corresponding sampling algorithms both formally and experimentally. Whereas their formal analysis is restricted to the worst case sample complexity of algorithms, in this paper, we design and analyze an algorithm (“LUCB”) with improved expected sample complexity. Interestingly LUCB bears a close resemblance to the well-known UCB algorithm for regret minimization. We obtain a sample complexity bound for LUCB that matches the best existing bound for single-arm selection (that is, when m = 1). We also provide a lower bound on the worst case sample complexity of PAC algorithms for Explore-m.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit offers several choices, each producing uncertain rewards. This paper studies how to sample those choices efficiently to identify a subset of m high-reward arms from n possibilities. The problem uses a probably approximately correct framework, so the goal is a selection that meets an accuracy requirement with sufficiently high confidence.

The authors introduce and analyze LUCB, an algorithm with improved expected sample complexity. This focuses on the number of samples needed on average, extending earlier analysis centered on worst-case sampling requirements. LUCB also closely resembles UCB, a familiar approach to regret minimization, although the problem here is identifying a good subset through exploration.

For selecting a single arm, the derived sample complexity bound matches the best existing bound. The paper additionally provides a lower bound on the worst-case sample complexity of PAC subset-selection algorithms. These two contributions address complementary questions: how efficiently a proposed method can operate, and what sampling burden the problem can impose on any qualifying algorithm in the worst case.
summary.tldr: LUCB improves expected sampling efficiency for PAC bandit subset selection, alongside a worst-case lower bound for the problem.

title: PAC Subset Selection in Stochastic Multi-armed Bandits

abstract: An efficient way to learn deep density models that have many layers of latent variables is to learn one layer at a time using a model that has only one layer of latent variables. After learning each layer, samples from the posterior distributions for that layer are used as training data for learning the next layer. This approach is commonly used with Restricted Boltzmann Machines, which are undirected graphical models with a single hidden layer, but it can also be used with Mixtures of Factor Analysers (MFAs) which are directed graphical models. In this paper, we present a greedy layer-wise learning algorithm for Deep Mixtures of Factor Analysers (DMFAs). Even though a DMFA can be converted to an equivalent shallow MFA by multiplying together the factor loading matrices at different levels, learning and inference are much more efficient in a DMFA and the sharing of each lower-level factor loading matrix by many different higher level MFAs prevents overfitting. We demonstrate empirically that DMFAs learn better density models than both MFAs and two types of Restricted Boltzmann Machines on a wide variety of datasets.

After learning each layer, samples from the posterior distributions for that layer are used as training data for learning the next layer. This approach is commonly used with Restricted Boltzmann Machines, which are undirected graphical models with a single hidden layer, but it can also be used with Mixtures of Factor Analysers (MFAs) which are directed graphical models. In this paper, we present a greedy layer-wise learning algorithm for Deep Mixtures of Factor Analysers (DMFAs). Even though a DMFA can be converted to an equivalent shallow MFA by multiplying together the factor loading matrices at different levels, learning and inference are much more efficient in a DMFA and the sharing of each lower-level factor loading matrix by many different higher level MFAs prevents overfitting. We demonstrate empirically that DMFAs learn better density models than both MFAs and two types of Restricted Boltzmann Machines on a wide variety of datasets.

paragraphs: A deep density model represents data through several layers of hidden variables. This paper develops a way to train such a model using mixtures of factor analysers, which are directed graphical models. Training proceeds greedily, learning one layer before moving to the next.

After each layer is learned, samples from its posterior distributions become training data for the following layer. This adapts a layer-wise strategy commonly used with Restricted Boltzmann Machines to a different model family. The resulting Deep Mixture of Factor Analysers can be converted into an equivalent shallow mixture by multiplying factor loading matrices across levels.

Despite that equivalence, the authors report that the deep representation makes learning and inference much more efficient. Sharing lower-level loading matrices among multiple higher-level mixtures also provides protection against overfitting. Across a wide variety of datasets, the deep models empirically learn better density models than shallow mixtures and two types of Restricted Boltzmann Machines. The findings emphasize the computational and learning benefits of the layered representation.
summary.tldr: Greedy layer-wise training produces deep mixtures of factor analysers with efficient computation and better empirical density modeling than the tested alternatives.

title: Deep Mixtures of Factor Analysers
